en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Purifier of Boundaries:
The Bestower of Boons, the most excellent Bestower of Boons, like the lotus born of the water, shining like the sun.
I bow to the Awakened One, the Awakener of beings, the God of gods.
I bow to the Peaceful One, the Bringer of peace, who has forever transcended the cycle of existence for his offspring.
I bow to the Extinguished One, the Savior from extinction, the Supreme Dharma.

Whatever has been heard repeatedly in existence, whatever is not worthy of being bowed to by those who bow—men and non-men have always performed these acts; yet I pay homage to the most excellent Saṅgha.
Thus, while bowing to that Triple Gem which is worthy of being praised by those who bow with absolute devotion;
I have obtained a vast increase of merit, and by its power my obstacles have been destroyed.
When the Vinaya exists and stands firm, the Teaching remains established;
when the Vinaya is lost, the Teaching will perish.
Therefore, having now illuminated my own vision within the Teaching and having shattered the discourse of doubt,
I shall bring about unity. [I shall abandon] the state of self-exaltation and the tendency to disparage others.
Without directing my mind toward those [worldly things], but rather for the great flourishing of the Teaching—
if such a mind as this were mine, yet evil intentions should arise,
I would experience the terror of hell on account of that base disposition.
Striving to make the Dispensation easily accessible, conducting myself with mindfulness,
may I now be united for a long time with the purity of the True Dhamma.
Having obtained the very rare going-forth in the Conqueror’s Dispensation, I shall strive.
Having resolved upon the excellent teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One to dispel my solitary doubt,
I shall compose this work titled *Sīmavisodhanī*, compiled from various texts;
may the virtuous, preeminent among poets, listen to it.
Having plunged into all of that— the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, the Mātikā, and the Padabhājaniya—
again and again without remainder, [he examined] his own works on the Abhidhamma,
as well as the various commentaries and word-explanations (*gaṇṭhipada*).
Having made everything complete and without exception, and having harmonized it all into one, this commentary has been set forth to delight those who possess discernment.
It covers the Vinicchaya, the Vimati, and the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathās.
For the arising of a Buddha is rare, as are the going forth and the full ordination. Indeed, it has been said:
"A Buddha is rare in the world, and the hearing of the True Dhamma is also rare;
the Saṅgha is rare in the world, and truly worthy persons are exceedingly rare."
“Human birth is difficult to obtain; the arising of a Buddha is difficult to encounter;
the perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to find; and the True Dhamma is supremely difficult to attain.
1. The Chapter on Ordination (Upasampadā-khaṇḍa)

For if this discourse connected with the qualities of the Buddha were spoken while standing in this place, it would both gladden the hearts of the virtuous and establish the fact that this treatise is the word of one who is not insane.
And once its status as the word of one who is not insane is established, people will consider it worthy of being heard;
therefore, we shall praise the qualities of the Buddha. It is said that for us, the Blessed One was preceded by the Buddhas such as Brahmādeva.
Having performed [these deeds] by way of mental aspiration from the time of the ancient Sakyagotamas down to the Kaṭṭhavāhana Jātaka,
and by way of vocal factors from the Majjhimadīpaṅkara Jātaka onwards, and starting from the feet of Majjhimadīpaṅkara,
having combined all [deeds] by way of both bodily and vocal factors until the Vessantara existence— thus fulfilling the perfections for twenty asaṅkhyeyyas.
For the sake of omniscient knowledge alone, the head of the Omniscient Bodhisattva—who gave away his head even after it was adorned—is greater than all the hearths of those dwelling in Jambudīpa;
the eye of him who gave away his eyes after plucking them out is greater than the multitude of stars in the cloudless sky, the expanse of the firmament;
and [the flesh of] his heart or his right arm, having been cut off...
The flesh given by one who gives it is greater than even Sineru, the king of mountains, which measures one hundred thousand eight hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas];
the blood drawn and given by one who gives it is greater than the water in the four great oceans;
and for one who gives away a wife like Maddī and sons like Jālī and Kaṇhājinā for the sake of others’ slavery, there is no way to calculate [the merit].

They have transcended [all defilements]. It was while fulfilling the perfections in this very way that he reached Buddhahood—having contemplated for seven *saṅkhyeyyas*, or nine according to other accounts;
and having purified body and speech through the fourfold practice.
For one who, while being neither a coward nor overly brave, thinks only of Buddhahood according to the method described, seven *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons pass by.
For one who is not overly brave but merely utters the words [of aspiration], nine *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons pass by.
For one who is overly brave and fulfills [the perfections] through both body and speech, four *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons pass by. These are the four.
These [perfections] are to be understood as having been fulfilled over incalculable eons, beginning from the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha’s feet.
However, it should be understood that the internal perfections were fulfilled at the end of one hundred thousand eons.

Furthermore, by means of the Vessantara existence, after giving the seven great gifts and causing the earth to quake seven times, he went to Vaṅka Mountain and [gave away] his two sons who resembled his own eyes.

Having given her away to serve as a slave to a brahmin, on the following day he gave his wife named Maddī— who was equal to himself— to Sakka, the king of the gods, who had arrived in the guise of a brahmin; having performed immeasurable meritorious deeds in that existence,
he then went to the Tusita heaven and remained there for the full span of his life, surrounded by distinguished deities who had come from ten thousand world-systems.
"O Lord, Great Hero, it is time for you to arise from the mother’s womb;
saving the world including the gods, awaken to the deathless state.
Thus was he entreated regarding these five great observations: the time, the continent, the region, the family, and the mother.
Having observed this, and having heard that the sons of King Okkāka— who was of the lineage of Mahāsammata— had been made to marry their own sisters out of fear of the destruction of their clan,
[the Bodhisatta] took as a sign of the circumstances the words spoken by the great king Okkāka, "These princes are indeed Sakyan," and thus became known by the name Sakyas among those kings.
Having been conceived in the womb of Sirimā Mahāmāyā, the chief queen of the great king Suddhodana,
and having emerged from his mother’s womb in the Lumbinī Grove midway between the cities of Devadaha and Kapilavatthu at the end of ten months,
he immediately upon birth took seven strides facing north and uttered a fearless proclamation.
Having caused his father to pay homage [to him], and having enjoyed the glory of sovereignty in due course when he reached the age of sixteen,
he went forth on the day Rāhulabhadda was born; after practicing the difficult ascetic life for six years,
he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment on the full-moon day of Vesākha, and for forty-five years served as a jeweled garland for gods and humans.

Having caused the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma to fall as if binding it together, and having thus fulfilled the Buddha’s work up until the conversion of the wanderer Subhadda, when the Blessed One, the Lord of the World,

had attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue at Upavaṭṭana near Kusinārā in the Sāla grove of the Mallas on the Vesākha full-moon day during the hour of dawn, the elder Subhadda who had gone forth late in life said: "Enough!..."
"Friends, do not grieve; do not lament! We are well freed from that Great Ascetic, who used to say, 'This is allowable for you;
this is not allowable for you. Now we shall do whatever we wish, and we shall not do what we do not wish.
Having observed these words spoken by the seven leaders of the groups, [he said:]...
After the Venerable Mahākassapa, the senior elder of the Saṅgha consisting of one hundred thousand bhikkhus,
had performed the rehearsal of the Dhamma, and while the Dhamma and Vinaya were thus purified, a hundred years later,
the Vajjiputtakas at Vesālī saw ten points being put forward and were causing the decline of the Dispensation; [the Elder Yasa] was then incited by the Venerable Elder Yasa, the son of Kākaṇḍaka.
After the Second Council had been held, later on— at the eighteenth year beyond two hundred years from the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata—
a king named Dhammāsoka attained the consecration of sole sovereignty over the entire surface of Jambudīpa.
Having established great material offerings and honor for the Buddha’s dispensation, the non-Buddhist sectarians (titthiyā), whose own offerings and honor had declined, [were affected].
Failing to receive even the mere necessities of food and clothing, yet longing for gain and honor, they went forth into the Dispensation and,
by propounding their respective speculative views, caused great corruption and defilement to arise within the Dispensation.
At that time, in the seventeenth year after King Dhammāsoka’s consecration, among six million monks...
Taking a thousand bhikkhus, the Elder of the Saṅgha named Moggaliputtatissa, having defeated the doctrines of others at the Great Pavāraṇā ceremony,
taught the *Kathāvatthu* treatise, and performed the Third Council; while the Word of the Buddha— including the commentaries— remained pure within the Dhamma and Vinaya, he,
grasping the shadow of the meaning from the texts and commentaries, [established] his own...
By the power of their own intellects, they compose various distinct treatises;
within these, relying on their own subjective interpretations of the meaning, they fabricate pseudo-reasoning and regard the words they have uttered as essential.

Consequently, disregarding the Suttas, the Suttas’ concordant teachings, and the traditional expositions of the masters, they reject the Pāḷi and its commentary, as well as the *Sāratthadīpanī*, which serves as an exposition thereof.

Furthermore, without reconciling other specific texts and without harmonizing the preceding and following passages even by means of their own judgment, some monks—setting aside the mere elucidation of the doctrine—do not abide by what is weighty among the weighty and light matters, even though they ought to abide by the weighty.
Thus they become split into two factions within the Teaching. And this schism [is described] in the Kosambaka Khandhaka.
Even more than this division, it is a hundredfold and a thousandfold stronger [cause] for the ruin of the Dispensation;
for this does not concern the monks alone in the human world, but also the lay followers, the protective deities,
their companions who dwell on the earth, and their companions who dwell in trees.
[The fame of those noble persons spreads] to their companions among the space-dwelling deities, to their companions among the deities of the Four Great Kings,
and to their companions among the deities of the Thirty-three; thus, by way of a succession of friends, it reaches even the deities of the six sense-sphere heavens,
and to the friends of those, the Brahma-parisajja [Brahma’s Retinue]— and so on, up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world, excluding only the noble persons themselves.
All ordinary beings, both gods and humans, become divided; because of that division, they produce much evil.

Therefore, having compared the commentary with the canonical text and having unified those various specific works by blending them together—like the waters of the Yamunā merging with the waters of the Gaṅgā to become one—[I have composed] this *Sīmavisodhanī*.
"I shall give him a name; listen to it well and attend to it thoroughly: 'Disciples of the Dharma King.
In this context, "the arising of a Buddha is rare" means that the time of a Buddha's appearance is difficult to encounter;
for during the periods when one has not arisen, an incalculable number of eons passes by without even the sound of the word "Buddha" being heard. Regarding the cause of becoming a Buddha...
The difficulty [of this] has already been stated above.
Here, in the phrase "pabbajā ca upasampadā ca," the suffix *-to* is used in the sense of inferiority (*lāmakatthe*) or in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyatthe*).
The intended meaning is that the appearance of a Buddha is rare, and following him and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) are likewise exceedingly rare. And as in the world...

Just as when one obtains something of great value that was otherwise unobtainable, or even something of little value that serves as an accessory to it, that [accessory] is called "of great value" and "rare";

even so, having come upon the arising of a Buddha, which is exceedingly rare, even following him into homelessness is called "rare. And just as on the upper part of a *nidiya* tree, by way of being a seven-day-old sprout and so forth...

Just as, when filling with water, a certain lower place where one is unable to cross is called "difficult to traverse," even so, regarding the difficulty of the task for the sake of Buddhahood, neither the going-forth nor the full ordination is said to be difficult or hard to obtain.
Otherwise, even for the Blessed Buddha, the state of having gone forth and received full ordination alone would be considered superior. Or alternatively:
It should be understood that this is also stated by way of metaphorical designation based on the cause (*kāraṇūpacāra*).

Just as in the case of "mucus-sugar," for instance, because of the condition of sugar, mucus increases; although people should say "mucus from sugar," they apply the name of the result, the mucus, to the cause, the sugar, and thus it is called "mucus-sugar.
Likewise, because the cause is difficult to accomplish, when the arising of a Buddha is rare...
Even the going forth (pabbajjā), which is an imitation of that [practice], is said to be "difficult to obtain" because it is rooted in the arising of a Buddha, which is its primary cause.
Even at the time when a Buddha has appeared, seeing a Buddha is difficult to obtain; how much more so when he has not yet appeared?

Furthermore, because all moments are like the ninth moment [of non-perception], for instance, in the lands of the mlecchas, the formless realms, the plane of non-percipient beings, the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm.
Or, among those being born in the Middle Country, even if they are born there, those who have fallen into wrong view;

or, even if born into a family of right view, those with deficient limbs due to the impairment of sight or hearing—such persons do not deserve to see the Buddha. Even if they do see him, it is merely a visual encounter.
Supaṇṇas, nāga kings, and others are not partakers of the path and its fruit in that existence, though some among them may be so.
“Born in a border region, without the higher faculties, physically impaired, born among the non-percipient beings;
holding wrong view, among the animals, as a hungry ghost, or even in hell—
these eight inopportune moments were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.”
"The arising of a Buddha is a unique moment; it is called 'the new'.
Here, although "going forth" (*pabbajjā*) is mentioned in general terms, it specifically refers to the novices (*sāmaṇera*), because "full ordination" (*upasampadā*) is mentioned separately.
And as for the novices, they are so called after having recited three times, "We go for refuge to the Buddha," and so forth, by way of the purification on both sides.
They remain on the level of a novice (sāmaṇera). However, for them, the ten precepts are merely a matter of training rules (sikkhāpada).
If one is unable [to explain] them according to the text (pāḷi), it is indeed permissible to point them out by way of their meaning (attha) as:

"Having undertaken this, you should practice it. There is nothing further to be said here. But full ordination (upasampadā) is of eight kinds: full ordination by the "Come, monk" formula (ehibhikkhu-upasampadā), full ordination by going for refuge (saraṇagamana-upasampadā), and so forth.

There are these types of ordination: ordination by receiving exhortation (*ovāda*), ordination by answering questions (*pañhābyākaraṇa*), ordination by accepting the eight weighty rules (*aṭṭhagarudhamma*), ordination by messenger (*dūta*), ordination by the eight proclamations (*aṭṭhavācika*), and ordination by the motion followed by three announcements (*ñatticatuttha*).
In this regard, the Blessed One, seeing a person endowed with the necessary support for the state of "Come, monk" (*ehi bhikkhu*), [took him] from within his red rag-robe... golden-colored.
Extending his right hand and uttering a Brahma-voice, he says: "Come, bhikkhu, lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
Immediately thereafter, the marks of a householder disappear, and there appear a set of three robes, an alms bowl, a razor, a needle, and a waistband.
"A bhikkhu who is devoted to yoga possesses these eight requisites, including the water-strainer.

When these eight requisites have been mentioned, he stands endowed with the four modes of deportment, like an elder of a hundred years, perfected in conduct, having the Buddha as his teacher and the Buddha as his preceptor, while paying homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One. This is the ordination by "Come, Bhikkhu" (ehi-bhikkhu-upasampadā).
[This is] the name. For at this time during his first awakening, the Blessed One conferred full ordination by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehi-bhikkhu-upasampadā*) alone.
These [disciples] ranged from the group of five to the end with the Elder Aṅgulimāla.
There were three hundred thousand, and another forty thousand;
And one elder who was wise; all of them were addressed as "Come, monk.

These are the ones designated as *ehibhikkhus* in the Vinaya Piṭaka. However, those not designated in the Vinaya Piṭaka include the Brahmin of the Three Hundred Retinue, Seḷa, and others—twenty-seven thousand and three hundred in total.
For all these are reckoned as "Come, O Bhikkhu" (ehibhikkhu) ordinations.
Summing up all of them, they total twenty-eight thousand six hundred and forty-one. This first Enlightenment lasted for twenty years.
For the Blessed One, having set in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma and having caused eighteen koṭis of brahmins to drink the Deathless (amata), [ordained them].
He spent the first rains retreat there. During the second, third, and fourth rains retreats, he spent the rains at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha;

for after spending his first rains retreat at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī on the full moon of the Āsāḷha constellation, the Blessed One arrived at Rājagaha on the full moon of the Phagguṇa month in the month of Phagguṇa, and stayed at the Veḷuvana built by King Bimbisāra.
Having stayed in the monastery for only one month, he went to Kapilavatthu in the month of Citta, surrounded by twenty thousand arahants.

In the midst of eighty thousand kinsmen who had fallen into wrong views, he cast the dust of his feet upon their heads, made them pay homage to him, and caused the rain of lotuses to fall; and having come there, [he established] those eighty thousand kinsmen.

Having related the Vessantara Jātaka and, having approached the mother of Rāhula, having related the Candakinnarī Jātaka, he established his father in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and returned to Rājagaha itself to take up residence there;
thus it is said that during the second, third, and fourth rains-retreats, he spent the vassa at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha. But in the fifth [year], in Vesālī...
He dwelt for one night. On the sixth [night], he dwelt for one night on Mount Makuḷa—or perhaps it was Puṇṇa who did so. Herein is the sequential account:
it is said that in a certain merchant village in the kingdom of Sunāparanta there were two brothers.
Sometimes the elder would take five hundred carts, go to the countryside, and bring back goods; sometimes it was the younger. Now at this time, it was the younger brother...
Having left [the goods] at home, his elder brother took five hundred carts and, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, eventually reached Sāvatthī.
Having parked the five hundred carts not far from the Jeta Grove, he ate his morning meal and, surrounded by his retinue, sat down in a comfortable spot.
At that time, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī, having eaten their morning meals, were observing the precepts of the Uposatha.

Having properly adjusted their upper robes and holding perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in their hands, they proceeded toward where the Buddha was, toward where the Dhamma was, and toward where the Saṅgha was;
leaning, inclining, and tending in that direction, they departed through the southern gate and went to Jetavana.
Seeing them, he asked a man, "Where are these people going? "What do you not know, noble sir? he replied.
"In this world, the Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—have arisen"; thinking thus, the great multitude went into the presence of the Teacher to hear a discourse on the Dhamma.
To him, the word "Buddha" pierced through his skin and hide, and having struck right down to the marrow of his bones, remained there.
Then, surrounded by his own retinue, he went to the monastery together with that assembly, and the Teacher, with a sweet voice—
Standing at the edge of the assembly while the Dhamma was being taught, he heard the Dhamma and conceived the desire for the going-forth.
Then, when the Tathāgata perceived the time had come and the assembly had been dismissed, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and invited him for the following day.
On the second day, having prepared a pavilion and arranged seats, [he offered hospitality] to the community headed by the Buddha.
After giving a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha, the Blessed One departed after delivering a discourse of thanksgiving at the conclusion of the meal.
Having eaten his morning meal and undertaken the observance factors of the Uposatha, he summoned the treasurer and, having explained everything—
stating how much of the goods had been distributed and how much remained— he said, "This property belongs to my younger brother."
Having offered everything with the words, "Please accept it," he went forth in the presence of the Teacher and became devoted to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
However, as he was attending to the meditation subject, it did not become manifest to him. Thereupon, he thought:
"This country is unsuitable for me; what if I were to take my meditation subject from the Teacher and go back to my own place?"
Then, having wandered for alms in the morning and emerged from seclusion in the evening,
Venerable Puṇṇa approached the Blessed One, requested a meditation subject, and after the Teacher had let out a lion’s roar, he departed. Then Venerable Puṇṇa,
having reached the kingdom of Sūnāparanta and entered the mountain named Sammata, arrived at the village of the merchants.

He entered for alms. Then his younger brother led him to his own home, gave him alms, and having made him give his promise, saying, "Venerable sir, do not go elsewhere, but dwell right here," he had him stay.
From there, he went to the monastery called Samuddagiri-vihāra.
There, the waves of the ocean came and struck against iron thorns and rocks, making a great noise.
The Elder, finding that his dwelling was not comfortable while he was attending to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), resolved to make the ocean silent.
From there, he went to the place called Mātulagiri. There, a great multitude of birds gathered, and their constant clamor day and night made it a single, unceasing noise.
The Elder, thinking, "This place is not comfortable," went from there to the monastery called Makuḷakārāmavihāra.

Thus, not too far from and not too near the village of Vāṇija, a place well-suited for coming and going, secluded, and quiet, the Elder—thinking, "This spot is comfortable"—had night-quarters, day-quarters, walking-paths, and so forth constructed there, and entered upon the rains retreat.
In this manner, he dwelt in four locations. Then, one day during that very same rains retreat, five...
Hundreds of merchants, saying, "Let us go to the other sea," loaded their goods onto a ship.

On the day they were boarding the ship, the Elder’s younger brother fed the Elder, received the precepts from him, and as he was departing, said, "Venerable sir, the great ocean is indeed unreliable and full of many obstacles; please keep us in mind."
He boarded a boat. As the boat was traveling with the speed of the waves, it reached a certain island.
Thinking, "We shall eat breakfast," the men disembarked on the island. There was nothing else on that island; it was solely a sandalwood forest.
Then, one man—or perhaps another—having struck a tree and recognized it as red sandalwood, said, "Sirs, for the sake of gain..."
“Let us go to the other sea; there is no gain greater than this from here. A single water-jar measuring only four finger-breadths is worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Let us take away whatever merchandise is suitable to be carried off and depart. They did so.
The non-human beings dwelling in the sandalwood grove became angry and thought, “This [grove] of ours has been destroyed by these men!”
Thinking, “We shall have them executed,” they said, “If these are executed, it will not become a single heap of corpses; therefore, we shall sink their ship in the middle of the ocean.

Then, as soon as they had boarded the ship and traveled for a short while, those non-human beings caused a storm to arise and themselves manifested terrifying forms. The terrified people [sought refuge] with themselves...
The deities paid homage to him. The householder Cūḷapuṇṇaka, the younger brother of the Elder, stood there paying homage to the Elder, thinking, "May my brother be my refuge.

It is said that at that very moment, the Elder, having reflected and perceived their impending misfortune, rose into the air and stood facing them. As soon as the non-human beings saw the Elder, they cried out, "The Noble Elder Puṇṇa!"
Saying, “Come! they departed. The storm subsided. The Elder, having comforted them by saying, “Do not be afraid,” asked, “Where do you wish to go?
They replied, “Venerable sir, let us go to our own place. The Elder stepped onto the ship’s deck and resolved:
“Let it go to the place desired by these men. The merchants [arrived at] their own place.
Having gone and reported the matter to their wives and children, they said, "Come, let us go for refuge to the Elder.
Thus, five hundred people, together with their own five hundred female relatives each, established themselves in the Three Refuges and declared themselves lay followers (*upāsaka*).
Then, having unloaded the goods from the ship and set aside one portion for the Elder, they said, "Venerable sir, this is for you..."
“[We have] a share,” they said. The Elder replied, “I have no need for a separate share.
But has the Teacher been seen by you before? “He has not been seen before, Bhante. “In that case, build a pavilion for the Teacher with this share and your own share.
In this way, you will see the Teacher. “Very well, Bhante,” they said, and with that share and their own share...
They began to construct the maṇḍalamāḷa. It is said that from the very moment its construction began, the Teacher made use of it.
Thus, when people saw a radiance there at night, they perceived that "there is a deity of great power.
Having completed both the maṇḍalamāḷa and the lodgings for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the lay disciples prepared the requisites for the gift.
“Venerable sir, we have performed our own duty; please summon the Teacher,” they reported to the Elder.
In the evening, the Elder arrived at Sāvatthī by means of his supernormal power and said, “Venerable sir, the inhabitants of the merchant village wish to see you;
please show compassion toward them. The Blessed One consented. Having understood the Blessed One’s consent, the Elder returned to his own place.
Having returned, the Blessed One addressed the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, tomorrow we shall go for alms in the merchant village of Sūnāparanta;

give voting tickets to the four hundred and ninety-nine monks. The Elder, saying “Very well, venerable sir,” announced this matter to the Saṅgha of monks and said, “Those who wish to go on the journey, take a ticket. On that day...

The Elder Kuṇḍadhāna took the first voting ticket. The inhabitants of Vāṇijagāma, thinking, "It is said the Teacher will arrive tomorrow," constructed a pavilion in the center of the village and prepared an array of offerings.

Early in the morning, the Blessed One, having attended to his bodily needs, entered the Fragrant Chamber and sat down, having attained the meditative absorption of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Sakka’s stone seat of the yellow blanket—
It became hot. Reflecting on what this might mean, he saw that the Teacher was going to Sūnāparanta, and he addressed Visukamma:
"Dear one, today the Blessed One will go for alms over a distance of three hundred yojanas;
construct five hundred gabled houses and place them ready for his journey at the gateway of the Jetavana. He did accordingly.
The Blessed One’s gabled chamber had four doors; those of the two chief disciples had two doors each; and the rest had one door each.
The Teacher, having emerged from the Perfumed Chamber, entered the foremost gabled chamber among those set out in succession.
Beginning with the two chief disciples, the four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus also went to the gabled chamber and sat down.
There was one empty gabled chamber. Five hundred gabled chambers also rose up into the air.
When the Teacher reached the mountain named Saccabandha, he set the gabled chamber in the sky;

on that mountain lived a man of wrong view named Saccabandha, who, having attained the pinnacle of gain and the height of fame, dwelt there while causing the great multitude to adopt wrong views. Within [the chamber]...
Within him, the proximate cause for Arahantship blazed like a lamp in the interior of a house;
seeing this, [the Blessed One] went, thinking, "I shall preach the Dhamma to him," and taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the ascetic attained Arahantship.

Higher knowledge came to him by way of the Path itself, and having become a *ehi-bhikkhu*, he entered the gabled hall with his supernaturally produced bowl and robes. The Blessed One [addressed] those who had entered the gabled hall...
Accompanied by five hundred bhikkhus, he went to the village of Vaṇijagāma; having made his peaked-roofed dwellings invisible, he entered the village.
After the merchants had given a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, they led the Teacher and his company to Makuḷakārāma.
The Teacher entered the circular pavilion. The great multitude waited until the Teacher’s fatigue from the meal was allayed.
Having taken his morning meal and undertaken the precepts of the Uposatha, he took perfumes and flowers and returned to the monastery to hear the Dhamma.
The Teacher taught the Dhamma. The great multitude was released from their bonds, and a great clamor arose concerning the Buddha.
For the sake of gathering the great multitude, the Teacher remained right there for several days until dawn.

However, he established it right there in the Mahāgandhakuṭī. Having stayed there for a few days and walked for alms in the village of Vaṇijagāma, he sent Puṇṇa Thera back, saying, "You stay right here.
Then, proceeding along the way, he reached the bank of the river named Nammadā.
The Nāga King of the Nammadā came out to meet the Teacher, led him into his nāga-abode, and [offered] the three...
He paid homage to the Jewels. After the Teacher had preached the Dhamma to him, he departed from the Nāga abode.
The Nāga requested, "Venerable Sir, please grant me a place where I may serve you. The Blessed One showed him the Footprint Shrine (*padacetiya*) on the bank of the Nammadā River.
When the waves approached it, it was covered; when the waves receded, it was revealed. It received great honor.
So it was. The Teacher then departed from there, went to Mount Saccabandha, and said to Saccabandha: “You have led the great multitude onto the path to the states of misery.
You must remain right here, cause them to abandon their false views, and establish them on the path to Nibbāna.
He, too, requested that he be allowed to attend upon him. The Teacher [placed] a lump of fresh clay upon a solid rock slab...

He showed the footprint shrine (*padacetiya*) like a seal-mark. Thus, within the kingdom of Sūnāparanta alone, he established two Wheel-Treasure shrines (*cakkaratana-cetiya*) until the disappearance of the Dispensation.

In the seventh year, however, at Sāvatthī, at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, while crushing the heretics, he performed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), for those who had come from ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

Having made the mother of the deities his personal witness, he spent the rains retreat at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the Paṇḍukambala stone in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven while teaching the Abhidhamma.
In the eighth year, he stayed for one year in the city of Saṃsumāra. In the ninth year, he stayed for one year in Kosambī.
At that time, Bhaddiya, Kimila, Bhagu, Ānanda, Anuruddha, and Devadatta—these seven—[were with him].
Six kṣatriyas went forth into homelessness; their detailed account is found in the *Dhammapada*.

In the tenth year, however, he spent a comfortable rainy-season retreat being attended upon by the elephant Pālileyyaka at the foot of a Bhaddasāla tree in the southern forest grove near the village of Pālileyya.
In the eleventh year, he stayed for one season in the brahmin village of Nālandha. In the twelfth year, he stayed for one season in Verañjā.
While experiencing the ripening of his own misconduct, it is said that because an unwholesome kamma— accumulated during the time of the Blessed One Phussa through verbal misconduct by his disciples—
had found its opportunity and manifested at that time, [the Buddha], although invited by the Brahmin of Verañjā,
did not perceive it due to Māra’s interference and instead went with the horse-dealers.
He ate for three months only barley and rice, as prescribed by the summary of the fixed practice (nibaddhavatta) starting from the *pattha* and *patthamūlaka* measures;
for this is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the dispensation of Phussa, I would revile the disciples;”
"Eat and consume barley, and do not eat fine rice.
By the ripening of that karma, I ate barley for three months;
invited by a brahmin, I dwelt there in Verañjā."
Therefore it was said: “In the twelfth year, he dwelt for one year at Verañjā, experiencing the ripening of his misconduct.

In the thirteenth year, he dwelt for one year at Jāliya-pabbata. In the fourteenth year, having spent the first year’s residence at the Jetavana monastery in the park of Anāthapiṇḍika at Sāvatthī, in the fifteenth year he went to Kapilavatthu for the purpose of gathering his kinsmen.
Having gone there, he made his dwelling in that very place alone. In the sixteenth year, for the purpose of subduing the yakkha Āḷavaka, he stayed for one residence in the city of Aggāḷava.
In the seventeenth year, he returned to Rājagaha and made his dwelling there.
In the eighteenth year, he returned to Jāliya-pabbata and stayed there. In the nineteenth year as well, he remained in that same Jāliya-pabbata.
"Vasi. For twenty years, he dwelt in the terrifying Bhesakaḷa Grove forest not far from Rājagaha;
these twenty years should be understood as the period of the First Enlightenment.

During this time, he ordained [people] primarily through the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) ordination alone, having made the Blessed One himself the preceptor and teacher (*ācariyupajjhāya*), thus [ordaining them as] "come, monk" [monks].
This was said with reference specifically to persons who have attained the state of being meritorious;

it does not apply to others who have not yet attained the state of noble ones, such as Sudinna and others, or the five hundred monks who previously lived as bats during the time of Kassapa Buddha and later went forth in the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera after gaining faith at the Twin Miracle. It refers to those very same monks.
Because his state of having gone forth was seen in the presence [of the Buddha], it was said by him:
"For at this time, during the first enlightenment, the Blessed One ordained him precisely through the *ehi bhikkhu* (come, monk) ordination.

However, in the twenty-five years following this, he resided for nineteen years in the Great Monastery of Jetavana, which had been built by Anāthapiṇḍika; [the remaining six years] were spent with Visākhā.
Having caused the Pubbārāma to be built at a cost of twenty-seven crores of wealth, he lived there for six years.
Relying on Sāvatthī, he lived there for twenty-five years out of consideration for the great virtue of two families.
However, in his final year, having stayed in the Beḷuva village, death-bed pains arose, and there he relinquished the life-faculty.
[He] did so. These [cases] are not intended here; they were spoken merely for the purpose of knowing the Blessed One’s sequence of years.

Ordination by going for refuge (*saraṇagamana-upasampadā*) means one who is ordained by the three goings for refuge, having uttered the words three times, beginning with “I go for refuge to the Buddha.
Ordination by receiving instruction (*ovādapaṭiggahaṇa-upasampadā*) means: “Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘Intense indeed... [and so forth].
"Shame and fear of wrongdoing shall be established toward the elders, the juniors, and those of middle standing"—thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself.

Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: "Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will attend to it thoroughly, mindfully, and with my whole heart; with ears pricked, I will listen to the Dhamma."
"I shall listen," thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself; therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:

"I will not abandon mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by pleasure"—it is by this acceptance of the exhortation that the Elder Mahākassapa’s admission to full ordination (*upasampadā*) is said to have been granted.

The "ordination through answering questions" refers to the ordination permitted for Sopāka. It is said that while walking about in the Eastern Monastery, the Blessed One asked the novice Sopāka ten questions based on the ten kinds of foulness:

"Sopāka, regarding these phenomena known as the 'perception of the bloated' or the 'perception of forms'—are they different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they the same in meaning and only different in phrasing?"
He asked. He answered him. The Blessed One, having given him his approval, asked, "How many years old are you, Sopāka? "I am seven years old, Blessed One.

"Sopāka, you have answered the questions in accordance with my omniscient knowledge," he said, and being pleased in heart, he granted him full ordination; this is ordination through the answering of questions.

The ordination by means of eight proclamations (*aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā*) refers to the ordination of a nun through these two formal acts (*kamma*): one from the community of nuns consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), and one from the community of monks consisting of a motion and three proclamations.

Ordination by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā*) is the ordination of monks nowadays; this alone is intended here, as it occurs both in cases of success and failure.

Why is he called "one who is fully ordained" (*upasampanna*)? Because he has reached, attained, or arrived at a superior state by means of a formal act (*kamma*) consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), performed by a harmonious Saṅgha that is irreversible and fit for the occasion; thus, "fully ordained" means he has attained the state of excellence.
For indeed, compared to the state of a householder, the state of a novice (*sāmaṇera*) is called excellent, and even more excellent than that is the state of one who is fully ordained.

In this context, "by a united Saṅgha" means: in the case of a formal act (*kamma*) to be performed by a quorum of five at the very least, it is one that has attained unity because all the monks who are entitled to participate have arrived, because the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forward, and because there is no objection from those present.
"By a motion and three proclamations" means by means of three formal announcements (*anusāvana*).

"And by what is to be done with a motion" (ekāya ca ñattiyā kattabbena). Here, although the motion (*ñatti*) is stated first, because there is no difference in meaning or phrasing among the three proclamations (*anusāvana*), the motion—which differs in both meaning and phrasing—is considered the fourth of them; thus it is called "the fourth [item] consisting of a motion" (*ñatticatuttha*).
"By a legal act" (*kammena*) means by a legitimate legal act (*dhammika-kamma*); the meaning is "by a Vinaya legal act."

"By one who has reached the unshakeable" means by one who has attained a state that is not to be disturbed and not to be rejected, because of the perfection of the site, the motion (*ñatti*), the proclamation (*anusāvana*), the boundary (*sīma*), and the assembly (*parisa*).
"By one worthy of the position" means by one worthy of the cause; the meaning is: by one worthy of the Teacher’s instruction.
The meaning is that he has attained the state of excellence through these causes. In this regard, [the distinction] arises by way of success (*sampatti*) and failure (*vipatti*).

The meaning is that the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) is accomplished by way of five accomplishments: accomplishment of the subject matter (*vatthusampatti*), accomplishment of the motion (*ñattisampatti*), accomplishment of the proclamation (*anusāvanasampatti*), accomplishment of the boundary (*sīmasampatti*), and accomplishment of the assembly (*parisasampatti*).
Therein, "accomplishment of the subject matter" means being twenty years of age and currently possessing a male body.
One who is less than twenty years of age, or one who has previously committed a terminal offense (*antimavatthu*), [is not qualified].
A paṇḍaka, one living in communion by theft, one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide,
a murderer of an arahant, a defiler of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic of the Saṅgha, one who sheds the blood [of a Buddha], and one possessing both sexual organs—
these thirteen persons are ineligible for full ordination (*upasampadā*). In this regard, although it is stated generally as "less than twenty years,"...

A person who has completed nineteen years from the time of emerging from the mother’s womb is a fit subject for full ordination (*upasampadā*); less than that is not a fit subject for full ordination. From the full moon of Kattika until the full moon of Phagguṇa is the winter season;
from the full moon of Maggasira until the full moon of Āsāḷha is the summer season;
the remainder is the rainy season, consisting of twenty-four Uposatha days.
"The fourteenth day occurs on the third and seventh fortnights of these [months];
the remaining days should be known as the fifteenth; thus there are eighteen Uposatha days.
And here, from the first day of the dark fortnight of Kattika until the full moon of Phagguṇa, there are four months.

The winter season (*hemantū*) is so called. From the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phagguṇa until the full moon of Āsāḷhī, these four months are known as the summer season (*gimhū*).

From the first day of the dark fortnight of Āsāḷha until the full moon of the latter Kattika, these four months are known as the rainy season (*vassū*). Thus, there are three seasons in one year. Among them, in one...
In each season, by taking two days from the third and seventh fortnights, there are six fourteenth-day observances (*cātuddasika*);

and by taking six days from the first, second, fourth, fifth, sixth, and eighth fortnights, there are eighteen fifteenth-day observances (*pannarasika*). Thus, in one year, there are twenty-four observance days (*uposatha*).
Since among these twenty-four observance days, twenty-nine days fall on the fourteenth day, in one year—
Six days are still lacking. By this method, in the nineteenth year, there are eighteen years plus six months.
Including the ten months spent in the mother’s womb, nineteen years plus four months are completed.
However, kings add one month at the end of every three years.
Together with the day, it is also a month; therefore, in the eighteenth year itself, there are six months and more.
By adding that to the nineteen years already including four months less, twenty years plus one month become completely fulfilled.
Thus, it should be understood that from the nineteenth year onwards, the twentieth year of conception is the basis for full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Now, regarding the phrase "the male state of existence" (*purisattabhāvo*): since there is no such thing as a female bhikkhunī [in this context], it is intended that only a male person (*purisapuggalo*) is suitable here.
For indeed, if women had been allowed to go forth, the True Dharma (*saddhamma*) would have remained for five hundred years;

however, because [the rule] was established [prohibiting it], it will remain for another five hundred years—thus, the True Dharma that has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) will last for exactly one thousand years.
The state of being established [in the Dispensation] has been stated. Furthermore, women are indeed characterized by weak wisdom, intense defilements, and inferiority.

Even though the Blessed One, from the very beginning of his first enlightenment, permitted the full ordination for Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī through her acceptance of the eight weighty rules (garudhamma), it was stated that the Dispensation would not endure for long. This is because women possess weak wisdom.
They do not remain long in the Dispensation because, due to their intense defilements, they are unable to maintain even the restraint corresponding to the training rules as they have been laid down.
Furthermore, because of their inferiority, even those who attain the eight meditative absorptions (aṭṭhasamāpatti) do not transcend the rank of a member of Brahmā’s assembly (brāhmapārisajja).
Thus, due to the absence of bhikkhunīs, it is now said, "a person who is male. In this context...
Having established [the duration], the four fields should be understood as follows: for it is said that because women have gone forth, the Dispensation will endure for exactly one thousand years;

this is stated with reference to those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and are free from taints (*khīṇāsava*). Beyond that, another thousand years will pass through those who are dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*) and free from taints;
another thousand years through non-returners (*anāgāmin*); another thousand years through once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*); and through stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*)...

"A thousand years" means that the True Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-saddhamma) remains for five thousand years. The True Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-saddhamma) also remains for exactly that long;
for there is no realization in the absence of the scriptures, nor does realization fail to exist when the scriptures are present.
However, the outward signs (liṅga) will continue to prevail for a long time even after the scriptures have disappeared; this is the view of the Khandhaka-reciters.

It should be understood that this was stated according to [a particular] opinion. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated thus: "The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) remained for a thousand years;
those possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*) for a thousand years; those possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*) for a thousand years;
dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*) for a thousand years; and the Pātimokkha remained for a thousand years. This too [is the view] of the Elders who were reciters of the *Dīgha*.

This was stated according to his opinion. In the *Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* as well, it is said that for a thousand years after the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas, people are able to develop the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*);
beyond that, they can develop the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*);

and when they are no longer able to develop even those, they develop the three true knowledges (*tisso vijjā*). As time passes further, being unable to develop even those, they become dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
By this same method, it is stated that there were non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers. This too is stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
However, in the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, it is said that at the time of the first enlightenment, the monks had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Then, as time passed, they were no longer able to attain the analytical knowledges, and became those possessed of the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā). Thereafter...
Even those unable to attain the higher knowledges (abhiññā) reached the three types of clear knowledge (tisso vijjā).

Now, as time passes, those unable to reach the three types of clear knowledge will reach the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya); those unable to do that will reach the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala);
those unable to do that will reach the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala); and those unable to do that will reach the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). As time goes on...
It is said: "They will not even be able to attain the fruit of stream-entry.
Since those teachers hold divergent views, it must be understood that the Master Buddhaghosa has recorded the opinions of those very teachers and reciters in various places;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of internal contradiction within the Master Buddhaghosa’s own work.
Indeed, having set aside the Sinhalese language, the word of the Buddha together with its commentary was written in the Māgadha language by no other teacher;
therefore, one must accept that only the words spoken in the commentary are authoritative. [Objection: But surely all four Nikāyas were included in the Council of the Commentaries;
then why are they thus divided? [Response: True, nevertheless, for some...
This was stated for the purpose of clarifying the argument of the elders, not that of the Saṅgāhaka elders; therefore, it is said that the word of the Aṭṭhakathā alone is the authority.

"One who has previously committed an ultimate offense" refers to a bhikkhu who has committed a pārājika; such a person is incapable of receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the Dispensation.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of paṇḍakas: the *āsittapaṇḍaka*, the *ussūyapaṇḍaka*, the *opakkamikapaṇḍaka*, the *napuṃsaka*, and...

"Half-month eunuch" (*pakkhapaṇḍaka*): therein, one for whom the feverish distress (*pariḷāha*) is pacified by receiving another's genitals into the mouth and being sprinkled with impurity is called an "eunuch by sprinkling" (*āsittapaṇḍaka*).
One for whom the feverish distress is pacified when envy arises upon seeing another’s sexual misconduct is called an "eunuch by envy" (*ussūyapaṇḍaka*).
One from whose seeds [the reproductive organs] have been removed by means of an instrument...

This is what is called an *opakkamika-paṇḍaka* (one who becomes so through external means). However, one who is born without virility even at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is called a *napuṃsaka* (neuter).

Furthermore, a certain person, by the power of unwholesome karmic fruition (*akusala-vipāka*), becomes a *paṇḍaka* during the dark fortnight, whereas his feverish distress subsides during the bright fortnight; this is called a *pakkha-paṇḍaka* (fortnightly *paṇḍaka*). Some, however, [define it as] one who, during the dark fortnight...
They say that one who is a woman during the dark fortnight and a man during the bright fortnight is a "fortnight-eunuch" (*pakkhapaṇḍaka*);
this is merely their opinion. Among these types, the admission into the order (*pabbajjā*) is not prohibited for the "eunuch by infusion" (*āsittapaṇḍaka*) and the "jealous eunuch" (*ussūyapaṇḍaka*).

However, it is prohibited for the "self-inflicted neuter" (*opakkamikanapuṃsaka*) and the "fortnight-eunuch. Even among those, in the case of the fortnight-eunuch, admission is permitted only during whichever fortnight he is a eunuch.

She was forbidden. And here, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that "having gone forth on the side of those who are not *paṇḍakas*, one who belongs to the class of *paṇḍakas* must be expelled.
However, some say, "One who has gone forth on the side of those who are not *paṇḍakas*, being such, attains the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*) and should not be expelled";
this is merely their own opinion, because the destruction of defilements is possible for a *paṇḍaka*, as in the case of one whose defilements are exhausted (*khīṇakilesa*).

And because the state of being a *paṇḍaka* cannot arise [subsequently], in the discussion on rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), it is stated without distinction that a *paṇḍaka* has rootless rebirth-linking;

furthermore, they say that for those who are "sprinkled" (*āsitta*) or *paṇḍakas* belonging to the side of envy (*ussūya*), the state of being a *paṇḍaka* exists from the very moment of rebirth-linking, and not only during the course of existence (*pavatti*).
For this very reason, in the description of rootless rebirth-linking, those such as the congenitally blind and the congenitally deaf [are mentioned].
The *paṇḍaka* is indicated as being distinguished by the word "birth" (*jāti*).

However, in the commentary on the fourth *pārājika*, while showing the persons who are incapable [of attaining the path], it is stated without distinction that the three types of those deficient in the basis—namely, the *paṇḍaka*, the animal, and the hermaphrodite—who possess rebirth-linking without roots (*ahetuka-paṭisandhika*), have heaven unbarred; thus, there are five kinds of *paṇḍakas*.
It should be understood that this was stated—“a paṇḍaka, monks, is not to be ordained”—by using the term “paṇḍaka” without making any distinction based on the commonality of being a paṇḍaka.
As for the "one who dwells in communion through theft": this refers to one who, having himself taken the outward signs of going forth and having counted his years as a monk, [claims], "I am a monk."

He accepts the formal acknowledgment, consents to salutation according to seniority, and because he is a thief regarding both his appearance and his communal life, he is called a "thief in both respects" (*ubhayatthenaka*).
However, he who does not consent to salutation according to seniority, being a thief regarding his appearance due to an impure state of mind, is called a "thief in appearance" (*liṅgatthenaka*).
Or again, he who, while remaining on the level of a novice (*sāmaṇera*), [acts] through false speech...

If one, having given his consent to be called a "bhikkhu," accepts such acts as salutation according to seniority by way of the bhikkhu’s formal year-count, he is not a "liṅgatthenaka" (one who deceives by outward signs) because he possesses the outward signs granted by the bhikkhus;
however, because he deceives regarding communal residence, he is called a "saṃvāsatthenaka" (one who deceives regarding communal residence).

Furthermore, in this context, even one who deceives both [regarding signs and residence] should be understood as included within the category of the "liṅgatthenaka" alone, due to his impure intention. Also, [the case of] a novice monk [deceiving] elder novice monks...

If one accepts a salutation, or if even a junior bhikkhu accepts a salutation from senior bhikkhus, he is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who dwells in communion through theft), because he is not dishonest.
Or again, as long as one who has actually committed a *pārājika* offense remains in the outward marks of a bhikkhu until he confesses it, his status as a bhikkhu still exists;
he does not fall into the category of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
For even though he consents to living together [with the Sangha], he is not one who lives in communion by theft;
he does not incur an offense such as sleeping in the same bed, nor does he incur a *pācittiya* for abusive speech. Therefore, it is said:

"An individual is impure, having committed one or another offense involving defeat (*pārājika*); if, while maintaining a view that he is pure, he requests permission [to speak] with the intention of reviling..."
"He speaks [of] an offense of abusive speech"—thus, for abusive speech, a *pācittiya* is prescribed.

For if he were not a monk, he would incur a *dukkaṭa*. However, a novice who, by means of his very status as a novice, commits the fivefold failure in virtue such as the taking of life—he too, having been brought before [the Sangha], must have his status revoked;
then, after the revocation, the refuge and the precepts must be given, and subsequently, through the self, the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

It does not even reach the state of being a formal offense (*avatthu*). However, for one who commits such acts as eating at improper times (*vikālabhojana*), the precepts must indeed be restored after having confessed the transgression in the midst of the Saṅgha by saying, "Venerable Sir, a transgression has overcome me," and so forth, or after performing a penance (*daṇḍakamma*).
One who has gone over to the faction of the heretics (*titthiyapakkantaka*) is clearly excluded.
"An animal" (tiracchānagata) refers to anyone who has become a non-human being, including those in the four states of misery (apāya); they are indeed ineligible for full ordination (upasampadā).
Because their rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is inferior, they are incapable of going forth in the Dispensation (sāsana).
If those in the four states of misery were ineligible for full ordination, then why was it stated that only "an animal" is ineligible, without specifying the others?

Because the remaining cases are not well-known, for instance, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One, a certain dragon king who had been reborn in the animal realm was distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by his birth in the dragon womb. Then it occurred to that dragon:
"By what means might I be released from this dragon womb and quickly regain human status? And so...

It occurred to that nāga: “These ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, are practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of righteousness, practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, virtuous, and of noble character.
If I were to go forth among these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, then I would be released from this nāga-birth and would quickly regain human status. Then...
That nāga, having approached the bhikkhus in the form of a young brahmin, requested the going-forth. The bhikkhus granted him the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon him.
Now at that time, that nāga was living in a frontier monastery together with a certain bhikkhu.
Then, as the night was ending, that bhikkhu rose from his seat in the early morning and went out into the open air.
He walked back and forth. Then, when that bhikkhu had departed, the nāga relaxed and fell asleep.
The entire monastery was filled with snakes, and their coils protruded from the windows.
Then, as that bhikkhu thought, "I shall enter the monastery," and pushed open the door, he saw the entire monastery filled with snakes and their coils protruding from the windows.
When they had gone out, [the snake] saw them and, being terrified, let out a cry. The monks ran up and said this to that monk: "Friend, why did you let out a cry?
"Friends, this entire monastery is full of snakes; their coils have come out through the windows.
Then that nāga, having woken up at that sound, sat down upon his own seat. The monks...
They said, "Who are you, friend? "I am a nāga, venerable sirs. "But why, friend, did you do such a thing?
Then that nāga related this matter to the monks. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled.
He said this to that nāga: "You indeed, nāga, are incapable of growth in this Dhamma and Vinaya. Go, nāga;
right there observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight.
In this way, you will be released from the nāga womb and will quickly regain human status. Then...
Then that nāga, thinking, "I have indeed not grown in the Dhamma and Vinaya," being pained and dejected, shed tears and departed with a cry.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, there are two conditions for a nāga to reveal its true nature:
when it engages in sexual intercourse with its own kind, or when it sees its own reflection in water."
"And when, being let loose, he falls asleep—these, monks, are the two conditions for revealing the true nature of a nāga.
A beast, monks, should not be ordained; if already ordained, he is to be expelled.
Thus, it is because the conduct of a beast is made manifest. And here, by way of showing the frequent manifestation of his true nature during his activities—
“Two conditions,” it is said. However, for a nāga, there is the manifestation of his true nature at five times:

at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), at the time of shedding his skin, at the time of mating with one of his own species, at the time of waking from sleep, and at the time of death (*cuti*).

But are not the gods also indeed in a state of full ordination (*upasampadā*)? Then why are only the four [beings] belonging to the states of misery (*apāya*) mentioned in relation to full ordination?

Regarding the statement that [the gods] are "not a basis" (*avatthu*): this is true; nevertheless, it should be understood that because the gods are incapable [of attaining the fruits], yet the teaching of penetration remains established, this was said specifically for the purpose of distinguishing them from those who are capable.
For the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, will say in the Mahāvagga: "In the phrase 'an animal, monks,' whether it be a nāga, or a supaṇṇa, a māṇavaka, and so forth..."
“Or, including anyone from any non-human species, even down to Sakka, the king of the gods, all such beings are to be understood as ‘animals’ (*tiracchānagata*) in this context”;
thus it was said that “an animal is anyone who has become a non-human being. And here [the author] says:
“If nagas and supaṇṇas were inferior in terms of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), then why, in the *Vidhura-jātaka*...”
Four persons, aspiring for various respective abodes among the realms of the Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Sakkas, Dhanañjayas, and Korabbas, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and so forth.
At the end of their lives, one was reborn as a Nāga king in a Nāga realm together with his sons and wife;
another was reborn as a Supaṇṇa king in a Simbali-vimāna in the Supaṇṇa realm; and another...

It is stated that the manner in which rebirth-linking occurred for all four individuals—Sakka being reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and one being reborn in the womb of the chief queen of King Dhanañjaya Koravya—was solely through wholesome kamma.
If it were by way of wholesome kamma, [it is said]: "Wholesome volition is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*)."
In this *Paṭṭhāna* scripture as well, it would follow that even rootless states possess the status of a kamma-condition at the moment of rebirth-linking;
yet this should not be stated, so how then is it to be understood? It is said:

because of the strength of attachment (*nikanti*) and because of the sevenfold union of sexual intercourse, their wholesome volition (*kusalacetanā*) is impure; and being impure, [it does not function as such a condition].
They are unable to produce [rebirth] in a happy destination (*sugatibhūmi*).

Even when kamma is occurring in an unhappy destination (*duggatibhūmi*), at the time of its accumulation, it is through the power of prior volition (*pubbabhāgacetanā*) associated with craving (*taṇhā*) that one aspires for various specific destinations;
it is by this means that rebirth occurs in those animal realms, not by any other unwholesome state. For in this way, the aspiration thus made would be fulfilled. If...
It might arise through another unwholesome kamma, and even one’s desired aspiration would remain unfulfilled.
This craving is indeed capable of obstructing even a volition associated with powerful jhāna;

for instance, the ascetic teacher of Gopaka-Devadatta, instead of being reborn in the Brahma-worlds by the power of his jhāna, was obstructed from that jhāna and, through another kamma, was reborn among the Gandhabba devas.
It arises that "Monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity";
the detailed account of this is found in the Dīgha Nikāya and should be consulted there by those who seek it.
Furthermore, beings are not liberated from suffering even through the seven types of sexual union, for it was said by the Blessed One: "In this case, Brahmin, a certain ascetic or brahmin..."
Or, while claiming to be a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārī*), one does not engage in sexual intercourse with a woman;
yet, one consents to a woman’s anointing, bathing, massaging, and rubbing of the body.
One relishes that, desires that, and finds one’s livelihood through that. This too is a corruption of the holy life of a brahmin.
It is broken, it is perforated, it is spotted, and it is flawed. This, O Brahmin, is called one who leads an impure holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Being fettered by the bond of sexual union, he is not liberated from birth, aging, and death...
[as before] ...I say that he is not liberated from suffering. Furthermore, O Brahmin, here some ascetic... [as before] ...claiming to be such. Not...
In this way, one enters into the act of sexual intercourse with a woman;
yet one does not even consent to being massaged by a woman... [and so on] ...but rather laughs, plays, and sports with a woman, and finds gratification therein...
[and so on] ...I say that this is suffering. Furthermore, O Brahmin, here a certain ascetic or... [and so on] ...does not indeed [engage in sexual intercourse] with a woman... [and so on].
He enters into communion with her. He does not consent to being anointed by a woman.
Nor does he laugh, play, or dally with a woman. Yet he gazes intently and stares at a woman’s eyes;
he relishes that... [as before] ...I say it is suffering. Furthermore, Brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin...
Or... [and so on] ...it is not that he looks at a woman, nor at a woman's [belongings], nor does he look with a woman;
yet he hears the sound of a woman from beyond a wall or beyond a fence—whether she is laughing, speaking, singing, or weeping—and he relishes it...
[and so on] ...I say this is suffering. Furthermore, O Brahmin, here someone else...
Whether it be a recluse or a brahmin... [as before] ...neither with a woman nor for a woman, neither by means of a woman nor for a woman, nor even when she is weeping...
[as before] ...but rather he recollects those things that were previously laughed at, talked over, and played with together with a woman.
He gives that to her... [as before] ...I say this is suffering. Furthermore, O Brahmin, here someone else...
Whether it be a recluse or a brahmin... [and so on] ...he does not even [do this] with a woman, nor for a woman...
nor does he recall those things formerly laughed at, spoken of, and played with together with a woman;
rather, he [recalls] a householder or a householder’s son accompanied by, endowed with, and enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure. He...
He relishes that... [as before] ...I say it is suffering. Furthermore, O Brahmin...
[as before] ...he does not even recall having dallied with a woman... nor does he recall a householder or a householder’s son while they were enjoying themselves;
rather, he leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas, thinking: "By this virtue, or by this vow, or by this austerity..."
"Or: 'By means of the holy life (brahmacariya), I shall become a god or some other kind of deity'—he relishes that, he desires that, and he finds satisfaction in it.
This, O Brahmin, is the breach, the flaw, the blemish, and the stain of the holy life.
Thus, through this division caused by gain and so forth, as well as by the sevenfold union of sexual intercourse, there occurs the state of being breached and so on.
He should be understood as one who is included [in the Saṅgha].
However, in the case of a matricide, even if he killed a mother who was a human female but not his biological mother— such as a nurse, a foster-mother, a stepmother, or a grandmother—
or even if he killed a biological mother who was not a human female, his admission into the order is not forbidden.

And one is not an immediate neighbor [to hell]. Even female animals, having approached human males, give birth to children who have become human, just like the two brothers, the elders Kontaputta and Dvebhātika; for they too were indeed egg-born (*aṇḍaja*).
Thus, in these three realms—the realm of ghosts (*peta*), the animal realm (*tiracchāna*), and the human realm (*manussa*)—the four modes of birth (*yoni*) occur. Among humans...
In this regard, some are indeed of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), such as Prince Mahāpaduma and others;
there are also those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*), like the two brothers, the Elder Kontaputta. The detailed account, however, should be looked up in the *Sīhaḷavatthu*.
And here, "Konta" means a *kinnarī*; her sons are the "Kontaputtas. For she was, during the time of King Asoka Dhammarāja, [taken] by a forest-dweller...
Having attained human society and given birth to two sons, she thought, "Now she will not leave the children," and so the forest-dweller gave her a *pottha* (a protective amulet).
Having received the *pottha*, she leapt up and returned to her own place;
for *kinnarīs* are unable to leap up without a *pottha*. Therefore, the ascetic said, "Do not [give] the *pottha*..."
He said, “He gave me the horse. For their beauty is produced by temperature conditioned by kamma, like the Wheel-Treasure of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).
Thus, the Universal Monarch’s ability to travel through the air and so forth is called psychic power (*iddhi*) belonging to one possessed of merit;
it is not that he can go by his own inherent nature alone without the Wheel-Treasure or the Elephant and Horse Treasures. In this regard:

The wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*) of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), because it arises through the power of his karma, is called "arisen from temperature conditioned by karma" even when it is produced in the midst of the ocean.
The elephant and horse treasures, however, are called "arisen from karma conditioned by karma.
The psychic power (*iddhi*) of birds, such as traveling through the air, is born of the maturation of karma (*kammavipākajā*). As for the *kinnaris*, however, without a lute...

They are unable to leap forth by means of their own intrinsic nature; therefore, it should be understood that for them, the physical form (*pottha*) is produced by kamma-conditioned temperature (*kamma-paccaya-utu-samutthāna*).
Some, however, say that it comes along with rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) like the ornaments of the gods;
that should not be accepted, because such a thing is impossible for those born from eggs or from a womb. Others say it is produced during the course of existence (*pavatti-kāla*).

To say that [the intermediate state] does not exist is likewise incorrect; for even those born by moisture (*saṃsedaja*) are produced within the interior of lotuses or within bamboo, such as the brahmin Pokkharasāti, Queen Padumāvatī, Queen Veḷuvati, and others.

Those born from a womb (*jalābuja*), however, are indeed evident. Even he who, being himself an animal, killed his mother who was a human woman, did not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantarika-kamma*);
yet, because he was an animal, his admission into the order of monks was prohibited.
But his karma is heavy; having reached an immediate offense (*ānantariya*), it remains standing.
Even human women give birth to offspring by approaching animals, just as the mother of Bhūridatta did. Indeed, for women, conception occurs through eight causes:
through sexual misconduct, physical contact, grasping the garment, drinking impure fluids, touching the navel, [and so forth].

"By seeing forms, by sounds, and by odors. In that regard, through misconduct, Sudinna’s former wife became pregnant and gave birth to a son named Bījaka, who was like a golden image and destined for his final existence.
Sometimes, at the time of her season, certain women, impassioned by desire and lust, [engage in] taking the hands of men, grasping their necks, or touching their limbs and members.
Even those who consent conceive a fetus. Thus, conception occurs through physical contact.
However, the nun who was formerly the wife of the Elder Udāyī took some of that impurity with her mouth and placed some of it along with a cloth into the organ;
she conceived a fetus by means of that. Thus, conception occurs through the taking of the cloth.
It occurs thus: At the time of her season, the doe who was the mother of the ascetic Migasiṅga came to the place where the ascetic relieved himself and drank [the urine] along with its essence;
having conceived a fetus by that means, she gave birth to an ascetic boy named Migasiṅga. In this way, conception occurs through drinking impurity.
However, the mother of the Bodhisattva Sāma, at the time of her season, [conceived] by touching his navel.
Having conceived, she gave birth to the ascetic boy Sāma; likewise, Maṇḍabya and Caṇḍapajjota were born because their mothers, at the time of their seasons, touched their navels.
In that regard, Maṇḍabya’s birth came about through Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā touching his mother’s navel.
A scorpion crawled over the navel of Caṇḍapajjota’s mother and passed away there.

And by that means, the birth of Caṇḍapajjota occurred. In this world, some women, not obtaining contact with a man during their fertile period, gaze upon a man from within the house alone out of desire and lust, like the queen of a king; she thereby conceives a fetus.
Thus, conception occurs through the sight of a form. However, among cranes, there is no such thing as a "man."
At the time of their season, they conceive upon hearing the sound of thunderclouds; or sometimes, like a cow, they conceive by the scent of a bull.
Thus, conception occurs through scent. In this way, women conceive by means of these eight causes.
And herein, the sons are exactly like their fathers; therefore, Bhūridatta and others [were born] from Dhataraṭṭha.
Dependent upon a nāga king, there are only nāgas. However, in the case of Caṇḍapajjota, a human was born dependent upon a scorpion, because he was not born from a [human] womb.
The same principle applies to a patricide as well.
But an arahant-killer [is reborn] as a non-human, either as a deity who was an arahant or as one of the remaining types of noble persons (ariyapuggala) within the human birth.
Having killed [an animal], one does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), nor is his going forth (*pabbajjā*) forbidden; however, the kamma is powerful.

On the other hand, even having killed an Arahat who is a non-human being (*amanussa*), one does not incur an immediate retribution; yet the kamma is grave because of the victim’s status as a non-human, and for that reason, his going forth is forbidden.
The cases of violating a nun and causing a schism in the Saṅgha are well known.
Furthermore, one who causes blood to flow— being unable to cut through the skin by means of another's assault due to the Tathāgata’s indestructible body,
yet causing blood to collect in a single spot within the body itself,
which then becomes manifest and accumulated through resentment— generates much demerit and incurs an immediate retribution.
He exists, and even his going forth [into homelessness] has been forbidden, just like Devadatta.
However, he who—like Jīvaka—cuts open [the body] for the sake of pacifying disease, removes putrid flesh and blood, and restores one to health, is not a shedder of blood;
rather, he generates much merit, he generates Brahma-merit, just like Jīvaka Komārabhacca.
Furthermore, the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) is twofold according to female and male;
therein, for the female hermaphrodite, the female characteristic is manifest and the male characteristic is concealed.
For the male hermaphrodite, the male characteristic is manifest and the female characteristic is concealed. In the case of the female hermaphrodite, there is masculinity within females.
When he performs [the act], the female characteristic becomes concealed and the male characteristic becomes manifest.
When a man with both sets of characteristics (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) assumes the female state among men, the male characteristic becomes concealed and the female characteristic becomes manifest.
A woman with both sets of characteristics conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive. The man...
But one who possesses both sexual organs does not take [the precepts] himself, yet causes another to take them. This alone is the distinction between them. Regarding the term *ubhatobyañjana*:
here, "organ" (*byañjana*) means "sign" (*nimitta*). You will explain it as *ubhatobyañjana* by way of the grammatical analysis:
"one who has organs on both sides. Does this mean there are two faculties for one person, or only one? It is only one.
Not both: "In one for whom the female faculty (*itthindriya*) arises, does the male faculty (*purisindriya*) arise?
No. Or rather, in one for whom the male faculty arises, does the female faculty arise? No.
This is because the two faculties are not found together in a single continuum (*santāna*). And that [female faculty] belongs to a hermaphrodite woman (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*).
