"In the case of a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), there is only the male faculty (*purisindriya*). If there is only one faculty, how can there be the state of being a hermaphrodite?
It has been stated that the faculty is the cause of the physical marks (*byañjana*), yet that [hermaphrodite] lacks it. To this it is replied:
the female faculty is not the cause of the male marks, nor is the male faculty the cause of the female marks.

Why is it that they do not always exist? Because, for instance, when a female hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) is impassioned toward a woman, at that time the male organ becomes manifest and the female organ becomes concealed;
the same applies to a male hermaphrodite. If those two organs were the cause of the two sexual characteristics (*byañjana*), then both characteristics would always be present together.
It might remain [as such], but it does not; therefore, one must conclude that there is only a single faculty (*indriya*).
Setting aside the physical characteristic (*byañjana*) as the cause of the faculty, it should be understood that here the lustful mind itself is the cause for both characteristics.

Consequently, a female hermaphrodite (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*) both conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive, whereas a male hermaphrodite (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*) causes another to conceive.
But [the text] itself does not state that [it] takes [the sex organ], because conception occurs only for one who possesses the female faculty (*itthindriya*).

However, in the *Kurundi* commentary, the arising of the sex organ at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is stated thus: "If the male characteristic (*purisaliṅga*) arises at rebirth-linking, the female characteristic (*itthiliṅga*) arises during the course of existence (*pavatta*); if the female characteristic arises at rebirth-linking, the male characteristic arises during the course of existence. This is what was said.
This is indeed illogical. Why? Because the female gender and so forth arise only during the course of existence (*pavatti*), not at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
It cannot be said that the sense-faculty (*indriya*) itself is the gender-mark (*liṅga*), because the sense-faculty and the gender-mark have distinct intrinsic natures (*bhinnasabhāva*).
And just as a tree comes into being when there is a seed, but not when there is none, even so, the gender-marks and so forth come into being when there is a sense-faculty.
For the faculty is like a seed, while the gender-marks and so forth are like a tree.

In the same way, among those individuals, the eleven types of persons beginning with the *paṇḍaka* are not capable of entering the fixed course (*niyāma*) in that very same existence; therefore, they are called "incapable" (*abhabba*).

Those under twenty years of age and those who have previously committed one of the ultimate offenses (*antimavatthu*) are merely unfit for the ground of full ordination (*upasampadā*), due to the lack of necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*).
Since they are capable of entering the path of certainty (niyāma) within that very same existence, they are therefore called "capable" (bhabba).
The discussion on the perfection of the basis is concluded.
Now, the perfection of the motion (ñatti).
“Lax and forceful, long and short, heavy and light, and the nasal stop (niggahita);
connected, distinct, and released—thus is the tenfold classification according to the intellect regarding phonemes.
Having thus considered the ten kinds of phonemes mentioned, even for one who is unable [to analyze them] in this way, [one should consider] the lax and the forceful...

The perfection of the motion (*ñatti-sampatti*) is that which is spoken without violating the phonemes as they have been uttered—either by way of release or by way of restraint—and without making a mispronunciation.
The failure of the motion (*ñatti-vipatti*) consists, first of all, of these five defects of the motion: (1) omitting the motion entirely; (2) failing to mention the subject matter (*vatthu*);

(3) failing to mention the Saṅgha; (4) failing to mention the individual (*puggala*); and (5) formulating the motion after [the proposal has already been made]. In this context, "this person named so-and-so" refers to...
Not mentioning the candidate for full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*) is called "not touching upon the subject" (*vatthu-aparāmasana*).
Having said, "Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs," but not saying "the Sangha," is called "not touching upon the Sangha" (*saṅgha-aparāmasana*).
Not mentioning the preceptor by saying, "The candidate for full ordination of such-and-such a name," is called "not touching upon the person" (*puggala-aparāmasana*). In every respect...
The failure to recite the motion (*ñatti*) is called "the non-apprehension of the motion.

Having completed the first part of the formal act (*kammavācā*), saying "This is the motion" and then stating "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha," thus proclaiming the motion afterwards, is called "the subsequent establishment of the motion.
These five faults of the motion are known as "deficiency of the motion" (*ñattivipatti*). When the motion is free from these faults, it is called "perfection of the motion" (*ñattisampatti*).
The Discussion on the Perfection of the Motion is concluded.

As for the "Perfection of the Proclamation" (*anusāvanasampatti*): it consists in speaking while avoiding these five faults of proclamation—namely, failing to state the subject matter, failing to specify the Saṅgha or the individual, omitting parts of the proclamation, and proclaiming at an improper time. This is called the perfection of the proclamation. Regarding that:

The non-handling of the robes and other items is exactly as described in the formal motion (*ñatti*). However, during the three proclamations (*anusāvana*), the non-handling of these items at any point constitutes non-handling indeed.
Alternatively, without reciting the entire ritual formula (*kammavācā*) in its entirety, one may simply recite the motion four times;
or, even within the ritual formula itself, one may omit four syllables.
Or, having mispronounced a syllable or a word, the proclamation is called "deficient" (hāpana) for each subsequent proclamation;

for indeed, the four types of consonants—by way of being lax (*sithila*), hard (*dhanita*), released (*vimutta*), or suppressed (*niggahita*)—vitiate the act within the formal procedure (*kammavācā*).
In that regard, when it should be said in a lax manner, "May he hear me," the statement "Hear me! is [an example of] the lax.
The term *dhanita* refers to this: where one should say "Bhante," the word "bhanteti" is called *sithila* (slack) when it is *dhanita*.
Where one should say "suṇātu esā ñatti," the word "suṇantu esaṃ ñattī" is called *niggahita* (suppressed) when it is *vimutta* (released).
Where one should say "pattakallaṃ," the word "pattakallā" is called *vimutta* when it is *niggahita*. Thus are these four phonemes.

They vitiate the formal act by means of an internal *kammavācā*. Even one who speaks without violating these four [rules] commits what is called "speaking incorrectly" (*durutta*) if he utters a different syllable when another syllable ought to be uttered.

Regarding the other six points—namely, the long and short vowels—one must use a long vowel in the place of a long vowel and a short vowel in the place of a short vowel; thus, in each respective place, that very same syllable [must be used].
While reciting, one must perform the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*) without destroying the traditional lineage that has descended in succession.

However, if one fails to do so and speaks a short vowel where a long one should be spoken, or speaks a long vowel where a short one should be spoken; likewise, if one speaks lightly where something heavy should be spoken, or speaks heavily where something light should be spoken;
or if one speaks in a general connection where a specific distinction should be made, or speaks with a specific distinction where a general connection should be made—[the procedure is invalid].
When one speaks the connection [of the formula] while it is being recited, even so the *kammavācā* is not invalidated. These six syllables do not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*).
This is precisely the common consensus among the teachers. However, others say that these syllables now corrupt the formal act within the *kammavācā*;
if that were the case, those who have not received full ordination would become the majority. Having investigated this, [one should conclude as follows].
However, it must be accepted. Or rather, the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) should be studied even more thoroughly.
To perform the proclamation at an improper time, having first set forth the motion (*ñatti*) when there is no opportunity for the proclamation, is called "proclamation at the wrong time.

Thus, a proclamation that is free from these faults is called "endowed with the perfection of proclamation" (*anusāvanasampattisampanna*). If one ordains a person who is devoid of bowl and robes, [it is a fault].
Because the formal proclamation (*anusāvanā*) has been performed with the words "the bowl and robes are complete," there is no invalidation of the legal act (*kammakopa*);
however, the Sangha of performers incurs an offense of transgression (*sātisāra*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:

"Even in the absence of the bowl and robes, because the formal act was recited with the words 'the bowl and robes are complete,' one does not speak of an invalidation of the legal act, but rather speaks only of a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). This applies if [the candidate] is without a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*).

If one ordains [someone], saying, "He seeks ordination from such-and-such a person, with such-and-such a person as preceptor," or if one announces the preceptor [to the assembly] by saying, "[He seeks ordination] with such-and-such a person as preceptor," he becomes one who is well-ordained. If one does not announce the preceptor, he is not ordained. For it will be said in the *Vimativinodanī*:
"The formal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated; this means that even in the absence of a preceptor, [one may say] 'He seeks ordination for such-and-such a person, with such-and-such a person...'"

"By means of a preceptor"—this is stated because the proclamation of a preceptor has been performed in all cases by mentioning the name of anyone who is no longer present, whether it be one who is dead, one who has disrobed, or one's former preceptor.

For if one were not to perform the proclamation of a preceptor, there would be the same fault as that mentioned in the rule: "He does not designate a person. Therefore, in the Canon it says: "One without a preceptor."

...it is said. If one grants full ordination with a Sangha as preceptor or a group as preceptor, the performing Sangha commits an offense of transgression (*sātisāra*), yet the formal act (*kamma*) itself is not invalidated; for the *Vimativinodanī* will state: "With the Sangha as preceptor":
this person named so-and-so desires full ordination from the Sangha; this person named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Sangha. By the Sangha...
"By the preceptor"—the meaning is that one has designated the Saṅgha itself as the preceptor by means of this formal act (*kammavācā*).
Likewise, in the phrase "by the group-preceptor," the construction should be understood as: "This person, [named] so-and-so, desires ordination from the group," and so forth.
Even when spoken in this way, the formal act is certainly not invalidated, because only a *dukkaṭa* offense has been stated; otherwise, that individual...

‘[One] who says, “He is not fully ordained. If one confers full ordination with a paṇḍaka or other such person as the preceptor who is not fully ordained, then—excluding them—if the quorum of five or more members is fulfilled without abandoning hand-contact, the formal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated;

however, the performing Saṅgha commits an offense of transgression. Thus it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*: “In cases where [the act] is being performed by paṇḍakas and others acting as preceptors...”
“Even without a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) or others, the quorum of five or more for a group is fulfilled, and the formal act (*kamma*) does not fail; otherwise, it fails.
If four teachers recite together, how is this to be understood?
It is said that in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), two or three teachers each [recite] separately to one person at a time, so that two or three [recitations] occur simultaneously.

The formal proclamation (kammavācā) must be performed. However, if they have different teachers and different preceptors, it is permissible provided that the group is complete—for instance, if the Elder Tissa recommends the student of the Elder Sumana, and the Elder Sumana recommends the student of the Elder Tissa.
But if they have different preceptors, there must be at least one common teacher; it is not permitted if they do not even share a common preceptor.

It is stated only that it is not permissible because it has been rejected. However, even though no shadow of a failure in the ritual (*kamma-vipatti*) is seen in the discussion regarding the deliberation of the four persons, nevertheless, it must certainly not be done, because it has not been deliberated upon in any of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

If one confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) on someone whose hair and beard have grown long while they are still wearing clothes, ornaments, and so forth, he becomes fully ordained immediately; afterwards—

It is proper for one to shave off the hair and beard and don the saffron robes, because it is free from the thirteen grounds [of disqualification] and because the excellence [of the candidate] is itself the measure here.
The discussion on the excellence of the proclamation is finished.
Now, the turn has come for the commentary on this verse, which is titled "The Purification of the Boundary" (*Sīmavisodhanī*) and is drawn from various texts:
"The wisdom of that Great Sage extended over all things to be known,
and his compassion toward infinite beings proceeded according to his will."
Urged by her, the Teacher, for the sake of the welfare of the bhikkhus, authorized a boundary;
concerning that, a question arises.
The bhikkhus have doubts and uncertainties in some places and in all places.
Even my books have become difficult to understand because they were composed by myself.
If, having heard such a discourse of mine, you remain indifferent,
then my going forth under the excellent teaching of the Fully Awakened One has been in vain.
Profound and subtle is the meaning, the domain of the Omniscient Victor.
Even for the Elder Sāriputta of great wisdom, it was beyond his reach;
how then could you possibly be able [to fathom] the domain of the Omniscient Victor?
"Thus they may criticize me," yet the Great Sage persevered.
Like a great sal tree in full bloom, lofty as Mount Meru,
the Perfectly Awakened One spoke thus at the time of his final nibbāna.
"Do not weep, Ānanda; do not grieve, Ānanda.
I alone have attained Nibbāna, for many Buddhas are still living.
These eighty-four thousand perfectly enlightened ones—"
"You shall give counsel, O Bhikkhu; you have performed meritorious deeds and shall become one who has done so.
While the Pāḷi together with its commentaries remains—the domain of the Omniscient One—then even though the Sambuddha has attained Parinibbāna, he is not absent from this generation."
Having reflected thus, day and night, without weariness,
while the Fully Awakened One was still living, my divisive talk was out of place.
Having abandoned that divisive talk and discarded the notion of my own conduct, I [proceeded].
"Now I shall explain it for the long-term purification of the True Dhamma.

In this context, "the Purification of the Boundary" (*sīmavisodhanī*) means they will compose a treatise that abandons the failure of boundaries (*sīmavipatti*), and having abandoned the failure of boundaries, elucidates the characteristics of success.
Regarding that, "boundary" (*sīmā*) refers to fifteen kinds of boundaries. What are the fifteen?

"Fragmentary boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), common-residence boundary (samānasaṃvāsasīmā), non-separation boundary (avippavāsasīmā), profit boundary (lābhasīmā), village boundary (gāmasīmā), town boundary (nigamasīmā), city boundary (nagarasīmā),
inner boundary (abbhantarasīmā), water-throw boundary (udakukkhepasīmā), province boundary (janapadasīmā), kingdom boundary (raṭṭhasīmā),

realm boundary (rajjasīmā), island boundary (dīpasīmā), world-system boundary (cakkavāḷasīmā). Therein, "fragmentary boundary" refers to [the boundaries] for going forth, full ordination, and so forth.

For the sake of making the formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha easy to perform, [the boundaries] were formally authorized by being divided and delimited within either a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) or a village field (*gāmakhettaka*).

The detailed explanation of this is stated in the *Mahāvagga* of the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, which is divided into seventy-two sections, beginning with the words: "First, the marks (*nimitta*) must be proclaimed. Even though it is stated here as well, it would be stated in exactly the same way.
Therefore, we shall not speak further; rather, having extracted certain points that are difficult to understand, we will make them clear.
In this regard, if there is a cave inside beyond the boundary of the upper limit, the boundary does not extend outside.
Likewise, if the cave is outside within the boundary of the upper limit, it is inside the boundary.
"Does not descend" (*na otarati*)—these two [terms] have the same meaning; only the phrasing differs. Herein, this is the meaning:
from the near side of the boundary's limit, one pierces through the mountain slope at the foot of the mountain in the shape of a cave (*umaṅga*), and there is a dwelling (*leṇa*).
Beyond the boundary's limit, both within the dwelling and on the ground outside the dwelling at the base of the mountain, there is the boundary.
It does not extend [into the space] above the shelter; rather, the boundary exists only above it.

Even if there is a shelter on the side of the mountain, pierced at its base by a tunnel in the shape of a cave, which lies outside the near side of that upper boundary-limit, the boundary does not extend into the shelter, nor into the area of the ground below the mountain that is beyond the shelter. Of the shelter...
"Or there is a boundary on the upper part. This investigation has also been carried out in the *Vimativinodanī*. "Inside" means inside the mountain; the meaning is "at the foot of the mountain.
To specify that very word "inside" by way of the delimitation of the boundary, it is said: "beyond the delimitation of the upper boundary.
However, with reference to the base of the mountain, although it should be called "on this side," [it is not].
It should be understood that the word "beyond" (*parato*) is said with reference to the mountain peak as the basis for the boundary (*sīmānissaya*);
for that very reason, in the phrase "outside the cave" (*bahileṇa*), he specifies the word "outside" by saying "on this side of the upper boundary-limit.
In the expression "the boundary does not extend outside," the word "outside" is said with reference to the cave at the foot of the mountain; [it means] above that which is external to the cave.
The meaning is that the boundary does not descend into the lower part of the boundary-delimitation.
"Within the boundary" means that it does not descend into a place within the cave or the mountain base that is suitable for its own descent; the meaning is that the boundary does not descend outside.

And here, regarding the phrase "the boundary does not descend," it means that by way of being a cave, the boundary is in every respect a total "non-descending" in the place suitable for its own descent.
It should be understood as "shown. Regarding this, the *Vimativinodanī* states: "In that case, 'not entering' means that the boundary exists only above.
However, some say that the "cave" (*leṇa*) is merely a hollow, like the hollow of a bamboo shoot; that is incorrect.

What is called the "proximate boundary" (*upacārasīmā*) extends, according to whether it pertains to a village, a forest, a town, or the like, as far as the Brahma-world, being the dwelling-place of those respective beings.

The "proximity boundary" (*upacārasīmā*)— referring here to places suitable for the vicinity of celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*), and so forth— is not intended in this context,
because such places are outside the domain of monks. However, it refers to that area which, having been demarcated and made into a courtyard (*pariveṇa*),
or having been enclosed by a wall and the like, or even in an unenclosed place, having demarcated an area suitable for the vicinity, or in whatever place monks [dwell].

They dwell; this very [area] is intended as the "proximate boundary" (*upacārasīma*). Because it is the place where monks enter for the rains retreat and perform the spreading of the *kaṭhina* cloth, it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada* on all three [texts]:
"of the boundary where the *kaṭhina* has been spread," referring to the proximate boundary, because there is no arising [of requisites] within the natural boundary (*khandhasīma*).
"Supported by what arises therein" means supported by fields, lands, and so forth belonging to the monastery.
The construction should be understood as follows: "Whatever robe belonging to the Saṅgha arises [for them], that shall belong only to those monks who have performed the *kaṭhina*-spreading ceremony.
Regarding the phrase "by means of fields, land, etc.," the word "etc.
includes either a robe for the deceased, or what has been given specifically for the Saṅgha, or what belongs to the Saṅgha; this is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. In that [context]...
It includes all robes that come into existence within the boundary of the precincts; for this very reason, it is said: "Now at that time, a certain lay follower had a monastery built for the Saṅgha.
When that monastery was finished, he wished to give an out-of-season robe to both Saṅghas. Now at that time, the kaṭhina had been spread for both Saṅghas."
Then that lay follower approached the Saṅgha and requested the lifting of the kaṭhina.
In this matter, the Blessed One prescribed the lifting of the kaṭhina for the sake of establishing its benefits;
yet, because the nun Thullanandā did not acknowledge those benefits, she obstructed the lifting of the kaṭhina, thinking, "The robe will be ours."
Therefore, within this limit of the spread-out kaṭhina, as long as the kaṭhina has not been withdrawn, for five months up until the full moon of Phagguna,
whatever robe-material belonging to the Saṅgha is given— whether it be a robe for the deceased, dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters on behalf of deceased kinsmen,
or given by way of alms-offering, or through the duties of a monastery festival, or by any other means— all that is included.

It belongs only to those monks who performed the *kaṭhina*-spreading ceremony. It does not belong to those whose rains-residence was interrupted, nor to those who arrived there during the later rains-retreat, nor to the monks residing within the boundary (*sīmā*).
If they take it without knowing [this], it must certainly be given back.
If that robe-cloth is made into food such as rice or other hard foods, it indeed belongs to others as well. Why?

This is because of the absence of that specific benefit. For that very reason, those who have arrived merely to complete the quorum of the assembly—whether they have completed their rains residence, or have entered during the later period (*pacchimikā*), or have spent the rains in another monastery—do receive hard food, soft food, and so forth.
However, the formal act of giving the cloth for one whose *kaṭhina* has been spread is only permissible within a delimited boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*). In that monastery...
If there is no other monastery available, it must indeed be performed within a delimited boundary (baddhasīmā) or within a water-sprinkling boundary (udakukkhepasīmā), and so forth.
Why is that? Because those who entered that monastery during the earlier session are not skilled in the spreading of the Kathina cloth.

Elders who are reciters of the Khandhaka and are skilled in the spreading [of the Kathina] should be sought out and brought there. Having announced the formal act (kammavācā), one should cause the Kathina to be spread.
"Having consumed the gift, they will depart, but the merit belongs to the others.
This is because the commentary states that the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) may be performed even by monks residing within another boundary.

Those who have arrived during the later rains-retreat (*pacchimikā*) after their retreat has been interrupted, or those who have completed their retreat in another monastery and arrived during the earlier rains-retreat (*purimikā*), receive only the status of completing the quorum.

The benefit belongs only to the others. Even if those who have had their rains-retreat interrupted and so forth offer an expression of appreciation (*anumodana*), the *kaṭhina* robe-offering is considered broken;

this has been examined in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, others say that because it is stated, "It was said with reference to the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) within the *kaṭhina*-spread boundary," they perform the formal motion (*ñatti*) for the *kaṭhina*-offering only within the precinct boundary. That is improper.

Because it is difficult to purify [the robe]. For indeed, once one has entered the village boundary within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), who would be able to bring the robe down there, or to establish a boundary outside?
By the phrase "the boundary where the kaṭhina has been spread," only the state of having the kaṭhina spread is expressed, not the formal act of giving the cloth for the kaṭhina.

And that investigation should be illustrated by the fourfold classification of formal acts (*kamma*). In this context, there are: the act of intimation (*apalokana-kamma*), the act consisting of a motion (*ñatti-kamma*), the act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiya-kamma*), and the act consisting of a motion and a fourth resolution (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*). Among these, an "act of intimation" is as follows:

having cleared the Saṅgha within the boundary, having brought the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it, and having announced the Saṅgha with the approval of the entire assembly, one says: "Does it please the Saṅgha?"

That which is to be performed after having announced three times is now stated. A *ñattikamma* (act by resolution) is an act to be performed with a single resolution (*ñatti*) by the consent of a united Saṅgha, according to the method already described.

A *ñattidutiyakamma* (act with a resolution as the second member) is an act to be performed with one resolution and one announcement (*anusāvanā*), thus consisting of a resolution as the second member, according to the method already described by the consent of a united Saṅgha.

A formal act (kamma) to be performed by means of proclamation (*anusāvana*). A "formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations" (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is a formal act to be performed by means of one motion and three proclamations through the consent of a harmonious Saṅgha, according to the method already stated.
Among these, a formal act by way of mere notification (*apalokanakamma*) is obtained only for light formal acts at times such as the distribution of the fruits [of the alms-bowl].

Even when giving a cloth for the purpose of spreading the *kathina*, if the *kathina* has not yet been spread, one may obtain a cloth with many benefits from that [donor] and spread the *kathina* with that very cloth;

there is no need for the formal act (*kammavācā*) of giving again, as it should be given with the consent of the Saṅgha through an act of intimation (*apalokana-kamma*). A single *kammavācā* for the giving of the cloth for the purpose of spreading the *kathina* is sufficient. Again...

There is no formal act consisting of a motion and proclamation (*ñattivācāyakicca*). However, at the time of the compilation of the Dhamma, when the Elder Mahākassapa and others appointed themselves, only light formal acts (*lahukakamma*) were obtained.
As for the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), it includes:

the authorization of a boundary (*sīmāsammuti*), the removal of a boundary (*sīmāsamūhana*), the offering of the Kathina cloth (*kathinadāna*), the suspension of the Kathina privileges (*kathinuddhāra*), the designation of a site for a hut (*kuṭivatthudesanā*), and the designation of a site for a monastery (*vihāravatthudesanā*).

It is not permissible to perform these six heavy formal acts (*garukamma*) after merely seeking permission (*apalokana*); they must be performed only after the motion and the second proclamation of the formal act (*ñattidutiyakamma*) have been announced.

Regarding the subsequent formal acts, such as the authorization for being apart from one’s robe (*cīvaravippavāsasammuti*), they may be performed even by seeking permission alone, because they are light formal acts (*lahukakamma*).

However, the formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*)—namely, the present act of full ordination (*upasampadākamma*) and the four [other such acts]—must be performed only after the motion and the third proclamation have been announced.

When it is impossible to purify the deeds within a fixed boundary (*baddhasīmā*), or in its absence within a water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), they must indeed be performed within an unfixed boundary (*abaddhasīmā*).

Others say this: "At the time when the site for a hut (*kuṭi*) or the site for a monastery (*vihāra*) is being prepared, how could those sites for the huts and monasteries be made to stand within a boundary? Therefore, right there [in that specific location]..."
The statement that "it should be done only at the very site where the hut-monastery is to be built" is merely their word; it should not be accepted as authoritative.
In this matter, the examination of the site (*vatthuparāmasana*) alone is the standard.

For, after performing the examination of the site by means of the request, "Look at the site for the Saṅgha’s hut," and so forth, one must avoid the faults of the motion regarding the site and the characteristics of failure, and then [proceed] with a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
The monks who have been appointed must go to that site for the hut-vihāra and inspect it; for it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Those appointed monks, having gone there, must inspect the site for the hut.

Otherwise, if they were to confer full ordination upon a person who is devoid of bowl and robes, or one who lacks a preceptor, [they would be contradicting the rule] "for one whose bowl and robes are complete."

Or, even when the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) has been recited, saying, "The candidate for full ordination is named so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor," the act might still fail to be accomplished.
Others say this: "But [the act fails] if it is performed at the time of the boundary-authorization (*sīmāsammuti*);
for at the time of the boundary-authorization, the monks recite the formal proclamation while standing in that very place; therefore, in that case too—"

"In that place, there is no formally established boundary (*abaddhasīmā*). If there were a formally established boundary, there would have to be either a transgression of the boundary or a breaking of the boundary.

This is true; nevertheless, because that site for the formal authorization of the boundary has been made free [of such restrictions] by means of the formal act of authorizing the boundary, monks standing within the village boundary of a separate village are not able to invalidate the formal act of those monks authorized in that [other] village.

If one were to think that the boundary should be established only after making the site of the boundary-agreement free from ownership, then how could the group of six monks have established boundaries as they pleased during the lifetime of the Blessed One? This, however, should not be viewed in such a way;
for instance, Migāramātā Vāsabhakhattiyā, having acquired land with nine hundred million [pieces of gold], built the great monastery named Pubbārāma.

Likewise, after Anāthapiṇḍika had caused the prince Jeta’s park to be purchased by means of a layer of kahāpaṇa coins and took possession of it, he had the great monastery named Jetavana built; thus, those desiring merit build monasteries by constructing a pariveṇa.
Therefore, it should be understood that the monks of the group-of-six (Chabbaggiyā) were binding the boundary (sīmā) as they pleased. This is...
There is deliberation regarding the boundary of formal conduct (*upacārasīmā*).

A "boundary of common residence" (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*) is a boundary authorized for a group of monks—characterized by their unity in view, virtue, and communal life—to dwell together in a state of oneness through sangha-acts such as the Uposatha.
A "boundary of non-separation" (*avippavāsasīmā*) is [the area] within which one may be separated from the three robes...
The *sammata-sīmā* (formally agreed boundary) and these two types of boundaries—since they can also exist as far as three *yojanas*—are given the name "great boundary" (*mahāsīmā*).
The investigation of these has been stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* after being treated in its entirety; therefore, we shall not discuss them here.
Even if it were discussed here, it would be stated without distinction [from what already exists]; therefore, we shall not discuss it.

The "boundary for acquisitions" (lābhasīmā) refers to whatever village, town, lotus pond, lake, forest, or other location that has been demarcated and established by kings, royal ministers, or high officials for the sake of providing the four requisites to the Saṅgha; this is called the boundary for acquisitions.
It was neither authorized by the Perfectly Enlightened One nor established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma; nevertheless—
It was indeed established by those who provide offerings. In the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Mātikā*, it is also stated: "The boundary of offerings (*lābhasīmā*).
This refers to when kings, royal ministers, and others, having built a monastery, demarcate a perimeter of four *gāvutas*, half a *yojana*, or one *yojana* all around, saying:
"This is the boundary of offerings for our monastery; whatever arises within this area, all of that [belongs to us]."
"Give it to our monastery," they set aside [the land]; this is what is called a "boundary for acquisitions" (*lābhasīmā*).
Regarding this section on the boundary for acquisitions: one year after the passing of King Mahācetiya-dāyaka, during the time of his eldest son, King Dhamma, such merit was performed in the past.
For if anyone among the kings, royal ministers, and so forth— [The text continues: ...if anyone... [the passage ends abruptly].
If one gives the ponds, fields, building sites, and so forth belonging to a monastery to an individual after having given that monastery itself to a group (saṅgha),
then in such a case, is it permissible for that individual to receive that monastery belonging to the group as his own personal property (puggalika),

or must it be received only as belonging to the Saṅgha? However, a monastery that is entirely personal (puggalika) and devoid of ponds, fields, building sites, and so forth— [is that what is meant here?]
If someone dies after saying, "I give this to others," does it become the property of the Saṅgha, or does it remain the personal property of that individual? Herein is the answer:

If anyone among kings, royal ministers, and so forth, gives a monastery’s ponds, fields, sites, and so on, it should be understood that in such a case it is not permissible to refuse it; thus it was stated in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā.
“When it is said, ‘We give this pond, this field, and this site for the monastery,’ it is not permitted to refuse. And:
“When they say, ‘We give a female slave, a male slave, a field, a site, and cattle and buffalo for the palace,’ there is no need for separate acceptance;
once the palace is accepted, these are already accepted. This is also stated in the *Vinayavinicchaya-pakaraṇa*.
“Whether it be fields, building sites, or ponds, or cattle, goats, and so forth—if one says, ‘I give these to the monastery,’ it is not permissible to refuse.
And in the *Khuddasikkhā* it is stated: “When [fields and so forth] are spoken of as being for the monastery, it is permissible to say, ‘I give them. “For the monastery...”
And here, it should be understood that "we give" refers specifically to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, not to a private dwelling;
for thus it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*: "'We give to the monastery' is said with reference to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.
And although "of the palace" is stated in general terms, [it is specified] by the passage: "Now at that time, Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, [gave] for the sake of the Saṅgha..."

In this context, regarding the passage, "He desired to have a gabled mansion with elephant-protuberances built," it is understood that this was said with reference specifically to a mansion belonging to the Saṅgha, because the use of such a mansion had been permitted. For thus it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:

"The entire use of a mansion. Furthermore, in the section of the commentary on the *Pāḷi* concerning the description [of the mansions], it says: "Variegated with gold, silver, and so forth," and so on.

This was said with reference to bedding belonging to the Saṅgha. However, it is not even permissible for an individual monk to accept personal property such as gold and so forth that is adorned with various ornaments, because it has been stated:
"In no way whatsoever should gold or silver be accepted.

For this very reason, it is not mentioned here in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) whether it is in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha or one belonging to an individual. [The phrase] "in the context of describing the Dhamma and Vinaya for monks" refers to this.

Because it has been so stated, it should be understood that only lodgings made of gold and other precious materials belonging to the Saṅgha, as well as the requisites for those lodgings, are permissible, and not those belonging to an individual (puggalika).
Therefore, a monastery together with its ponds, fields, lands, and so forth, belongs exclusively to the Saṅgha and not to an individual;
this is how those skilled in the Vinaya should regard it. However, if anyone among kings, royal ministers, or others...
If one gives a monastery together with its ponds, fields, buildings, and so forth, having informed the individual that it is being given as such a combined monastery,
then it should be understood that it is permissible for the individual to accept it precisely as a communal (saṅghika) monastery,

and not as a private (puggalika) monastery. This is because, regarding the ponds, fields, buildings, and so forth that were given after saying, "We give these to the monastery," they belong to the Saṅgha alone.
Because it is allowable. For this very reason, it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*: "Regarding the statement 'We give it to the monastery,' it is allowable for the Saṅgha, not for an individual;
it should be regarded as being like [the giving of] fields and so forth. Herein, the application is as follows:

having said "We give it to the monastery," fields and so forth that have been given are allowable for the Saṅgha, not for an individual; likewise, regarding the statement "We give it to the monastery," [this applies to] gold and other such variegated items.
It should be understood that an improper bed is permissible for the Saṅgha, but not for an individual.
It is likewise permissible for the Saṅgha alone to accept fields and so forth under the designation of "proper requisites" (kappiya-vohāra). For it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:
"If one gives [land] saying, 'Let him enjoy the four requisites,' it is permissible; here, for the purpose of the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha's enjoyment of the four requisites, a reservoir..."

Whether one says, "I give," or "I give a pond for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to enjoy the four requisites," or "I give from this pond the four requisites that arise therefrom"—all such statements are permissible.

However, this is said specifically with reference to what is being given to the Saṅgha; for an individual, even if given in this way, a pond, field, or the like is not permitted. [This applies] to one of pure mind.
However, wells, lotus ponds, and so forth are permitted for the purpose of utilizing water. Since it is stated in all such cases—such as "the Saṅgha has a tank;

what of that?"—that it is by way of the Saṅgha alone; and because it should be understood that "fields and so forth are permitted for the Saṅgha as a whole, since they were not authorized to be taken as private property in the Canon";
whereas for an individual or for several individuals, fields, lands, and so forth [are not permitted].
It is not even permissible to accept [these things] by means of allowable terminology (*kappiyavohāra*).

Having said this, it is understood from the *Vimativinodanī* that even fields, land, and so forth are not permitted to be taken for an individual (*puggala*) even by means of allowable terminology, because it has been stated:
"He abstains from accepting fields and land," and so on; for among those things prohibited, taking them for an individual alone is not authorized.
It has been stated that "thereby it is established that other things must likewise be accepted [as belonging to the Saṅgha]";

therefore, it should be understood that a monastery together with its ponds, fields, lands, and so forth, must be accepted solely as the property of the Saṅgha. This is the answer to the first question.
However, a monastery devoid of ponds, fields, lands, and so forth, may also be accepted as the private property of an individual (puggalika).

And while that person is still living, that dwelling belongs to that individual. However, it should be understood that if one has not said, "I give this to others," then upon his death it is neither to be distributed nor divided;
it remains the property of the Saṅgha alone. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes.
Furthermore, those who tend to the sick have been of great service; therefore, I allow you, bhikkhus, [to assign these] by the Saṅgha.

And the three robes are to be given to those who have attended to the sick. Whatever light goods or light requisites there are therein, these are to be distributed by the Saṅgha assembled before them.

Whatever heavy goods or heavy requisites there are therein, these are not to be sold nor divided, but belong to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future. And in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* [it says]: "In that..."
It is said: "While they are alive, [the property] belongs to the individual; when they have died, it belongs only to the Saṅgha.

Thus, even requisites set aside for others become the property of the Saṅgha alone in that case. When [an object] belongs to two people and has not been divided, upon the death of one, the other becomes the owner.
This same principle applies even when [the object] belongs to many; when all have died, it becomes the property of the Saṅgha.
And here, regarding the terms "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*) and so forth, heavy goods are fivefold by way of category, but twenty-fivefold by way of specific form.
Therefore, one should understand that even a monastery which has become the property of the deceased is considered heavy goods;
thus it is said in the Commentary: "Whatever there is there that is light goods, whatever there is there that is heavy goods."
"Thus, with five groups, the Lord whose eyes are fivefold pure proclaimed the twenty-five kinds of heavy property.
Herein, the status of the monastery as "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa) should be understood. This is the answer to the second question.
This is the response regarding the leading Mahātheras of Haṃsāvatī. However, the Mahātheras residing in the kingdom of Rāmañña state that it may indeed be accepted even as a private gift (puggalika);

likewise do the Mahātheras residing in the kingdom of Jaṃbūdīpa, likewise the Mahātheras residing in the kingdom of Sūnāparanta, and likewise the Mahātheras residing in Isinagara [regard it] as a private gift.
Regarding those who say, "There is no fault in accepting [the robe]," the intention of these great elders is as follows:
this so-called "boundary for acquisitions" (*lābhasīmā*) was neither authorized by the Fully Enlightened One nor established by the elders who compiled the Dhamma.
Rather, it was established by donors seeking merit; therefore, kings, royal ministers, and others seeking merit [established] the monastery...
Having had it built, they demarcate a portion of land for the purpose of providing for that monastery, saying, "Whatever arises within this area, we give all of that to our monastery.
Then, they [assign] that monastery to whichever individual they please, saying, "I give this monastery to you; let it be your monastery," or they [assign it] to themselves.
If one gives out of personal preference, that person also accepts only a dwelling that has been authorized by such statements as, "Bhikkhus, I authorize five kinds of dwellings:
a vihāra... and so forth, because only a dwelling authorized by the Blessed One is accepted.
If it is argued that fields, lands, and so forth exist within that dwelling, [the answer is: "He abstains from accepting fields and lands," and so forth. What [is prohibited]...
The acceptance of grounds such as fields and so forth has been prohibited;
because such grounds as fields have not been accepted, when only a monastery itself is accepted, then robes, alms-food, requisites for the sick,
and medicinal supplies arising on those connected grounds belong to that very person by way of what is allowable (kappiya), whether through the person’s acceptance or through their use.
There is no fault, because it is the consumption of a permissible requisite (kappiyapaccaya) authorized by the Blessed One himself. If you ask for a scriptural passage (sutta), [it is]:

"I allow you, monks, the use of all palaces. But was it not Visākhā Migāramātā who built the palace with verandas and elephant-trunk towers for the sake of the Saṅgha alone? True; nevertheless, the individual is included within the Saṅgha.
When the use of a monastery by the Saṅgha is authorized, it is indeed authorized for an individual included therein as well.

Otherwise, even if the Saṅgha were performing a formal act (kamma) within the boundary of that very monastery while sitting inside the dwelling with an individual present, there would be no invalidation of the act;
for it will be stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "I authorize you, monks... [and so forth].
From the statement, "all [items] for the use of the palace," it follows that even in the case of a private dwelling,
although it is permissible to use items such as golden jars that have been designated for the use of the lodging, it is not permissible to use them by making them one's own personal property;
by this statement as well, the entire contents of a private monastery are established as being allowable.
It is understood from the observation of the indicative statement: "Monks, I allow the use of all palaces. Regarding the phrase "golden jars, etc.," the word "etc.

(*ādi*) here has the sense of a limit or the sense of a category; by this, it includes silver, bronze, brass, crystal, and other unallowable jars, as well as bowls, ladles, and other requisites for lodgings made of gold, silver, bronze, brass, crystal, and so forth.

These items are not permitted for a bhikkhu as personal requisites; likewise, female and male slaves, cows, and buffaloes are not permitted. Similarly, fields and other lands are not permitted for a bhikkhu to accept as his own property;
however, there is no prohibition regarding a monastery (*vihāra*), because the word "all" is seen [to include it].
For this very reason, it was said in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya: "Regarding lodgings..."
"However, for door panels, window shutters, and so forth, everything—even if made of precious gems—is permissible as a smooth, polished finish.
Regarding lodgings, there is nothing to be prohibited except for a conflicting lodging (*viruddha-senāsana*).

By this [statement], with the exception of the village and its precincts, and with the exclusion of the "conflicting lodging," all things—both allowable and unallowable—are permitted for a monastery (*vihāra*).
It is understood that there is nothing, however slight, that is not permitted and must be prohibited; for this very reason it is said in the *Vinayavinicchaya*:
"Even if one says, 'We give a field or a site, a pond, or cows, goats, sheep, and so forth, to the monastery,' it is not allowed to refuse them."
Now, it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* that the phrase "we give [this] to the monastery" was spoken with reference to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.

For it is said there: "According to the intention of the Teacher, when it is said, 'We give the fields, the dwellings, and so forth to a private (puggalika) monastery,' one must refuse it, saying, 'It is not permitted, O lay follower. Why? Because the person [is not the owner] of that monastery..."
"Venerable sir, when a monastery is given, it is as if it were given to an individual;
if this were so, one would incur the offense prescribed by the training rule stating, 'He abstains from accepting fields and lands,' and so forth.
However, a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha should not be refused. Why? Because that individual has no ownership over that Saṅgha monastery. It belongs to the four quarters."
Whatever has been given for the sake of the Saṅgha, whether small or large, even one who takes it by encroaching upon a portion does not incur a *pārājika* offense;
this is because it is impossible to relinquish responsibility for the entire Saṅgha of the four quarters.
Therefore, when what was given to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha is withheld, one becomes an obstructer of the Saṅgha’s gain. This very point—
It might have been said that "we give it to the monastery" refers to a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha;

thus, it should not be accepted even as private property. And this being so, regarding the phrase "by the relinquishment of responsibility by the owners," in the case of a pond or a field belonging to a single individual, there is a *pārājika* offense upon that very person's relinquishment of responsibility. However, if...
That pond is for the common use of all, while the fields are individual; if he abandons his responsibility regarding that [pond], it is theft (*avahāra*).
Now, if the fields too are for the common use of all, then the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) occurs only upon the abandonment of responsibility by everyone;

thus, there would be no contradiction with the statement in the *Vimativinodanī* that "it is not [theft] when [the owner] is absent," because [the offense applies] to one who possesses [the property] such as fields, lands, and so forth.
Since the monastery is the private property of an individual, how could there be a legal claim against that individual regarding fields, land, and so forth?
And as for the statement, "He lays down the burden," this refers specifically to ponds and fields belonging to householders;
thus it should not be said [that the rule applies to monastic property]. Even so, it should not be stated.
Why is it said, "He lays down the burden"? Because the phrase, "But when [the husband] thinks: 'This man is stubborn and harsh;

he might even create an obstacle to my life or my holy life (brahmacariya); enough now for me with him,'" is seen [in the source], it is for that very reason that it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī*:
"The fields are individual property, and upon his laying down the burden. Likewise: "I allow you, monks, all..."
There would be no contradiction with the statement in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:

"Because of the expression 'use for a palace,' even in the case of a lodging belonging to an individual, gold jars and the like—which are restricted as being intended for the use of the lodging—though their use is permitted, it is not permissible to use them by making them one's own private property. Likewise [with the passage]: "In the lodging, anything..."
This is also consistent with the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "There is nothing that should be prohibited, except for a lodging that is unsuitable.

Likewise, it is consistent with the conformity to the Sutta: "Monks, whatever has not been forbidden by me as 'this is not allowable,' if it conforms to what is allowable and excludes what is unallowable, that is allowable for you. How so? "I authorize..."

By the passage beginning, “Monks, they dwell in five kinds of lodgings,” the acceptance of a dwelling has been authorized. Furthermore, because only those allowable requisites (kappiyapaccaya) dependent upon that dwelling—such as robes and so forth—are to be used, the lodging, almsfood, medicinal requisites for the sick, and other equipment are all allowable and conformable to what is allowable for a monk.
Thus, [this matter] is established by correlating it with the Suttas, what is conformable to the Suttas, the tradition of the teachers, and one’s own reasoning.
On the contrary, just as the water of the Yamunā is [mixed] with the water of the Gaṅgā, a monastery together with its fields, lands, and so forth may be accepted even in a private capacity;
thus should the permissible and impermissible matters be viewed by those skilled in the Vinaya.
This is the common response of the Great Elders residing in Isinagara.

“And those people who, having conspired over heavy property, steal it, yet there is an abandonment of responsibility (dhuranikkhepa), and they have not committed an offense of defeat (pārājika)—this question was considered by the wise.
This question was stated with reference to a monk who steals land belonging to the Saṅgha;

for in that case, because there is an abandonment of responsibility toward the present Saṅgha, there is no theft since there is no abandonment of responsibility toward the Saṅgha of the four quarters. This...
There is deliberation regarding the boundary of profit (*lābha-sīmā*).

However, the village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*), town boundary (*nigama-sīmā*), and city boundary (*nagara-sīmā*) are indeed well known. Their specific distinction, however, should be understood as follows:
in whatever location there is only a marketplace (*āpaṇa*) and no enclosure wall, or where there is only an enclosure wall [and no marketplace], [that is the respective boundary].
This place is not a market; that which is called a village (*gāma*) is a location where there is indeed a village, but no markets or walls.
That place where there are both markets and enclosures of walls is called a town (*nigama*).

And that place where there are markets and it is also surrounded by walls is called a city (*nagara*). This place is called "having lords" (*nāgarika*) because of the meaning of the word: "those who have lords (*nāga*) are here," or [it refers to] kings.
Alternatively, it is called a "city" (*nagara*) because it is a place suitable for the residence of great ministers. However, in secular treatises, it is said:
"A wise man should behold the city, with its various divine shrines, palaces, shops, and mansions, and its royal highway beautifully adorned."
It has been stated. Thus, having understood the distinction between a village, a market town, and a city, the meaning of those terms should be understood as follows:

the village itself is the village boundary, the market town itself is the market town boundary, and the city itself is the city boundary. In that regard, monks, in a place where a boundary has not been formally authorized nor established, whatever village or market town one dwells in dependence upon—that [is the basis for the boundary] of that [place].
It has been authorized that "the village boundary of a village, or the town boundary of a town—this is there a common residence and a single *uposatha*";
thus, the entire area of the village is included in that location.

Furthermore, even if within the same village field a certain area is demarcated and the king gives it to someone, saying, "Let this be a separate village," that too constitutes a separate village boundary.
Therefore, both that [boundary] and the other—the natural boundary of villages, towns, and market towns—are indeed similar to a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*).
However, they do not receive the exemption from the offense of being separated from one’s three robes (*ticīvaravippavāsa*). On this point, others say:
"Just as King Pasenadi of Kosala and others gave [lands] to Pokkharasāti and others by pouring out the water of dedication (*dakkhiṇodaka*),"

"The boundary of a separate village is established only by what has been given as a *brahmadeyya* (a royal gift to Brahmins), not by mere extent, because [the donor] lacks authority over cutting or breaking [the land]. This should not be viewed in that way;

for since cutting and breaking belong to the king, the measure is determined solely by the boundaries set by those in authority according to worldly convention and designation, such as: "This area is the limit of this village."
If it were something that could be cut or broken, it would be reckoned as a kingdom, just like a king.

That village district must be the boundary of a city-kingdom (*nagararajja*), and not merely the boundary of a village; for this very reason, the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, states:
"In whatever extent of territory the village lords of that village receive tribute—that territory, whether it be small..."
"Or, if it is large, it is reckoned as being within the village boundary itself. The same principle applies to the boundaries of towns and market towns.
This is the investigation of the boundaries of villages, market towns, and cities.
As for what is called the "internal boundary": "Monks, in a forest that is devoid of a village, the area extending seven *abbhantara*s all around is [the internal boundary]."
"In this case, those who share the same communion and perform the uposatha together" refers to the so-called "internal boundary" (abbhantarasīma) which has been authorized.

Regarding "seven abbhantaras all around": if a bhikkhu dwells in a forest such as the Viñjhāṭavi wilderness, then from his standing place, there are seven abbhantaras to the east, seven abbhantaras to the west, and seven abbhantaras to the south.
"Seven *abbhantara*s to the north" means seven *abbhantara*s all around.
"Fourteen in depth" means fourteen *abbhantara*s from east to west, and likewise fourteen *abbhantara*s from south to north;
thus, by calculating fourteen times two, there are twenty-eight *abbhantara*s all around. And here, one *abbhantara* is twenty-eight...
It is one *hattha* in measure; therefore, within the seven *abbhantara*s to the east, it measures nine hundred and sixty *hattha*s.
Likewise for the south, north, and west. Adding all these together, it measures eight hundred and eighty-four *hattha*s.
However, by way of its circumference, it measures one thousand six hundred and seventy-six [units].
But when measured according to the natural standard:
“A dead staff is five cubits; twenty staffs are a *usabha*;
a cow is more than a *usabha*; four cows are a *yojana*.”
By way of the stated measurements for each individual part, when separated out, there are seventy-eight cubits and two additional spans within the twenty-eight internal sections.
When all twenty-eight internal sections are combined, the total is one hundred and fifty-six cubits and four additional spans.
However, by way of the circumference, it is two hundred and forty-four cubits and six additional spans; this is according to the measurement of an ox.
However, by way of diameter, it is fourteen *abbhantara*, two less than four *usabha*, and two *ratana*.
Combining all these together, within twenty-eight *abbhantara*, there are four *ratana* and seven *usabha* plus sixteen *ayana*.
But by way of circumference, there are six *ratana* and fourteen *ayana* in addition.

There are eleven cubits. This is the analysis according to its essential meaning (*sārato*). However, some, having imagined that the term "internal sound" (*abbhantarasadda*) refers to the measure of a cubit (*hattharatana*), say this:

because it is stated that for one standing in the middle, there are seven [cubits] on all sides and fourteen by way of depth, they calculate seven cubits to the east and seven cubits each to the south, north, and west; thus...
By penetration, they are fourteen cubits. Adding them all together, the "inner space" is twenty-eight cubits;
however, this is merely their opinion and should not be accepted as authoritative. Why? Because it is stated in the Commentary that there is one inner space of twenty-eight cubits therein.
If, according to their view, the entire inner space added together were twenty-eight cubits...
If it were so, it would have to be stated in the commentary: "In that context, 'interior' (abbhantara) measures twenty-eight cubits;
for one standing in the middle, there are fourteen on each side by way of a seven-fold penetration.
But this was not stated; therefore, it should be understood as being merely their own opinion. In this regard, the meaning here is as follows: "In that context..."
*“Tattha”* is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). *“Ekaṃ”* is a limit of enumeration.
*“Abbhantaraṃ”* is a designation for that which is delimited, or a demonstration of what is determined. *“Aṭṭhavīsatihatthappamāṇaṃ”* is a designation of the collection of phenomena to be delimited;
therein, among those seven *abbhantaras* on all sides, one is called an *abbhantara*, measuring twenty-eight cubits (*hattha*).
The meaning should be understood as "it becomes. Here, however, the number must be explained. That is twofold, by way of measurement (*parimāṇa*) and counting (*mīna*).
Among these, the number of measurement should be known as follows: four handfuls make one *kuḍuva*; four *kuḍuva*s make one *pattha*;
four *pattha*s make one *āḷhaka*; four *āḷhaka*s make one *doṇa*; and four *doṇa*s—
One *mānikā*. Four *mānikās* make one *khārī*. Twenty *khārikās* make one *vāha*.

That same amount is called one "cart" (*sakaṭa*), as stated in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, regarding the phrase "nine thousand *vāhas*," it is said:
four *muṭṭhis* make one *kuḍuva*; four *kuḍuvas* make one *pattha*; four *patthas* make one *āḷhaka*. Four...
"Four *āḷhakas* make one *doṇa*; four *doṇas* make one *mānikā*; four *mānikās* make one *khārī*.
Twenty *khāris* make one *vāha*, which is the same as one cart (*sakaṭa*)," so it is stated in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and other texts.

However, having stated that "in this context, they say two carts make one *vāha*," it is written [elsewhere] that by the local usage of the border regions, when measured, [it is] one hundred and sixty [measures].

Regarding "one *vāha*": when measuring the rice harvested by King Dhammāsoka from the *sūvakāhata* fields, they say it amounts to one hundred and twenty plus one according to the local currency (*paccantavohāra*).
The calculation for this measurement should be understood as follows:
"Thirty-six atoms (*paramāṇu*) are said to constitute a single minute particle (*aṇumatta*);..."
Thirty-six *aṇu*s are called one *tajjārī*.
Thirty-six full *tajjārī*s are the measure of a *rathareṇu* (chariot-dust).
And thirty-six *rathareṇu*s are called one *likkhā*.
Seven *likkhas* make one *ekūka*; seven *ekūkas* make a *dhaññamāsaka*.
Seven grains [of rice] make one finger-breadth (*aṅguli*); twelve finger-breadths make one span (*vidatthi*).
Two spans make one *ratana*; seven cubits (*hattha*) make one *yaṭṭhi*.
"Eight *vīsa-yaṭṭhis* make one *usabha*; eighty *usabhas* make one *gāvuta*;
four *gāvutas* are called a *yojana* of Mount Meru.

Because this has been stated, a single *raja-paramāṇu* (mote of dust) is extremely subtle, imperceptible to the eye; even the body [of a Buddha], though composed of solid rock, is like Sineru, the king of mountains.
Having been discarded, they departed. Thirty-six of those [atoms] make one *tajarita* atom;
thirty-six of those make one *rathareṇu*. Thirty-six of those make one *likkhā*; seven *likkhās* make one *ūkā*.
Seven *ūkās* make one grain (*dhañña*); seven grains make one finger-breadth (*aṅguli*); twelve finger-breadths make one span (*vidatthi*). Two spans make one cubit (*ratana*).
Seven *hatthas* make one *yaṭṭhi*; twenty *yaṭṭhis* make one *usabha*; eighty *usabhas* make one *gāvuta*. Four *gāvutas* are called a *yojana* of Mount Meru.
Therein, the *aṇuraja* (minute dust) is seen in the sunlight when it is struck by the wind through the gaps in winnowing baskets, walls, and so forth.
The *tajjārī* (dust raised by a cart), however, is seen on the right and left sides of cart tracks and the like. The *rathareṇu* (cart-dust), however...
It is seen in the places where she clings. The *likkhā*, however, is exceedingly coarse and manifest. This has been stated by way of the scale of Mount Meru. Furthermore:
"Ten hairs equal one sesame seed; six sesame seeds would equal a barley grain."
"Four barley-corns [make] one finger-breadth; fifteen [finger-breadths] make one foot," so it is said.

Ten hairs are called one sesame seed (*ekatila*). Six sesame seeds are called one barley-corn (*yava*). Four barley-corns are called one finger-breadth (*aṅguli*). Fifteen finger-breadths are called one foot (*pāda*). This was stated according to what is found in the three Vedas. Furthermore:
“Ten hairs make one sesame seed; six sesame seeds make one barley grain;
four barley grains make one finger-breadth; eight finger-breadths make one fist; three fists make one *ratana*.
Because it is stated thus, ten hairs are called one sesame seed. Six sesame seeds are called one barley grain. Four barley grains are one finger-breadth.
A span (*aṭṭhaṅgula*) is one fist (*ekāmuṭṭhi*). Three fists are one cubit (*ratana*). Five cubits are one staff (*odaṇḍa*).
Twenty staffs are one *usabha*. Eighty *usabhas* are one *gāvī*. Four *gāvīs* are one league (*yojana*); thus it has been said.
"Five hands are considered a staff, and twenty staffs are an *usabha*."
“Eighty oxen make a cow; four cows make a league (*yojana*).
This was stated according to the natural measure of a league. However, according to the league-measure of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), it is said:
“A staff is considered to be seven cubits long, and twenty staffs make an ox.”
It is said: "Eighty oxen and a cow [make one yojana], and four cows [make one yojana].
Furthermore:
"Ten hairs make one sesame seed; six sesame seeds make one barley grain."
Four *yavas* make one finger-breadth (*aṅguli*); eight finger-breadths make one fist (*muṭṭhi*); three fists make one *ratana*;
twenty-eight *ratanas* make one internal fathom (*abbhantara*). Thus it is said. For this very reason, he said:

"In that regard, one [fathom] is the measure of twenty-eight hands. And here, in the phrase "in a non-village" (*agāmake*), what is the meaning of the negative particle *a-*? For such is the function of the particle *a-*.
The letter *a* is seen in the following senses as they have been stated:
negation, increase, another meaning, similarity, opposition, censure, emptiness, absence, and smallness.

Thus, in such cases as "not having produced" (*ajanetvā*), it is seen in the sense of negation. [In the phrase] "states not subject to decline" (*aparihānīyā dhammā*), [it is seen in the sense of another meaning].

In such cases as "growth" (*vuddhi*), it signifies increase; in "O Venerable One, it is blameless" (*anavajjaṃ bhante*) and so forth, it signifies that state (*tabbhāva*); in "syllables" (*akkharā*) and so forth, it signifies another meaning (*aññattha*);

in "King Amaru" and so forth, it signifies similarity (*sadisa*); in "spotless" (*amala*) and so forth, it signifies opposition (*viruddha*); in "this brahmin is not excellent, he is not a practitioner of the holy life" (*aseṭṭho ayaṃ brāhmaṇo abrahmacārī*) and so forth, it signifies censure (*garahe*);

in "a non-village" (*agāma*) and so forth, it signifies emptiness (*suñña*); in "a woman without a husband" (*apatikāyaṃ itthī*) and so forth, it signifies separation (*virahe*); and in "then this... (*atha nāyaṃ*)... [and so on].
In such instances as "a maiden," the term refers to something small. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of being empty or solitary.

In its sense of emptiness (*suñña*), the meaning is "in a non-village" (*agāmaka*), that is, in a purely forested area devoid of people. Or, in its sense of solitude (*viraha*), the meaning should be understood as "in a non-village," that is, in a region separated from a village.
Precisely because of these senses of emptiness and solitude, by the word "non-village" (*agāmaka*), [the presence of] villages, rivers, lakes, ponds, and oceans is excluded.

Having excluded everything without exception— including the water below that supports the earth, the wind that supports the water, and the cloudless sky— as well as everything up to the Brahma-world above,
including all the celestial palaces (*vimānas*) of the Asuras, Yakkhas, Suras, and other space-dwelling deities and Brahmas,
these are all comprised within "the forest" (*arañña*). Furthermore, even in the spaces between rivers and oceans, a place where fishermen cannot reach is a "peninsula" (*dīpaka*).
Or even a mountain—it too is reckoned as being within the forest boundary.

Therefore, this seven-league boundary is obtainable even on a plain of earth in the midst of a purely wild forest where there are no humans, and even in the celestial realm among the palaces, the wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth.
On the earth, however, in whatever village territory, or wherever beneath the surface of the earth gold, gems, and so forth have been dug up—
That area which they are able to occupy is indeed village territory (*gāmakhettam*). Beyond that, it extends even as far as the water that supports the earth and into the cloudless sky.
Is it not the case that in the six celestial realms of the sense-sphere (*chakāmāvacara-devaloka*), there are also divine palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, villages, market towns, and so forth?
If so, why is it called "forest" (*arañña*)? It is because non-human beings (*amanussa*) or such creatures, being of a different species, do not constitute a village.
For this very reason it was said: "In a non-human forest. Regarding the animal realm as well, it is stated:

"Whether it be a nāga, or any other non-human species such as a supaṇṇa, a māṇavaka, and so forth—even including Sakka, the king of the devas—everyone belonging to the class of non-humans should be understood as 'gone to the animal realm' (tiracchānagata) in this context.
Therefore, a forest is a dwelling place for non-humans because they differ in species.
It should be understood. This concludes the investigation of the internal boundary (*abbhantarasīmā*).
Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*). In that regard: "Monks, all rivers are without boundaries;
the entire ocean is without boundaries; every natural lake is without boundaries. Whether it be a river, monks, or the ocean, or a natural lake..."
Or, that which is the range of a splash of water from a man of medium height all around—this is what is prescribed there as "the same community" and "a single uposatha";

this is called the *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (splash-of-water boundary). In that context, regarding the statement, "Monks, all rivers are *asīmā*," the vowel *a* in the word *asīmā* has the sense of "devoid of";
the meaning is that they are devoid of a bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*). [The formal act] consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation...
"Even though it has been announced" means that it is free from the boundary of formal binding. Alternatively, it has the sense of negation, meaning "not to be authorized.
Or it has the sense of completion, as in the case of the "dhammas of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*), where it means those who have completed their training after having trained;

thus, the meaning is that they have reached the culmination of the functions of both the non-boundary and the boundary. Even when authorized by announcing the words of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
It is said that even without being formally demarcated, by its very own nature, it is like a *baddhasīmā* (a formally established boundary), similar to a village boundary.
By this, it is shown that rivers, lakes, and oceans do not constitute the domain of a *baddhasīmā*.
Thus, having rejected the status of a *baddhasīmā* for rivers, oceans, and lakes through such statements as "Monks, all rivers are non-boundaries" (*sabbā bhikkhave nadī asīmā*), therein—

Regarding these rivers and so forth, which are established by worldly convention and for which no formal boundary has been fixed, the Blessed One—desiring to establish a delimitation of the boundary by means of sand and other materials in order to avoid the failure of a formal act of a group (*vaggakamma*)—said:

"Monks, in a river, or in the ocean, or in a lake, [the boundary is] that which is within the range of a splash of water all around a middle-sized man. In this context, "of a middle-sized man" means...
In the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, it is said regarding a man of medium strength: “by a man of medium strength.
If a carpenter were intended, it would have been stated as “by a carpenter,” but it was not so stated;
therefore, it is understood to mean “by a man of medium strength. For there are three kinds of men.
The supreme person, the intermediate person, and the ordinary person. Therein, the "supreme person" refers to the omniscient Blessed One.
For that Blessed One is the most excellent of all beings by virtue of his steadfastness, majesty, perfection, sovereignty, and so forth. Such indeed is the steadfastness (*thāma*) of the Tathāgata:
"The Kāḷāvaka, the Gaṅgeyya, the Paṇḍara, and the Tambapiṅgala;..."
“Gandhamaṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta.
This should be understood according to the strength of the ten elephant breeds mentioned there. In that context, “Kāḷāvaka” refers to the ordinary elephant breed;
the bodily strength of ten men is the strength of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. That of ten...
The strength of ten black elephants is equal to the strength of one Ganges elephant.
The strength of ten Ganges elephants is equal to the strength of one pale elephant. The strength of ten pale elephants is equal to the strength of one tawny elephant.
The strength of ten tawny elephants is equal to the strength of one reddish-brown elephant. The strength of ten reddish-brown elephants...
The strength of one [ordinary elephant] is the strength of a single scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*).
The strength of ten scent-elephants is the strength of a single auspicious elephant (*maṅgala*). The strength of ten auspicious elephants is the strength of a single golden elephant (*hema*).
The strength of ten golden elephants is the strength of a single Uposatha elephant. The strength of ten Uposatha elephants—
The strength of one *Chaddanta* elephant is equal to that of ten *Chaddanta* elephants; the strength of ten *Chaddanta* elephants is the bodily strength of one Tathāgata.
This very thing is also called "the strength reckoned as Nārāyaṇa. In this context, "nārā" refers to rays;
because many various kinds arise from it, it is "nārayana," which is the thunderbolt (*vajira*). Therefore, it is called "the strength reckoned as the thunderbolt."
This is the meaning: according to the calculation of ordinary elephants, this amounts to ten million elephants;
according to the calculation of men, it possesses the strength of ten billion men. This is the bodily power of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the determination of his powers such as sovereignty and so forth should be understood by following the respective suttas. A "middle-sized man" refers to a carpenter, for he [possesses the strength] of the Tathāgata...

Just as one attempting to measure Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, with a mustard seed would be unable to do so even by a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand [seeds], he would likewise be unable to count even a single toe of that [mountain].
Because he stands in the middle due to his greatness compared to an ordinary man, he is known as a "middle-man" (majjhimapurisa). For it is thus:
A *sugata-vidatthi* (the span of a well-gone one) is three *vidatthis* of a carpenter; by the hand of a carpenter, it is one and a half hands.
Likewise, a carpenter’s *vidatthi* is two *vidatthis* of an ordinary man; by the hand of an ordinary man, it is a full hand.
Thus, what is called a *sugata-vidatthi* is now three *vidatthis* of a medium-sized man, measured by the hand of a carpenter.
"It is one and a half cubits" is stated in the commentary on the training rule regarding the building of a hut (*kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada*).

Here, this [measure] is not intended as the "middle-sized man's" cubit. Why? Because in the very same training rule regarding the hut, it says "three cubits," which refers to three carpenter’s cubits.
Just as a bed that conforms to the standard measure is called a bed measuring nine spans of a natural *vidatthi*, so too here it is by the "middle-sized man's" cubit.
Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Instead of saying 'here,' it is said 'by a man of average strength.

A "normal man" (*pakatipurisa*) is one whose bodily strength is equal to that of ten men; as it is said, "the strength of one such man is the strength of a black calf-elephant"—this is what is meant by a "normal man.
In this regard, although some are possessed of merit, such as King Ajātasattu or Jīvaka Komārabhacca...
Women such as Visākhā, Migāramātā, and others possess the strength of five elephants;

yet they are not called "middle-sized men" (*majjhimapurisa*), but rather are simply "ordinary men" (*pakatipurisa*) who are distinguished as "special men" (*visesapurisa*) due to their possession of merit.
However, in this context, only the ordinary man whose physical strength is that of a middle-sized man is intended. "By the throwing of water" (*udakukkhepa*) means by means of splashing water.
It is delimited; for that very reason, it is said in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Mātikā*:
