"In the phrase ‘by the throwing of water’ (*udakukkhepena*), the ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. This is the meaning here:
among rivers, oceans, and lakes, that place which is delimited by the throwing of water all around from the center of a medium-sized man—this is what is meant there.

Regarding rivers and other such things established by worldly convention, when their boundaries have not been formally fixed, there may be doubt as to whether they constitute a common residence (*samānasaṃvāsa*) or a single *uposatha* area;

however, in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, it is stated: "the distance of a 'water-splash' all around for a man of medium stature" refers to that place delimited on all sides by the water-splash of a man of medium strength. In this regard, just as gamblers [do not stake against one another within the same gaming circle]...
They throw a wooden ball; likewise, one should take water or sand in the hand and throw it with all one's might by a man of medium stature.
Wherever the water or sand thus thrown falls, that is called "water-throwing" (*udakukkhepa*).
In this case, those who are equal therein share the same community and the same *uposatha*; this refers to those [boundaries] in rivers and so forth that are delimited by water-throwing.
Having established the meaning as "the boundary is both a common residence and a single Uposatha," this [boundary] is obtained only within these rivers and so forth,
not outside them; therefore, in the case of a river or a lake,

it extends over as much an area as is flooded by water during the four months of the normal rainy season, and in the case of the ocean, it extends to the place where the natural waves roll in and subside.

From that point onward, it is a *kappiya-bhūmi* (a place where food may be prepared). During times of drought or in the summer, even when rivers and lakes have dried up, that very spot remains a *kappiya-bhūmi*.
However, if they dig a well or construct a reservoir in a dried-up lake or pond, or if they cultivate crops there, that location becomes village territory (*gāma-khetta*).
As for what is called a *kappiya-bhūmi*, beyond that is the *udaka-ukkhēpa-sīmā* (the boundary determined by the splash of water).
"It does not go [far], it goes only within; therefore, starting from their inner boundary, the demarcation of the water-splash all around must be made"—so it is said.

However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, regarding the phrase "the water-splash all around for a man of medium height," it is explained that when the Saṅghas of four or more members perform separate formal acts (*kamma*) such as those requiring a quorum of four, [this measurement applies] to this river.

The teachers say that this was stated for the purpose of showing the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmā*), and also for the purpose of showing the delimitation of the separation from the three robes (*ticīvara-vippavāsa*);
it is like the demonstration of the delimitation of the seven-abhantara boundary. Therefore, it has been written:

"It is established that it is permissible to perform [the ceremony] within a river even in the absence of a delimitation by the throwing of water. In this context, the phrase "even in the absence of a delimitation by the throwing of water" refers to...

Either by the statement in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, “The site is demarcated on all sides by the throwing of water,” or by the statement in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, “The demarcation by the throwing of water should be made on all sides,” or [by the reasoning]: “For even there, the middle-sized man is not specified;
likewise, it is the throwing with the full force [of one’s strength],” or [as stated]: “It is for this very purpose [that the boundary is marked] by sand and so forth.”
This does not accord with either the words "delimiting the boundary" (*sīmaparicchindana*) or the words from the *Vimativinodanī*.

Furthermore, the author of the text, in order to avoid the censure of others, did not say "this is our own patience," but rather indicated other authors by saying "the teachers. Later, in the conclusion, he states:
"All of this should be accepted after careful investigation; having attended upon those of noble lineage, one should accept what is appropriate."
It has been stated, "The other [version] must be discarded"; therefore, it should be understood that this was written according to the opinion of other teachers.

Otherwise, the words of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) included in the three councils, as well as the statements of the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* and *Vimativinodanī*, would have to be defiled, the texts themselves would become mutually contradictory, and even the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the Blessed One would be undermined.
While it may be appropriate to adapt [the practice] according to the opinion of the disciples, the training rule (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Blessed One must not be defiled;
one must proceed exactly as it was prescribed. For he will say that even if a monk knows [the nature of the drink], drinking alcohol constitutes an offense of expiation (pācittiya);
however, for a novice (sāmaṇera), drinking while knowing [it is alcohol] results in a breach of virtue (sīlabheda), whereas drinking without knowing does not.

The reason for this should be sought therein; or rather, it need not be sought, because the formulation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is the domain of the Buddhas alone, and one must simply act in accordance with what has been prescribed. Therefore, "within an area reached by the splash of water" means:
either it is demarcated on all sides by the splash of water in accordance with the formulated training rule, or water is to be splashed [around it], or by the splash of water...
Whether it be a delimited boundary or one extending beyond it, the measurement of the limit by the throwing of water all around is indeed the authority of the Elder Dhammasaṅgāhaka;
for he was one who knew the Buddha’s intention. This statement, however, is neither a direct word of the Blessed One nor a word of the Elder Dhammasaṅgāhaka himself;
rather, it is [the definition]: "that which is the distance of the throwing of water all around for a man of medium height."
Since the teachers (ācariyā) state that this was said for the purpose of showing the boundary-delimitation— just as one shows the delimitation of a seven-fathom boundary within this river—
it is established that it is permissible to perform [the ceremony] within the river even in the absence of a water-splash boundary; thus,
neither the Elders who compiled the Dhamma nor the author of the manual have entered into this interpretation of the meaning.

[The opponent] has been refuted. Why? Because in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* included in the three councils, as well as in the *Sīlakkhandha-ṭīkā* which serves as its commentary, they write in many ways regarding the boundary of the water-sprinkling (*udakukkhepa-pariccheda*) alone, such as:
"delimited by the sprinkling of water," "water must be sprinkled," and "the boundary of the water-sprinkling must be made.
Therefore, even the Elder Theras who compiled the Dhamma [did so].
"It is understood that [the author] has not entered [the text]" means that even the author of the treatise, in order to avoid the censure of others, indicates another agent by saying "the teachers";
therefore, it is understood that the author of the treatise has also not entered [the text]. And this statement is the personal opinion of certain elders;
for such a personal opinion is indeed very weak, like one who attempts to measure Sineru, the king of mountains, with a mustard seed.

Who indeed could dare to defile the words of Mahākassapa, Yaśa, Moggaliputtatissa, and others—beginning with them—as well as their disciples and grand-disciples, the residents of the Mahāvihāra, when they explain the meaning of the training rule regarding the "throwing of water" (*udakukkhepa*) as prescribed by the Omniscient Buddha?

Furthermore, because the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and other such rites are weighty ceremonies and the very root of the Dispensation, one must remain respectful toward them. “Yaṃ... [text continues]”

Regarding the Blessed One’s prescription that “the boundary for a medium-sized man is the distance of a water-splashing all around,” the commentator of the Aṭṭhakathā—anticipating the objection as to whether the area reachable by a water-splash from a medium-sized man constitutes the water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), or whether it is by the act of splashing itself that the water-splashing boundary is established—says: “But how is the water to be splashed? and so forth. In this regard:
"How" is a question expressing a desire to speak; "how" means for what reason or by what means should water be thrown?
The meaning is that it should not be thrown in the manner of pouring water, but rather in the manner of throwing a clod of earth or a wooden ball.
Although "gamblers" is stated as a general term, just as in the expression "the lion sings his tail" or "the lion wags his tail," here it refers specifically to the wooden ball.
Because they are thrown in proximity to other sounds, it is understood that "players" refers to gamblers by way of meaning;

for the word *akkha* is conventionally established in the sense of gambling. "Wooden ball" (*dāruguḷa*) refers to a wooden artifact fashioned with a pointed tip and mounted on a spindle—this is the meaning here...
just as when dice-players, those gamblers, take a wooden ball in their hand.
Just as one might throw oneself down with all one's might while leaning forward as if displaying one's strength, in the same way,
a man of medium strength should take water or sand in his hand and, as if displaying his strength,
lean forward and throw it with all his might after walking around the perimeter of the assembly, whether [the person] is sitting or standing.
"In this way, wherever the mind—or water, or sand—falls, this is one 'water-splashing' (udakukkhepa)":

by means of this phrase, "this is one water-splashing," he shows the possibility of another water-splashing as well, because of the boundary (sīmantarika) that exists between two Saṅghas performing separate formal acts (kamma). For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*...

"But if two Saṅghas perform the Uposatha and other formal acts separately, another single 'water-sprinkling' (udakukkhepa) should be established for the purpose of defining the boundary between the two water-sprinklings," so it is said; and in the *Vimativinodanī* as well:
"Within that" means within that place delimited by the water-sprinkling, and not only within that [specific] one...

It is stated [in the *Sāratthadīpanī*]: "The statement that 'it is not permissible to stand within even a single splash of water beyond that' arises from a suspicion of the invalidation of the formal act (*kammakopa*) because the boundary of the water-splash is difficult to discern. However, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it says:

"By the phrase 'one standing outside that boundary, having left the reach of the hand (*hatthapāsa*), invalidates the act,' [it is meant that] one standing anywhere outside that boundary invalidates the act..."
Having stated, "He explains it as 'he does not provoke anger,'" he also rejected the statement from the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*;
that [rejection] should be understood as having been spoken with reference to a single communal assembly (*ekasaṅgha*).

And just as boundary-interstices (*sīmantarikā*) are established for the purpose of avoiding mutual confusion among partial boundaries (*khaṇḍasīmā*) that have been bound by dividing a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), even so is the village boundary by its own inherent nature.
"Furthermore, because rivers, oceans, and natural lakes possess an immense extent,

the Blessed One has permitted a water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) where the limit is naturally established by its own nature; nevertheless, just as with two fixed boundaries (*baddhasīmā*),
another splash of water must be placed between two water-splashing boundaries to serve as a boundary-intervener (*sīmantarika*) for the purpose of avoiding mutual confusion."

It has been stated: "The *baddhasīmā* (formal boundary) is with its defining marks (*sanimittā*); the *udakukkhepasīmā* (water-splashing boundary) is with the throwing of water (*saudakukkhepā*). A single water-splash should be regarded as being like a boundary-line (*sīmantarikā*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Vimativinodanī*:
"In this context, this rule for the boundary-line should be understood as established by way of conformity with the sutta that permits a boundary-line between two formal boundaries. In one [case]...
Furthermore, it should be understood that even if one person stands outside during an assembly of the Saṅgha, he does not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*).
For it is stated in the *Vimativinodanī* by the Blessed One, by way of an introductory narrative:

"For two contiguous villages with a common boundary that have established a formal boundary (*baddhasīmā*), there is mutual penetration and overlapping [of their boundaries] only when there is no intervening space between them, except for a boundary-interval (*sīmantarika*)."
Knowing that this place was indeed approved by the Blessed One, the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) have established the rule for the boundary-line (sīmantarikā) here as well.

For even in the case of dissimilar boundaries, it should be understood that a place becomes subject to division without a boundary-line only when it possesses two factors—namely, being situated within a single boundary and having a single common nature—and not when these are absent. Thus it is with rivers, oceans, and natural lakes.
Regarding the phrase "on all sides by the throwing of water": having shown the boundary by the throwing of water in accordance with the prescribed training rule (*sikkhāpada*),

he says "if it is not too long, starting from its source," and so forth, in order to show that even in a place where a river originates, there is complete suitability (*kappiya*) by its own nature— even without the throwing of water— just as there is within the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
In this context, "starting from the source" means starting from the upper part of that place where the river flows for a maximum of four months.
"As far as the mouth" means that here the very bank of the river is intended by the term "mouth.
"Everywhere" means that since there is no establishment of a water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) in any part of the river, it proceeds by means of the water-throw.
The *sīmā* is the water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*). "To be performed" (*karitabba*) refers to an act (*kamma*); it is derived from the verbal root *kṛ* (to do) with the suffix *-tabba*.

Regarding "performance" (*karaṇa*), it is a bodily application that is a modification of the air element produced by the seventh wholesome impulsive consciousness (*javana-citta*) in the mental-door process (*manodvāra-vīthi*).

By means of that bodily application, the act which is thrown forth and raised up is called *kamma* in the ultimate sense (*paramattha-vasena*). However, [in the conventional sense], it is [defined] as that which is reckoned as the bodily application...
The mind, through the expansion of the element of motion (*javāyodhātu*), originates only as a mass of eight aggregates that reach other locations.
"A boundary established by the throwing of water" (*udakukkhepasīmā*) refers to the formal act (*kamma*) regarding such a boundary;
the meaning here is that there is no rapid flow of a river at this place. This is the meaning: if the river is not very long—whether it be half a *yojana*, a *gāvuta*, or half a *gāvuta*— [...]*
Alternatively, starting from the point where the river begins its course and extending everywhere across the river’s location as far as its bank, the Saṅgha sits;

in that river location, because there is no other river remaining on all sides, there is no fear of a *vagga-kamma* (a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly), and thus there is no *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (water-throw boundary);
it is simply the river itself that constitutes the boundary—so it is stated in both the *Sāratthadīpanī* and the *Mātikāṭṭhakathāyalīnatthappakāsani*.

This very point is the established conclusion. However, in the *Vimativinodanī*, it is stated that where, in a small forest, there is no need to consider a seven-abhyantara boundary because there is no suspicion of a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act by an incomplete assembly) due to the presence of a large number of monks, the seven-abhyantara boundary does not arise there;
rather, only the forest boundary (*kevalāraññasīmā*) exists, and within that, the Saṅgha performs the formal act.
The same method applies to rivers and so forth; for it will be said:

"If a river is not very long, the Saṅgha sits everywhere from its source down to its mouth, and there is no need for the ritual of the water-splash boundary (udakukkhepasīmā)," and so on in both cases.
In whichever direction there is no space for seven *abbhantara*s or for the water-splash, [that is the limit].

In that case, how could there be measuring or throwing [of the boundary]? Since it would enter village fields and the like, the boundary would enter what is not a field, and thus the *atisīmā* (extra-boundary) would fail.

However, when a boundary arises through dependence, wherever it extends, the seven-fathom water-throw boundary (*sattabbhantara-udakukkhepa-sīmā*) is produced there of its own accord as complete. But wherever it does not extend, there—
It is stated that they arise only according to the measure of one's own field and not outside of it.

Furthermore, regarding this, because it is said, "By depending on the boundary (*sīmā*), the seven-cubit water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) itself arises complete," some explain the meaning as: "The water-throwing boundary arises by depending on the [other] boundary even without the water-throw.
This appears to be improper. Why? Because it contradicts the method of the canonical text (*pāḷinaya*).
This is because it contradicts the statement made later on, and because this statement might have been uttered by the Master for the purpose of clarifying the arguments of certain individuals. Why?
Because it does not harmonize with the statement spoken later, and because it conflicts with the words of the *Pāḷi*, the *Aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Ṭīkā*; we shall explain that further below.
Just as in the world, when one has not enclosed a fence, one says, "This is the place for the fence";

and just as when one has not plowed with the tip of a plow, one says, "This is the place for plowing"; and just as people making a site cut down trees with axes, hatchets, and so forth, saying, "This is the place where my axe fell";
and just as [one does] without having marked it with a line—

Nor can it be said, "This is my place for washing"; in the same way, without having splashed water or sand with the hand, one cannot say, "This is a single scoop of water," nor can it be called "the place where the water falls.
And here, two monks engage in this dispute in the *Vimativinodanī*: "In a small forest where there are large..."

Because there is no suspicion of a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly) due to the presence of monks, there is no need for a seven-abhyantara boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*) there;
consequently, a seven-abhyantara boundary does not arise in that case. Only a forest boundary (*kevalāraññasīmā*) is to be established there by the Saṅgha.
This same principle applies to rivers and so forth as well. For it will be said: "If a river is not very long, [the boundary] starts from its source... and so on.
"Until the Saṅgha is seated everywhere within the mouth-gate [of the hall], there is no need for the ritual of the water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*)," and so forth;

because it has been stated that "it should be understood that the water-sprinkling boundary and the seven-cubit boundary arise only when there is a dependence on a formal boundary (*sīmā*) for the purpose of avoiding a factional act (*vaggakamma*),
and not when there is none," [the boundary] exists even without the water-sprinkling, from the very edge of the assembly.
Since the water-throw boundary arises simultaneously with the expectation of the boundary starting from that point, there is no need at all for the water-throw;
therefore, they should be told: "O good men, do not speak thus, and do not misrepresent the excellent teacher.
This statement is merely a provisional word of the excellent teacher; furthermore, the excellent teacher will state his final decision later."
Your statement does not even accord with the words spoken in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* itself and in the *Sāratthadīpanī*;
furthermore, it does not cohere with the words spoken later in the *Vimativinodanī*. How can it be a statement of what is merely to be understood (*neyya*)?
[The passage reads: “When there is a dependence on the boundary... [etc. ...it will perish. Here, without the dependence on the boundary, there is the going on the path, bathing, and so forth.
For monks who have entered a forest or even a river and so forth, it does not arise at the very moment of entry; rather, if there is mindfulness regarding the boundary,
an internal boundary arises in accordance with the training rule prescribed as "seven *abbhantara*s all around in the forest," and in the case of rivers,
oceans, and lakes, it is "all around the water's edge for a man of medium height."
The water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) arises together with the water-splash in accordance with the prescribed training rule (*sikkhāpada*);

it does not arise without the water-splash—this is the meaning to be understood (*neyyattha*). "Not being non-existent" (*nāsatīti*): here, even the meaning of "by means of the water-splash" is not obtained.
And this being so, in the *Vimativinodanī* itself, it is stated again: "In those three, such as rivers and so forth, which are established by worldly convention (*lokavohāra*)."

The intention [of the author] is to show the delimitation of the "unbound boundary" (abaddhasīmā)—which is established by the terminology of the Dispensation—for the purpose of avoiding the invalidity of a formal act performed by a group (vagga-kamma) in cases where no boundary has been formally bound.
In the Canon, in passages such as "that which for a man of medium height," the term *udakukkhepa* refers to the place or location of water;
it is so called because water is thrown (*ukkhipeyyati*) there. This, then, is the meaning here.
The meaning [of the boundary] is established by way of connection with the words:

“Starting from the limit of the assembly, extending all around as far as the place where water thrown by a man of medium height falls—that delimited area is, in this context, another ‘water-throw boundary’ (udakukkhepasīmā) within rivers and the like, belonging to the same communal affiliation. This is identical in meaning to the words stated there.
Some indeed say that the boundary is produced only by measuring the interior on all sides and establishing a demarcation,
and not by itself; having rejected that view with the words "that should not be accepted," etc.,
and having shown the fault in measuring and throwing [the sand], he states the purpose of the act of throwing the sand and so forth for the measurement of the interior here.
And that [mention of] "seeing" is made for the purpose of showing the delimitation of the location where the self-arisen boundary (sayaṃjātasīmā) stands;
it is like the demonstration of throwing a clod or a stone to discern the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) and the house precinct (gharūpacāra).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "They either bind a boundary or establish a delimitation by the throw of water. Even when such a delimitation has been made, because of its origin...
Or [it might mean] that because it is impossible to know [the exact distance], one should recognize it as "thūla" (large) and stand in a place free from fear while remaining inside;
or that those who exclude others should send them to a very distant place free from fear.

Therefore, the arising of these seven-abbhantara and water-throw boundaries must be understood precisely by reference to the aforementioned boundary, and their disappearance occurs through the removal of that [reference].
"Our patience must be tested before it is accepted, or else another method more suitable than this should be sought," he said.
By these words of the teacher— namely, "It must be tested before it is accepted" and "Another method more suitable than this should be sought"—
he [the pupil] demonstrated both that this statement was merely his own opinion and that the teacher had not yet attained analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*).
This shows [the following]. Furthermore, this statement is not the word of the Blessed One, nor is it the word of the Elders who compiled the Dhamma;
it is not included in any of the three councils (saṅgīti), nor is it the teacher’s exposition of his own views in the commentary (aṭṭhakathā).

Therefore, it should not be regarded [as authoritative]. Even in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, in the section concerning this commentary, regarding the phrase "if the river is not too long," [it is stated that this is not the Buddha's word].

Regarding the statement that there is no formal act (*kamma*) for a water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*): because the entire river area is encompassed by the monks, there is no need for water-splashing since the river does not exist on all sides;
thus it is said, "Because the river does not exist on all sides, there is no purpose for water-splashing.
This is either by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or by way of logical implication (*atthāpatti*).
Or, when there is water on all sides of a river, the purpose of throwing water [to mark the boundary] exists;
the meaning is that it serves to avoid a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act by an incomplete assembly). This meaning is also found in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Mātikā*:
"It is said with reference to a sufficient space that 'the delimitation by the throwing of water should be made on all sides'; however, where this is not possible in a small stream, there..."

It is said: "In a suitable place, the boundary for the throwing of water should be established. By this statement, "the boundary for the throwing of water should be established," it is understood that the establishment of the boundary does not arise by its own nature alone, but only together with the act of throwing water in view of the boundary;
for otherwise, in the absence of a person acting as the establisher of the boundary for the throwing of water, how could there be a boundary for the throwing of water?

Therefore, the statement that "the *udakukkhepa*-boundary and the *sattabbhantara*-boundary arise only when there is a dependence on a formal boundary (*sīmā*) for the purpose of avoiding a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly), and not when there is none," appears to be mutually contradictory with the words spoken in both the *Sāratthadīpanī* and the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, in the *Vimativinodanī* itself it says: "But by a great flood, from a high place..."
It has been said: "By one falling into a place where the water is still, even a small or large mark that possesses the characteristics [of a boundary] must be established as if it were newly arisen;

here too, there is no requirement for the 'water-splashing' (udakukkhepa) in the case of a small [lake], but in the case of the ocean, the formal act (kamma) must be performed within the very limit of the water-splashing boundary, because it is difficult to purify [the area].
For this reason, this eminent teacher previously stated: "For the purpose of avoiding a factional act (vaggakamma)..."

Having stated, "When there is an expectation of a boundary, the *udakukkhepa-sattabbhantara-sīmā* (the boundary consisting of the distance of a stone's throw across water) arises, but not when it is absent," the Master subsequently says in his discourse, "In this case as well, there is no need for the act of throwing a stone across water," and so forth. Herein, the analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows:
it is called *udakukkhepa* because a stone is thrown (*ukkhipitvā khipīyati*) here after being thrown across the water; thus, it is the place where the water falls.
However, in the expression "kiccaṃ karaṇaṃ" (the performance of what is to be done), the suffix *ya* is applied to the verbal root *kṛ* (to do) with the prefix *sthā* (to stand).

As in the phrase, "Exertion (*ātappa*) is the duty (*kicca*) to be performed this very day," so too "the performance of the duty of water-sprinkling" (*udakukkhepakiccaṃ*) means the doing of the sprinkling of water.

Regarding the word "pana" in the phrase "samudde pana," the particle *pana* here has the sense of specification (*visesa-attha*); others say it has the sense of an alternative position (*pakkhantara-attha*). However, in the sense of specification, [it applies] to rivers and lakes (*nadījātassaresu*).

In large [bodies of water], it must be performed within the *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (the boundary defined by the splash of water) alone; however, in small ones—even in mere rivers or lakes—it may be performed [therein];
but in the ocean, specifically, it must be performed only within the *udakukkhepa-sīmā*. This is the specific meaning of the word (*sadda*).
"In every way" (*sabbathā*) means in every respect (*sabbena sabbaṃ*). Regarding the phrase "only within the *udakukkhepa-sīmā*," the particle *eva* here has the sense of restriction (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
The meaning that this formal act (kamma) must be performed only within a boundary defined by the splash of water (udakukkhepasīmā), and never within a boundary defined by the ocean,
is indeed logical. Furthermore, the meaning that it should be performed within a boundary of the splash of water in large rivers and lakes, but not in small rivers and lakes,
is obtained by implication from the distinction between the small and large nature of those rivers and lakes.

Regarding the objection, "Why are two [types of] boundaries not obtained in the ocean by way of the throwing of ocean water—namely, the 'river-born' and the 'lake-water-throwing'?"—the author, keeping this in mind, says:
"Because it is difficult to purify. In that context, "because it is difficult to purify" refers to the ocean.

The intention of the excellent teacher is this: for a monk who has entered the ocean due to its immense size, it is exceedingly difficult to perform either hand-clapping or the "making of the outer ocean" [as boundary markers];
therefore, in every way and entirely, the act must be performed only within the *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (the water-throwing boundary).
This applies provided there is a need for the boundary in order to avoid the invalidity of a formal act (*vaggakamma*) performed by an incomplete assembly.

If the water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) were to arise [in the ocean], then, when a multitude of monks has descended into the sea, one would have to cast them outside the reach of the hand;
and since that would be difficult to accomplish, even the causal phrase [stating the reason for the boundary] would become meaningless.
But it cannot be said that this is so; therefore, it is known that "the purpose of the water-splashing is to prevent a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly)."

Furthermore, according to the intention of those teachers, if they were to desire, "We shall not perform [the formal act] within the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), but only in the ocean itself," how would they be able to do so?

Therefore, according to their opinion, since the water-throw boundary occurs simultaneously with the expectation of a boundary, a water-throw boundary would exist in every place one goes; and this being the case—

Furthermore, the statement, “In the ocean, however, the formal act (kamma) must be performed only within the boundary defined by the splash of water, because it is difficult to purify [the area] beyond that,” would likewise be rendered meaningless; and if one were to say:

“…the words beginning with ‘In the ocean, however’ were spoken by the venerable teacher with reference to the fact that a boundary for the entire ocean cannot be obtained”—even so, this should not be said. Why?
And if such a meaning were intended, it would have been necessary to state: "But in the case of the ocean, a boundary is obtained everywhere up to the high-water mark," yet it was not stated thus.
Alternatively, even when the meaning of a word is analyzed according to its context and other factors, there remains a contradiction:
how is it that when one says, "Bring the cow with the calf," the word understood is "cow" (gāvī) by virtue of association?
It is not a mare. Just as when it is said, "a cow that has recently calved," one understands it to be a cow and not a mare,
so too here— since the quality of not being excessively long, which would have to be excluded by the word "only" (*eva*), cannot be found in a river as it is in the ocean—
it should not be stated with the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) that "the ritual act must be performed in the ocean exclusively within the boundary of the water-splash."
It may be so; for indeed, when it is said, "a cow with a calf" or "a cow without a calf," one understands it to be a cow (*gāvī*), not a mare (*vaḷavā*).
And as for a mare, because her birth canal is excessively narrow, she is unable to give birth;
rather, when the fetus has matured, she takes the noble colt by tearing open her belly. Thus...
They die within a single womb; therefore, it is not appropriate to say "a mare with a foal" or "without a foal.

In the same way, since [the ocean] is never found even in an ocean that is not excessively long, it is certainly not appropriate for one who is turning [the discussion] back to refer to it by means of the word "only" (*eva*), as in:
"But in the ocean, the ritual act must be performed exclusively within the water-limit (*udakukkhepasīmā*)."
Therefore, one must conclude that the boundary arises by means of the throwing of water; thus it was said:
"And if such a purpose were intended, then it might be said that in the case of the ocean, only a boundary defined by the throwing of water would be possible, yet it was not so stated.
From this it is understood that sand and other materials are thrown for the purpose of avoiding a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly (vaggakamma).
Furthermore, in the *Vimativinodanī* itself, in the section of the commentary on this passage—"It is not permitted to perform [the formal act] on a boat that is moving. Why?

Because the boundary (*sīmā*) consists merely of the splash of water, and the boat quickly passes beyond it; thus, there would be a motion (*ñatti*) in one boundary and the proclamation (*anusāvanā*) in another"—the text states:
"by the phrase 'quickly passes beyond,' [it means] without having passed beyond that [boundary]."

This shows that it is permissible to perform [the formal act] only for one who is within the boundary. For it is precisely for this purpose that the delimitation of the boundary is made by means of sand and so forth;
otherwise, there would be the suspicion of a violation of the procedure (*kammakopa*) as to whether or not one has moved outside the boundary.
Regarding "another proclamation," the Master of Teachers stated: "It is the proclamation for a river-boundary alone. If, with regard to such a [river-boundary], together with oneself...

If a water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) were to arise by its own inherent nature (*sabhāvena*), then in every place where a boat has gone, a water-splashing boundary would arise surrounding it on all sides like a hall.
Furthermore, when it arises, one would have to say that it is the proclamation (*anusāvanā*) of another water-splashing boundary, yet this has not been stated; moreover—
If one were to say, "The expectation of the boundary exists only at the place where it was first crossed, and not at every place subsequently traversed," that statement is also entirely illogical.
Why? Because until the formal act (*kamma*) is completed, it is impossible to proceed without the expectation of the boundary;

therefore, it is understood that for the purpose of avoiding a *vaggakamma* (an incomplete or invalid assembly), the casting of water (*udakukkhepa*) is unnecessary, and the boundary is established together with the expectation itself.
One must reach the conclusion that, by its very nature, a water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) does not arise [on a moving vessel].
Therefore, those performing an act (*kamma*) on a boat should do so having made the boat very stable and rendered it immovable.

In the *Sāratthadīpanī* as well, regarding the statement "it is not permissible to perform [an act] on a moving boat," it is explained that this refers to a boat turning around without crossing over the water-splash boundary.
"It should be understood that it is proper to do so. And furthermore, one might say: "As long as the assembly increases, the boundary also increases;

because it is stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* that 'the measure is only the splash of water from the edge of the assembly,' the [boundary] increasing by way of the assembly increases even without the splashing of water, just like the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*)."
"Therefore, there is no purpose whatsoever in the throwing of water. Now, this is the meaning here:

This so-called "water-throw boundary" (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) increases by way of expansion (*parisavasena*), whereas an established boundary (*baddha-sīmā*) increases by way of aggregation (*samūhavasena*).
Why must the throwing of water be performed from the edge of the assembly when it is increasing by way of expansion?
Others say as follows: "In the past, the throwing of water alone was the measure; there is no further need for the act of throwing water.
This is like the formal ritual (kammavācā) for the giving of the robe when the kaṭhina has been spread; for at the time of giving the robe when the kaṭhina is spread, only one single ritual is valid.
Once the kaṭhina has been spread, even after receiving another excellent robe, there is no further need for the ritual act of giving."
"There is none"—in this case as well, they say that the previous limit of the water-sprinkling alone is the measure, and there is no further need for the water-sprinkling;
thinking it to be like a precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), they speak thus.

For in the case of a precinct boundary, the place where a man sits is itself increased by the status of being a precinct boundary; but here, it is increased only from the edge of the assembly by the measure of the water-sprinkling.
It is not accomplished without the throwing of water. But how is the water to be thrown?
Just as dice-players throw a wooden ball, so one should take either water or sand in the hand and throw it with all the strength of a man of medium build;
the area where the water or sand thus thrown falls is one [boundary].
They are said to "contradict" the commentarial statement: "the throwing of water. If one asks, "How so?

it is because those who claim that "kamma alone performs the act of kamma-making and there are no wardens of hell" are, as it were, contradicting the *Devadūta Sutta*, which states: "There are, monks, wardens of hell in hell.
And if one should say this: "Those [actions] which succeed along with the throwing of water..."

The intention is that even if a thousand monks remain, from the outer limit of the space they occupy, a boundary of seven *abbhantara*s arises spontaneously along with the expectation of a boundary for the purpose of avoiding a *vagga-kamma* (a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly) among the monks;
thus, they are "of common communion. However, in a small forest where—

They indeed contradict the statement made in the *Vimativinodanī*, which says: "Because there is no suspicion of a *vaggakamma* (an illegal act performed by an incomplete assembly) due to the presence of monks [within the boundary], there is no need to refer to a seven-abbhantara boundary;

in that case, a seven-abbhantara boundary does not arise, and the Saṅgha must perform the formal act (*kamma*) solely within the forest boundary (*araññasīmā*). This same principle applies to rivers and so forth as well."
That is not so; therefore, there is no loss for us, and thus there is indeed no contradiction whatsoever in our position. Why is that?
Because these two verbal formulations are unrelated, possessing different characteristics and different scopes. How are the verbal formulations unrelated?
Just as, in the forest, a "seven-abhyantara" boundary does not arise there, but only the forest itself [is established].

It is said: just as one does not say, "The Saṅgha sits everywhere even in a river, so that a water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) does not arise," but rather says, "There is no formal act (*kamma*) involving a water-throwing boundary," this is stated by way of referring to the action itself.
[The question is: What is the formal act to be performed? It is the throwing. Even in this way, the phrasing of the words remains disconnected. "[For the purpose of avoiding a factional act]... etc."

Regarding the statement, "The water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) arises when there is a seven-fathom boundary (*sattabbhantarasīmā*), not when it is absent," the meaning of "not when it is absent" (*nāsatī*) is indeed appropriate even as "even without the water-splashing [boundary].

Why? Because by the phrase "only when there is a regard for the boundary" (*sīmāpekkhāya sati eva*), the meaning "it does not arise when there is no regard for the boundary" is appropriate according to the method of positive concomitance (*anulomanaya*). Some, however, [interpret] "within a fathom on all sides... [as follows].
The claim that "a boundary arises only through the act of delimitation, not by itself" should not be accepted. For if...
[as follows]... just as it is here, so too with the water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) in rivers and the like;

for even there, a "middle-sized man" is not known, since they throw [the water] with all their might—by this statement also, [the boundary is established] by the water-throwing of the excellent teacher.
The intention is understood to be that the *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (water-throw boundary) arises only when there is a perception of a boundary, and not when it is absent.

How is it that they have different characteristics? Although the village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*) and the seven-abhantara *udakukkhepa-sīmā* are identical in being unbound boundaries (*abaddha-sīmā*), they are not identical in their specific characteristics;
for it is said: "Monks, in a boundary that has not been formally resolved (*asammatā*) and has not been established..."
"In whatever village or town one dwells in dependence upon, the boundary of that village or the boundary of that town—this is here the common residence and the single *uposatha*.
In this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), every portion of a village area, whether small or large, is authorized as the "village boundary" (*gāmasīmā*);
it is not like the seven-abhyantara (*sattabbhantara*) boundary.

The area within the boundary that is permitted by the throwing of a clod of earth all around is not, however, permitted as "forest boundary" for the forest in which one dwells, even if it is a non-village wilderness.

Likewise, in the case of rivers, oceans, and lakes, just as with the village boundary, the entire area of the river, ocean, or lake is not permitted as "river, ocean, or lake boundary. It is exactly thus that [the interior] is not permitted.

Likewise, just as in the case of the internal boundary (*abbhantarasīmā*), it has not been authorized that [the boundary] extends seven *abbhantara*s all around; thus, these village boundaries and water-sprinkling boundaries (*udakukkhepasīmā*) have different characteristics.
Therefore, according to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the Blessed One, whether small or large, every portion of a village area constitutes a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*).
Regarding the seven-*abbhantara* boundary as well, [it is defined as] "seven *abbhantara*s all around."
"In accordance with the training rule (sikkhāpada) that has been prescribed, the seven-fathom boundary (sattabbhantara-sīmā) arises by itself together with the intention for a boundary.
However, any deliberation regarding measuring or non-measuring is indeed useless;

likewise, for the water-sprinkling boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā), it arises together with the water-sprinkling in accordance with the prescribed training rule: "the water-sprinkling all around a man of medium height."
There is no purpose in deliberating over the tossing and non-tossing [of the boundary]. How so? The seven-intermediate-space boundary has the forest as its domain;
the water-throw boundary has rivers, oceans, and lakes as its domain. Thus, these—the village boundary, the seven-intermediate-space boundary, and the water-throw boundary—have distinct domains.
Therefore, even when it is said, "The same principle applies to rivers and so forth," [this is stated] with reference to the seven-intermediate-space boundary.

Just as the boundary of seven *abbhantara*s arises simultaneously with its own inherent nature, so too, in dependence upon the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), the water-throw boundary arises precisely at the moment the water is thrown, for the purpose of avoiding a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly (*vaggakamma*); it does not arise later.
Therefore, no formal determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*) need be made. But is it not stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* that within the limit of the enclosure, the handspan (*hatthapāsa*)...?

If it is argued that this does not contradict the statement found in all the *Aṭṭhakathās*—namely, "Even one who has left [the boundary] but remains outside the demarcation, provided he does not exceed another demarcation of the same size, still commits an offense"—that is not so.
For in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "But if two Saṅghas perform the Uposatha and other rites separately..."

"Between two water-sprinkling boundaries (udakukkhepa), another single water-sprinkling boundary must be established for the sake of the precinct (upacāra)," because it is stated that the two Saṅghas have separate authority to perform the formal acts (kamma). Also, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"In this regard, even if one stands without overstepping another boundary of exactly the same extent, one still invalidates the act; this [point] is found neither in the Pāḷi..."

This is not found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. If this were said with the intention that—because it has been stated in the context of two Saṅghas performing separate formal acts such as the Uposatha—that a Saṅgha standing outside the water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepa*) commits a failure of the act (*kamma*) due to the possibility of a breach of the boundary (*sīmāsambheda*) when performing the Uposatha and so forth without crossing over to another water-sprinkling boundary; [then it would be so].
If this were so, it would be logical; for that very reason, in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Mātikā*, it is stated: "There is another section of exactly that same size:
even one who does not cross the second *udakukkhepa* (water-throw) boundary incurs an offense. Why?

Because there is a 'conflict of boundaries' (*sīmāsambheda*) since his own *udakukkhepa* boundary has encompassed the *udakukkhepa* boundary of others; therefore, he incurs an offense. This [is what is meant].
It should be understood that this was stated with the intention: "the conclusion in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Since in all the commentaries the breaking of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*) is not desired, it is therefore said that between one's own water-sprinkling limit (*udakukkhepapariccheda*) and those of others, another water-sprinkling limit must be established for the purpose of a boundary-line (*sīmantarikatthāya*). However, others here [hold] otherwise.
Having stated, "They proliferate; that should not be grasped," it was rejected.

Furthermore, by the statement in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, "One standing outside the boundary [of the area] defined as 'within arm's reach' spoils the legal act (kamma)," it is demonstrated that one standing anywhere outside that boundary does not spoil the act.
Thus, even in a single assembly of the Saṅgha, [one standing] elsewhere outside the boundary...
It should be understood that even if one stands without exceeding that very boundary, one does not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*);

this point is established for the sake of strengthening the argument in the *Sāratthadīpanī* itself. Furthermore, another splashing of water is performed as a mark of courtesy so that the intermediate space between the boundaries (*sīmantarika*)—measured by the extent of the water-splash—is more easily discernible, and so that no suspicion of the overlapping of boundaries (*sīmāsambheda*) might arise.

"It should be established for the purpose of marking the boundary-line," so it was said. However, it is indeed permissible to establish as much as is necessary so that there is no overlapping of boundaries;
therefore the ancients said: "It is permissible to establish even as much as does not cause a confusion of boundaries, but a very small amount is not permissible.
This is because the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) may increase by way of its surrounding extent.
There might be a suspicion of a confusion of boundaries; it was stated precisely for the purpose of preventing that.
Having repeatedly examined the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, the Ṭīkā, the Vimati, and so forth, may the preeminent among poets reflect [upon this].
This concludes here the investigation regarding the water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*).
As for the "district boundary" (*janapadasīmā*): it refers to each individual region within the dominion of a single king, inhabited by great ministers; such a place is called a district boundary.
The "kingdom boundary" (*raṭṭhasīmā*) refers to the sixteen great districts, such as Kāsi, Kosala, and so forth. They are also known as the "sixteen great cities."
As for "name": therein, the sixteen great provinces (mahājanapada) are as follows:

the kingdom of Aṅga, the kingdom of Magadha, the kingdom of Kosala, the kingdom of Vajji, the kingdom of Cetī, the kingdom of Kuru, the kingdom of Pañcāla, the kingdom of Majjha, the kingdom of Surasena, the kingdom of Assaka, the kingdom of Avanti, the kingdom of Gandhāra, the kingdom of Malla, and the kingdom of Kamboja. These are they.
The "sixteen great provinces" (soḷasa-mahājanapadāni) are as follows. These sixteen great provinces existed specifically within the Middle Country (majjhima-padesa);

however, there were many other "great kingdoms" (mahā-raṭṭha), such as the Sunāparanta kingdom and others. Likewise, in the border regions, there were indeed many various kinds of great kingdoms, such as Rāmañña and so forth;
all of these are also called "provincial boundaries" (raṭṭha-sīmā). However, in the worldly treatises (lokiya-sattha)...
That region where the four castes—Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas—dwell is called a "Great Kingdom" (mahāraṭṭha).
For it has been said by the ancients:
"In that region where the four castes do not exist..."
Thus the region of the Mlecchas has been described; beyond that is the Land of Merit (Puññabhūmi).
What is called the "kingdom boundary" (rajjasīmā) is the area where the commands of a single king prevail; this is what is called the kingdom boundary.
What is called the "island boundary" (dīpasīmā) refers to islands situated either in the midst of the ocean or in the middle of a river; these are called island boundaries. Furthermore, in which...
In the island of Dīpa, villages exist; it is reckoned as being within the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*). For it will be said:
"If they dig a pond or a reservoir in a dried-up lake, or cultivate a crop, that place becomes the domain of the village (*gāmakhetta*).
As for what is called the "world-system boundary" (*cakkavāḷasīmā*), it measures one million two hundred and three thousand four hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
As for its circumference:
“All together it is one hundred thousand,
thirty-six thousand, and four hundred and fifty.”
It is said that one world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) is called the world-system boundary (*cakkavāḷasīmā*). Thus, the boundary is of fifteen kinds.

In this regard, whatever boundary a person possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*) performs a formal act of the Saṅgha, such as the Uposatha, within, the monks who have gone there are entitled to give their consent (*chanda*) for the purpose of either extending the hand-measure (*hatthapāsa*) or for the establishment of an external boundary. Consent is required from those who are eligible to give it.

The criterion is simply whether one would be able to fetch [the materials] and perform [the rite]. With reference to individuals lacking supernormal powers who are unable to do so, a boundary of seven *abbhantara*s on all sides was authorized in a very large forest.
In that case, the boundary of seven *abbhantara*s on all sides arises by its own inherent nature along with the expectation of the boundary;
likewise, it is the same for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes for a person of medium stature.
A water-sprinkling boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) extending all around a person was authorized;

even there, for the sake of avoiding a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly (*vaggakamma*), a water-sprinkling boundary arises in dependence upon that [person] along with the water-sprinkling itself.

Likewise, for the sake of avoiding a formal act performed by an incomplete assembly, a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*) was authorized for villages, market towns, districts, cities, kingdoms, and realms. Beyond those, however, are the village boundary, the seven-abhantara boundary, and the water-sprinkling boundary.
By virtue of the method of conforming to the *nuññāta-sutta* (the "authorized" discourse), having cleared the monks who have gone here and there among small villages,
market towns, districts, and cities, and having brought the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it, the formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha, such as the Uposatha,
must indeed be performed with the approval of a harmonious Saṅgha; likewise, this applies even in small forests, by rivers, and at lakes, as one pleases.
The formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the Uposatha, must indeed be performed.

Thus, although there is no difference in terms of the characteristic of being demarcated, they are twofold according to whether they are "bound" or "unbound. According to their subdivisions, they are fifteenfold;

however, by way of their specific forms, they are: the broken boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), the boundary of common affiliation (samānasaṃvāsasīmā), the boundary of non-separation (avippavāsasīmā), and the boundary for acquisitions (lābhasīmā).
The village boundary; the town boundary, the city boundary, the inner boundary, the forest boundary, the water-throw boundary, the river boundary, the lake boundary,
the ocean boundary, the district boundary, the kingdom boundary, the realm boundary, the island boundary, and the world-system boundary—
having abandoned the characteristics of failure regarding these nineteen types of boundaries, this treatise named *Sīmavisodhanī*, which elucidates the characteristics of success, is completed.
Thus:
"I shall compose this work called the *Sīmavisodhanī*, compiled from various texts;
may the virtuous, the preeminent among poets, listen to it."
Having plunged into all of that— the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā,
the Mātikā, and the Padabhājaniya— again and again and without exception, [he examined] his own works on the Abhidhamma and the various sections of the Ṭīkās and Gaṇṭhis.
"Having made everything without exception from the *Vinicchaya*, the *Vimati*, and the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* concordant together,
this commentary has been composed to delight those who possess discerning vision."
The meaning of these verse lines has been fully explained. The discussion on the perfection of the boundary is concluded. Regarding the perfection of the assembly:
having excluded the twenty-one persons who should be avoided, [the Saṅgha] now proceeds by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*).

When fully ordained monks are seated without having left the reach of one another’s hands—starting from a group of five in border regions and starting from a group of ten in central regions—this is called "perfection of the assembly.
In this regard, there are twenty-one persons to be excluded, based on the statement: "Monks, [one should not confer ordination] from an assembly that stands together."

The nun, the trainee (sikkhamānā), the male novice (sāmaṇera), the female novice (sāmaṇerī), one who has renounced the training, one who has committed an offense involving defeat (antimavatthu), one suspended for not seeing an offense, one suspended for not making amends for an offense, and one with an evil view— these were mentioned below by way of the passage beginning: "Monks, the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in an assembly where a nun is seated."
The meaning is that those who have been suspended for non-renunciation, a paṇḍaka, one living in communion by theft, one who has gone over to another sect,
an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, a defiler of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic, one who has shed blood [of a Buddha], and one with both sexual organs—
these sit by virtue of being excluded from the boundary (sīmā). If they are within arm’s reach...

Or they may be within the same boundary; if, excluding those [offenders], a group consisting of at least five regular monks (pakatatta) remains seated without relinquishing hand-contact, the performing Saṅgha is blameworthy, yet the legal act (kamma) does not fail. Why? Because it lacks the required quorum.
Others, however, say this: because one who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu) is not mentioned among those "not to be saluted" (avandanīya), therefore, for one who lies down with him...
Because there is no offense of sleeping together and because that acceptance [of the robe] has been abandoned, it is understood that this [latter case] alone is more appropriate;
nevertheless, one should be saluted as long as he continues to claim the status of a bhikkhu.
However, when he claims, "I am no longer a samaṇa," then he is not to be saluted—this distinction should be understood here. Regarding one who has committed an ultimate offense:
For the status of a bhikkhu belongs only to one who claims the status of a bhikkhu, and not beyond that.
Since it is stated in the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada* and the *Sāratthadīpanī* that one who does not claim the status of a bhikkhu belongs to the side of those not fully ordained,
a bhikkhu who has previously committed an *antimavatthu* (an offense involving defeat) may, without even knowing his own case, [perform an act] together with a group of five bhikkhus.
To say that "the Saṅgha performing a formal act such as the Uposatha is blameless, and the act itself is not invalid," is merely their own opinion. Why?
Because even though there is no offense regarding sharing a sleeping place [with him], it is because his status as a monk is established by the perception of him as a monk;
and because he is trusted as a "monk" in that person regarding the acceptance and the cultivation [of requisites], there is also the offense of sharing a sleeping place with that person.

There is no offense; and the acceptance [of the act] is valid. Since even among the twenty-one persons who should be avoided, there is no such deliberation [regarding their status], a group of five monks performing a formal act of the Saṅgha—such as the Uposatha—in their company constitutes a "performing Saṅgha" that is blameless provided it acts unintentionally.
However, it is our view that the formal act itself becomes invalid; therefore, one should certainly seek out someone more suitable than this.
The discussion on the perfection of the assembly is concluded.
Thus, it is called "fivefold" because it is endowed with five factors by way of the subject matter, the motion, the proclamation, the boundary, and the perfection of the assembly;

or alternatively, it is so called because it has attained a superior state through a unanimous Saṅgha performing a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations, which is unshakeable and fit for its purpose.
Or rather, because it is obtained through two causes—the motion (ñatti) and the fourth [proclamation]—the state of full ordination (upasampadā) is exceedingly rare.
Thus, the meaning of these three terms—"the arising of a Buddha" (buddhuppāda), "going forth" (pabbajjā), and "full ordination" (upasampadā)—has indeed been stated.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sīmavisodhana* composed by the Elder Sāgarabuddhi.
The First Chapter: The Section on Ordination (Upasampadākaṇḍa).
2. The Section on the Destruction of the Aeon (Kappavināsakaṇḍa).
Now follows the discourse on the rarity of the arising of a Buddha.
“The Buddha is rare in the world, and the hearing of the True Dhamma is rare;
the Saṅgha is rare in the world, and true persons are rare.
The turn has come for the commentary on this verse. In this regard, within this world of sentient beings or the world of space, the Omniscient, Perfectly Enlightened One—
For this world is indeed difficult to understand; it is threefold, consisting of the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), the world of beings (*satta-loka*), and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*).

Their success and failure should be understood in this way. In that context, the "world of beings" (*satta-loka*) is to be understood according to the etymological definition: "it breaks up and disintegrates" (*lujjati palujjati*), thus it is called "the world" (*loka*).

The "world of space" (*okāsa-loka*) is to be understood according to the etymological definition: "the groups of beings find their footing and establish themselves therein" (*lokenti patiṭṭhahanti ettha sattanikāyā*); thus it is called "the world" (*loka*).
It should be understood thus: for beings enter into it, and therefore it is called "space" (*okāsa*).

By way of plane, that space is fourfold: the plane of the states of misery, the plane of the sense-sphere happy destinies, the plane of the fine-material sphere, and the plane of the immaterial sphere.
Among these, hell, the animal womb, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras are called the four planes of the states of misery. Humans, the deities of the Four Great Kings, ...

The thirty-three gods (Tāvatiṃsa), the Yāma gods, the Tusita gods, the Nimmānarati gods, and the Paranimmitavasavatti gods—thus there are seven kinds of planes of fortunate rebirth in the sense-sphere.
Because craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā) ranges over these eleven types [of beings] as well, it is called the "sense-sphere plane" (kāmāvacarabhūmi) in the sense of the word’s derivation.
The Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārisajja), the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita), and the Great Brahmās (Mahābrahmā) constitute the plane of the first jhāna; this is [the realm] of fire.
The realm encompassed by water consists of the Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara heavens;
this is the second jhāna plane. The realm encompassed by air consists of the Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha heavens; this is the third jhāna plane.
We shall describe their destruction later. [Also included are] the Vehapphala and Asaññasatta realms.
The Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) and the plane of the fourth jhāna constitute the sixteenfold form-sphere plane (*rūpāvacara-bhūmi*).
The Pure Abode plane itself is fivefold: the Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭha.

The fourfold [formless-sphere plane] consists of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is the formless plane (*arūpabhūmi*). Up to this point, the thirty-one-fold plane is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because the categories of beings (*sattanikāya*) descend into it;
in the sense of being a locus, it is called "space" (*okāsa*). Among these, the eight great hells are called the "plane of misery" (*apāyabhūmi*).
For animals, the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), and the host of asuras, there is no separate plane; they exist within the human plane itself.
In certain places, such as forests and woodlands, they dwell in fixed residences; that very location is their ground.
Forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the human realm is the ground of the Four Great Kings (*Cātumahārājika*), measuring the same as Yugandhara and forming the fifth terrace of Sineru.
Above that, forty-two thousand *yojanas* is the summit of Sineru, the ground of the Thirty-three Gods (*Tāvatiṃsa*). Above that, [another] forty-two thousand *yojanas*...
The station of the Yāma devas is their ground. Following this method, it extends up to the ground of the Vasavatti devas at thirty-two thousand yojanas.
Therefore, from the human world up to the ground of the Vasavatti devas, there are two hundred and fifty-two thousand yojanas; thus it is said.
From the human realm up to the plane of the Vasavatti gods,
the measurement in terms of *yojanas* is two hundred thousand, fifty-nine million, and two thousand.
“Enumeration refers to the levels; thus has the number been declared.
Beyond that, the three classes of deities beginning with the Brahmapārisajjā dwell on a level plane five hundred and fifty thousand and eight thousand yojanas from the Brahmā world.
The deities of the second and third levels also dwell on level planes of those same dimensions.
On the fourth plane, however, the Vehapphalas and the non-percipient beings reside on a level ground of that same extent.

The Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) likewise reside one above the other on grounds of their respective extents. The four formless planes (Arūpabhūmi) also reside one above the other on grounds of their respective extents.
From this point, from the human realm up to the peak of existence (Bhavagga), there are seven crores and eighteen lakhs of yojanas.
And there are five nahutas and sixty thousand; therefore this is said by the ancients:
"A great rock, fallen from the lowest Brahma-world, rises forty-eight [yojanas] in a single day and night."
The earth [below] extends for thousands of yojanas over four months;
according to the measurement thus stated, that is the lowest earth.
From here, there are one hundred thousand [yojanas], and another fifty-seven [thousand].
Sixty thousand [yojanas] are declared to be its height.
When the measurements in yojanas are stated, excluding those pertaining to sensual pleasures,
the remainder is the interval between the Vasavatti deities and their assembly members.
That is said to be fifty-five hundred thousand,
plus another eight thousand yojanas.
Beyond this, in all the Brahma-worlds, the yojanas—
They should be seen as being measured by the wise one who grasps the method:
from the earth up to the peak of existence, there are seventy-eight million,
five hundred and sixty-six thousand [instances] in total.
And this investigation was composed according to the tradition of the *Ṭīkā*;
it is with reference to this that it is said: "As far as the sun and moon revolve, as far as they shine, illuminating the quarters."
"Thus, for a thousandfold world-system, your sovereignty prevails here.
So it was said. Within this interval beings abide; because it would be impossible to explain their details by composing something unprecedented, we shall not speak of them.
In this world of beings and the world of space, only the Omniscient Sammasambuddha is difficult to encounter; likewise...
For there are indeed four types of Buddhas: the *anubuddha*, the *sāvakabuddha*, the *paccekabuddha*, and the *sammāsambuddha*.

In this context, by praising a learned (*bahussuta*) bhikkhu, and by acknowledging the state of Buddhahood in that learned bhikkhu when saying, "This Cunda is indeed a Buddha, though he is not called your disciple," [the Teacher has shown this].
"Since the Teacher is the Dhammakāya, the Dhamma is considered the Teacher’s body;
and the Saṅgha, being a treasury of the Dhamma, also receives the designation of 'Teacher.

When this is said, even an ordinary person (puthujjana) is called "one who has awakened" (anubuddha) by way of metaphorical usage, because of their awakening to the path of recitation. As for the noble disciple (ariyasāvaka):

However, one who awakens to the four truths by means of another’s instruction, being of the nature of awakening merely through the act of awakening, is called a *sāvakabuddha* (hearer-awakened one) in the sense of the word "awakening.

One who is like the horn of a rhinoceros (*khaggavisāṇakappa*), having awakened by himself through self-dependent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) without awakening [to them] through another, is called a *paccekabuddha* (privately awakened one) in the sense of awakening privately. The term *sambuddha* (fully awakened one) also applies to this very person.

As for the name: he who, by means of his own self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhū-ñāṇa*), having become self-become through the perfection of self-realization, has himself—without being awakened by another—rightly and thoroughly penetrated the entire range of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) categorized as conditioned and unconditioned, according to their actual nature and specific characteristics;

and who, through the meeting with the rays of the sun, has utterly dispelled the sleep of delusion along with its latent tendencies (*savāsana-sammoha*), thereby attaining the supreme excellence of most radiant beauty and glory.

Like a lotus in full bloom through the attainment of the knowledge of the supreme path, by reaching the omniscient wisdom adorned with an immeasurable multitude of virtues, he awakened to, understood, and fully realized all phenomena;
thus he is the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha), the Blessed One. He alone is rare in the world;
for even Paccekabuddhas, though they are rare because they appear only once in a period of hundreds of thousands of years, are not as extraordinary as he, since they arise individually.
Furthermore, because he lacks the necessary support for others to attain the paths and fruits [of enlightenment], the Perfectly Enlightened One alone is rare in the world;
this is the investigation of worldly prosperity.
How is the world’s decline to be understood? For in this way, when the world is perishing, it is destroyed by fire, by water, or by wind.

It perishes. Although its detailed exposition is stated in the *Visuddhimagga* and other works, because it represents a wrong grasp according to the opinion of certain individuals, it does not even correspond when measured by the lifespan of the Brahmās, and its limit of contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa-sīmā*) is contradictory.
Therefore, setting aside their doctrine and harmonizing it with the texts, we shall explain it. In this regard, there are four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*). Which ones?

There are four incalculable aeons: the aeon of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the aeon remaining in a state of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*), the aeon of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*), and the aeon remaining in a state of evolution (*vaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).

There are three types of dissolution: dissolution by water, dissolution by fire, and dissolution by wind. There are three boundaries for dissolution: the Ābhassara, Subhakiṇha, and Vehapphala heavens. This is the summary here.
In this context, "dissolution" (*saṃvaṭṭa*) refers to an eon that is declining. By that [term], the "aeon remaining in a state of dissolution" (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) is also [included].
It is included because it is the root of that [period]. When it is increasing, it is called the eon of evolution (*vivaṭṭakappa*);
by that term, the period of remaining in evolution is also included because it is the root of that [process]. In this context, "dissolution" (*saṃvaṭṭa*) means destruction.

When the eon, while undergoing destruction, dissolves by means of fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm—down to the level of the first jhāna—is consumed by flames. When it dissolves by means of water, [everything] from the Subhakiṇha realm...

Downwards, as far as the plane of the second jhāna, it dissolves by water. Or, when it is destroyed by wind, from the Vehapphala realm downwards, as far as the plane of the third jhāna, it is destroyed by wind.

As for its extent, however, among the three types of Buddha-fields—namely the field of birth (*jātikhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākhettta*), and the field of range (*visayakhettta*)—the field of authority perishes. When that has perished, the field of birth also necessarily perishes.

In this context, the field of birth (*jātikhetta*) extends as far as ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). It trembles even at times such as when the Tathāgata takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), relinquishes the life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*), and so forth.
The field of authority (*āṇākhetta*) extends as far as one hundred thousand million world-systems;

it is there that the power of these protective discourses (*paritta*)—namely, the *Ratana-sutta*, the *Khandha-paritta*, the *Dhajagga-paritta*, the *Āṭānāṭiya-paritta*, and the *Moraparitta*—exerts its influence.
The field of objects (*visaya-khetta*) is infinite and immeasurable. Within that, two fields—the field of birth (*jāti-khetta*) and the field of command (*āṇā-khetta*)—perish together;
likewise, when they re-form, they re-form together. Its destruction and its re-formation should be understood as follows:
at the time when the world-age (*kappa*) is destroyed by fire, first a great cloud that destroys the world-age arises.
A single rain-cloud poured over a hundred thousand million world-systems. Delighted, the people sowed their seeds;
yet when the crops had grown no more than the height of a cow’s footprint, the cloud let not even a single drop fall, while it brayed like a donkey.
When everything was completely cut off, those beings who lived by the rain died and were reborn in the Brahma-worlds among the Parittābha deities, subsisting on the fruit of their merit.
Deities arise right there in the Brahma-world; thus, after the passing of a long period of time, the water in various places goes to exhaustion.

Fish, turtles, and other water-dependent creatures, having passed away, are reborn in the human and deva worlds, and by developing meditative absorption (jhāna), they are reborn in the Brahma-world. As for the beings in hell, due to the manifestation of the seventh sun...
Even those who perish there are reborn in the Brahma-world by virtue of the jhāna they have attained in the world of the gods;
for at that time, the gods known as Lokabyūha, belonging to the sense-sphere realm, wander along the paths frequented by humans with their heads held high, disheveled hair, weeping faces,
shedding tears from their hands, dressed in red garments, and wearing extremely hideous attire, proclaiming as follows:
“Friends, after the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, there will be the emergence of an aeon; this world will be destroyed.
Even the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn away and perish.
Destruction will reach as far as the Brahma-world. Friends, cultivate loving-kindness; cultivate compassion, gladness, and equanimity.”
"Friends, cultivate the thought of motherhood; attend upon your mothers; attend upon your fathers; be respectful toward those who are senior in the family.
Having heard these words, most humans and earth-deities are moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);
with hearts softened toward one another, they perform meritorious deeds such as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and are reborn in the world of the gods. There, their food consists of ambrosia (*sudhā*).
Having eaten and performed the preliminary exercise for the wind, they attain jhāna; likewise, even beings in hell are reborn in the deva-world through karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
However, those who hold fixed wrong views experience the result of their own karma according to its nature in other world-systems, because that karma has not yet been exhausted.
For this very reason, it is said that in the case of "ineffective karma" (*ahosikamma*), there is nothing that need be done by way of wrong view.
There is no evil greater than this, for it is precisely the state of being a seed of saṃsāra; thus it was said: “Views, O bhikkhus, are the supreme obstacles.
This is because it has been stated that there is no such thing as a “sentient being” wandering in saṃsāra who is free from karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Therefore, having abandoned the undertaking of wrong view through reliance on true persons by means of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives, [one should proceed].
"It would be our wish that there might be an emergence from existence. Thus, by means of the jhānas attained in the world of the devas, all are reborn in the Brahma-worlds.
But after the cessation of the rain, when a long period of time has passed, a second sun appears. And when that has appeared, there is no longer any distinction between night and day.
It appears that one sun rises and one sun sets; the world remains under the continuous heat of the sun.
In the ordinary sun there is a son of the sun-gods (*sūriyadevaputta*), but in the sun that destroys the aeon (*kappavināsaka-sūriya*) there is none.
By the light of the ordinary sun, clouds and columns of smoke move through the sky; by the light of the sun that destroys the aeon, [the sky] is free from smoke and clouds.
The sky becomes as stainless as a mirror-disk, except for the five great rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarabhū, Aciravatī, and Mahī.
With the exception of these five great rivers, the water in all the remaining five hundred minor streams and so forth dries up.
After a long period has passed, the third sun appears; when it has appeared, even the five great rivers [dry up].
They dry up. Then, after the passing of a long period of time, the fourth sun appears.

With its appearance, these seven great lakes—the Sīhapatanaka, Haṃsapatanaka, Mandākinī, Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka, Rathakāradaha, Anotattadaha, Chaddantadaha, and Kuṇāladaha—which are the sources of the great rivers of the Himavat, dry up. Then, after a long...

After the passing of a long period, a fifth sun appears; with its appearance, even the water of the great ocean gradually does not remain even enough to wet a finger-joint. Then, after the passing of another long period, a sixth sun appears;
with its appearance, the entire world-system becomes a single mass of smoke due to the smoke of evaporated moisture.
