And just as it is with this [world-system], so it is with a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). After the passing of an even longer period than that, a seventh sun appears;
through its appearance, the entire world-system together with the hundred thousand times ten million world-systems becomes a single mass of flame.
The peaks of Mount Sineru, measuring hundreds of *yojanas* and more, crumble away and vanish right there in the sky. That mass of fire also...
Having risen, she seized the realm of the Four Great Kings; there, having incinerated the golden palaces and jewel palaces, she seized the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
By this means, she seized everything up to the plane of the first jhāna. There, having incinerated even the three Brahma-worlds, she stood reaching as far as the Ābhassara realm.
As long as there remained even the slightest trace of conditioned phenomena, she did not go out.
But with the total exhaustion of all conditioned phenomena, it was extinguished like a flame of fire fed by ghee and oil, leaving not even so much as ashes behind.
Below, together with the space, the upper space became one vast darkness.

Thus, from the great cloud that destroys the eon until the limit of the net, this period is called the "contraction" (*saṃvaṭṭa*), which constitutes one incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*). Then, after the passing of a long duration of time...

A great cloud having arisen, it first rains fine mist. Gradually raining with streams as large as lotus stalks, reeds, pestles, palm leaves, tree trunks, and so forth, it fills every scorched place throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems and then vanishes.
The wind, rising from below and from the sides, condenses that water. It forms a circular rim like a lotus leaf.

It is like a drop of water. Thus, from the extinguishing of the flames of fire up until the filling of a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) by a great rain-cloud of prosperity—this is called the "subsistence of the dissolution" (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*), the second incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*). If it is asked:
"How does the wind make such a vast mass of water dense? [The answer is: because it provides openings; thus, being gathered together by that [wind], it becomes solid.
As it becomes condensed and completely solidified, it gradually descends downward.

As the water has receded further and further, first the plane of the first jhāna appears in the former location of the Brahma-world, according to the divisions of the Brahmapārisajja, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā realms.
Then, as the water has receded further and further, the four sense-sphere heavenly worlds appear in their respective locations in due order.
The four sense-sphere heavenly worlds—Paranimmitavasavatti, Nimmānarati, Tusita, and Yāma—manifest.
Then, when the water has descended to the previous level of the earth, powerful winds arise;
these cause the water to become motionless, like water held in a bellows with its mouth closed, and then they cease. The sweet water is completely exhausted.
As it moves, it causes a layer of savory earth to arise;
this is endowed with beautiful color as well as fragrance and flavor, like a film upon boiled rice porridge from which the water has been removed.

At that time, beings who had previously been reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma-world fall away from there due to the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit, and are reborn here. Regarding the phrase "due to the exhaustion of merit":
By this it is understood that death occurs for the Brahmās through the exhaustion of their karma even before reaching the full limit of their lifespan.

They were self-luminous and moved through the air. Having tasted that earth of essence (*rasapathavī*) in the manner described in the *Aggañña Sutta*, they became overcome by craving and began to consume it by making balls of it.
Then their self-luminosity vanished, and darkness arose.

Seeing that darkness, they are afraid. Then, having dispelled their fear and producing a sense of courage, the solar disk appears, measuring a full fifty leagues in extent. Seeing it, they become joyful and elated, thinking, "We have regained light!
and [they say], "He has arisen, dispelling our fear and producing courage; therefore, he is the Sun (Sūriya)."
“Let there be light! they said, and so they gave him the name Sūriya (the Sun).
Then, when the sun had made light for the day and set, they became afraid again, thinking, “Even that light we obtained has vanished.
They thought, “Oh, that we might obtain another light from him! As if knowing their thought, the moon-disk, measuring forty-nine yojanas, appeared.
It became manifest. Seeing it, they were even more exceedingly joyful and delighted, and thinking, "He has arisen as if knowing our desire;
therefore, let him be 'Canda' (the Moon)," they gave him the name Canda.
From that time forth, nights and days became known, and gradually months, fortnights, seasons, and years followed. On the very day the moon and sun became manifest, however—
The Sineru world-system mountains and the Himavanta mountains appear; and they appear not one after another, but all at once on the full-moon day of the month of Phagguṇa.

Just as, for example, when millet porridge is being cooked, bubbles arise simultaneously—some places are high and mound-like, some are low and hollow, and some are level—exactly so, in the places where the mounds are to stand...

Mountains arise; in low-lying places there are oceans, and in level places there are islands—thus, when the human world has been established, the two sensual-sphere heavenly worlds of the Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa appear behind it.
These two heavenly worlds are called "earth-dependent. Thus, from the great cloud of prosperity until the manifestation of the moon and sun—this is [the first stage].
The "Turning Away" (vivatta) is called the third incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*).

Then, as those beings were consuming the savory earth (*rasapathavī*), through their karma some became beautiful and others became ugly. Thereupon, those who were beautiful looked down upon those who were ugly.
On account of that pride and arrogance, even that savory earth disappeared. The "earth-crust" (*bhūmipappaṭaka*) appeared.
Then, by that same process, that too disappears, and the *pātālatā* (underground creeper) appears;
by that same process, that too disappears. Unplowed, ripening rice appears—free from husks and red powder, pure, fragrant, and consisting of whole grains.
Then vessels appear for them; they place the rice in the vessels and set them upon stone slabs.
The flame itself rises up and cooks it. That rice becomes like jasmine flowers;
there is no need for it to be prepared with broth or condiments. Whatever flavor they desire to eat, that very flavor it becomes.
As they consume that gross food, from that time forth urine and feces are produced.
Then, for the purpose of their exit, the openings of the wounds burst open.
The masculinity of the male and the femininity of the female become manifest. Thereupon, the woman gazes excessively at the man, and the man likewise gazes excessively at the woman.
From this state of excessive gazing, a fever of sensual desire arises in them. Thence follows sexual intercourse.

They practice that which is contrary to the true Dhamma. Because of practicing that which is contrary to the true Dhamma, being censured and harassed by the wise, they build houses for the sake of concealing that unrighteousness.
While dwelling in those houses, they gradually follow the example of a certain person of a lazy nature.
As they began to consume [the grain], they stored it away. From that time on, even the husk and the chaff enveloped the rice grain, and the place where it had been harvested no longer grew back.
Gathering together, they lamented: "Alas, friends! Evil states have appeared among beings;
formerly we were mind-made. This should be expanded upon according to the method set forth in the *Aggañña Sutta*.
Then they established boundaries. Thereupon, a certain being took another’s portion without it being given.
After rebuking him twice, on the third occasion they struck him with clods and sticks.

When these matters—taking what is not given, quarrels, false speech, and the infliction of punishment—had arisen, they gathered together and reflected: "What if we were to appoint one being who, for us..."
“One should censure what is rightly censurable; one should blame what is blameworthy; one should ordain those who should be ordained;
and we, moreover, shall provide him with his portion of the fine rice.
When the beings had thus reached a consensus, during this very kappa, while the Blessed One was still a bodhisatta, he was at that time the most handsome among those beings.

He was more worthy of being seen and possessed greater authority; endowed with wisdom and capable of exercising restraint and encouragement, they approached him, requested his consent, and formally appointed him.
Because he was appointed by that great multitude, he is called "Mahāsammata" (Greatly Appointed);

because he is the lord of the fields, he is called "Khattiya" (Noble); and because he delights others through righteousness and equity, he is called "Rājā" (King)—thus he is known by these three names.
It was thus manifested. For whatever wonderful state exists in the world, the Bodhisatta alone is the first person therein;
thus, with the Bodhisatta as the starting point, when the circle of Kṣatriyas had been established, the other castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas gradually became established as well.
Thus, from the appearance of the moon and sun until the great cloud that destroys the aeon, this is the period of the world's expansion (vivattaṭṭhāyi).
This is called the fourth incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*). Therefore, it is said: "The dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*) is delimited by clouds;
the duration of the dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) is delimited by clouds. "The evolution (*vivaṭṭa*) is delimited by the sun;
the duration of the evolution (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) is delimited by the sun. These four [periods] constitute a great eon (*mahākappa*).
It is said that Buddhas and others arise only during the eon of the expansion and duration (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyi-kappa*).

For it is precisely in this eon of expansion and duration, and not in the three [preceding] incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*), that Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and Wheel-turning Monarchs (*cakkavatti*) arise.

Moreover, they arise only in an eon that is not empty (*asuñña-kappa*), and not in an empty eon (*suñña-kappa*). In that regard, by means of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and Wheel-turning Monarchs...
It is called an "unempty aeon" because it is not devoid of persons possessing merit. By contrast, its opposite should be understood as a "void aeon.

Furthermore, even among those unempty aeons, there are five types: the substantial aeon (*sārakappa*), the excellent aeon (*maṇḍakappa*), the superior aeon (*varakappa*), the substantial-excellent aeon (*sāramaṇḍakappa*), and the auspicious aeon (*bhaddakappa*).
Among these, that aeon in which only a single Buddha arises is called the substantial aeon. In that [aeon]...
In an aeon when two Buddhas arise, that is called a *maṇḍa-kappa*. In an aeon when three arise, that is called a *vara-kappa*.
In an aeon when four Buddhas arise, that is called a *sāramaṇḍa-kappa*.
In an aeon when five Buddhas arise, that is called a *bhadda-kappa*. These five types of aeons occur together.
Having brought together the origins of Jātattakī and Sotattakī:
"Nanda, Sunanda, Pathavī, Maṇḍa, Dharaṇī, Sāgara,
and Puṇḍarīka— these seven are proclaimed as belonging to the incalculable eons."
Five thousand Buddhas appear during the *asaṅkhyeya* aeon of Nanda;
nine thousand Buddhas appear during the *asaṅkhyeya* aeon of Sunanda;
ten thousand Buddhas appear during the *asaṅkhyeya* aeon of Pathavī.
Eleven thousand [Buddhas] were in that incalculable mandala;
twenty thousand Buddhas were on the earth in the incalculable [period];
thirty thousand Buddhas were in the ocean in the incalculable [period].
Forty thousand [aeons] in one *asaṅkhyeya* of Puṇḍarīka;
in seven such *asaṅkhyeyyas*, this much is said.
One hundred and twenty thousand [aeons].
“The remaining five thousand [Buddhas] were adorned by all the Buddhas.
Thus it was said. Furthermore, it was also said:
“Bhadda, Sabbaphulla, Sabbaratana, and Usabhakkhandha;”
Mānita-bhadda, Paduma, and Usabha-khantuttama;
Sabbabhāsa, Asaṅkhyeya—this is called the ninth.
In the Asaṅkhyeya aeon named Sabbabhadda, there were fifty thousand Buddhas.
Sixty thousand Buddhas appeared during the aeon of all-blossoming flowers;
seventy thousand Buddhas during the aeon of all-jewels;
and eighty thousand Buddhas during the aeon of the bull-shouldered ones.
Ninety thousand Buddhas were honored during the Asaṅkhyeya aeon called Bhadda;
twenty thousand Buddhas during the Paduma asaṅkhyeya;
ten thousand Buddhas during the Usabha asaṅkhyeya.
Five thousand Buddhas [arose] during the supreme *khantūttama* incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeya*).
And two thousand Buddhas [arose] during the *sabbabhāsa* incalculable eon.
It is said that in the ninth incalculable eon, there were this many [Buddhas].
"Three hundred thousand and seventy-seven thousand;
this is the number of Buddhas by which all the Buddhas are adorned.
Having thus combined all those Perfectly Enlightened Ones up to Ariṭṭha Metteyya—
To the Fully Enlightened One, twenty-eight and twelve thousand,
and five hundred thousand— I bow my head in homage;
and to their Dhamma and Saṅgha, I bow with reverence.
"By the power of this homage, having abandoned all calamities,
may even the many obstacles perish without remainder.
This *Namassanagāthā* (Homage Verse) must have been composed with a number of verses less than [the standard count], for thus it is for us...
The Blessed One, while reflecting mentally, passed through seven *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons beginning from the ancient Buddha Brahmadeva down to the ancient Buddha Sakyagotama;
and passing through nine *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons by means of mere speech, beginning from the ancient Buddha Sakyagotama down to the Buddha Dīpaṅkara of the Middle [Aeon].
From the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara of the Middle [Aeon] down to the Buddha Padumuttara...
By way of bodily and vocal actions, twenty *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons have been passed.
From the time of Buddha Padumuttara until Buddha Kakusandha, one *asaṅkhyeyya* has been passed.

Thus, within these twenty *asaṅkhyeyyas*, combining all together the seven *asaṅkhyeyyas* during the intervals between the Buddhas Brahmadeva, Porāṇa, Sakya, and Gotama, there are one hundred and twenty-five thousand [aeons].

And they are as follows: combining all nine incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) that occurred between the ancient Sakyamuni and the Buddhas Majjhima and Dīpaṅkara, there are three hundred thousand and eighty-seven thousand [aeons].
From the time of Dīpaṅkara up to Metteyya, combining all twenty-eight [aeons], there are five hundred thousand and twelve thousand and twenty-eight [aeons].
And because they are thus, they should be understood as a deficient number. Those who wish to do so should consider them according to a complete enumeration.
This investigation of numbers has already been explained in the Nidāna.
Thus: "The seven enumerations have been considered, as well as those expressing nine enumerations."
“Through body and speech, he attained Buddhahood after four *asaṅkhyeyya* [aeons].

This was stated by way of the *asaṅkhyeyya-kappa* (incalculable aeon) occurring within the twenty *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons mentioned. However, in terms of actual meaning (*attha*), it should be understood as fivefold, according to the *sārakappa*, *maṇḍakappa*, *varakappa*, *sāramaṇḍakappa*, and *bhaddakappa*.
These five names are found only in aeons during which a Buddha appears, not in aeons when no Buddha has arisen.
However, it receives the name "empty aeon" (suññakappa) for this reason: at the time of the formation of an aeon, first of all, a lotus bud arises precisely at the site of the Great Bodhi-throne.
At the time when one Buddha is to arise, a single lotus bud arises together with the eight requisites.
Seeing that, the Arahants who are the diviners of omens among the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas—
Thinking, "In this kappa one Buddha will arise," they become filled with joy and gladness;
taking eight requisites, they place them in the Brahma-world, saying, "When a Buddha arises, we shall give them.
In the same way, when two, three, four, or five Buddhas are to arise, then two, three, four, or five lotus-buds [appear].
They arise together with the eight requisites; moreover, they arise bound one by one within a single stalk.
Thus, it should be understood that these five names are obtained starting from the very time of the formation of the eon (*kappa*).
Up to this point, in this very *asaṅkhyeyya-kappa* of the evolving period (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*), there were those of great influence and merit, such as the Buddhas and others.
Universal monarchs appear, as do [periods of] lifespan and intermediate aeons (*antarakappa*). In this context, "lifespan" (*āyukappa*) refers to the limit of the life-span of various beings.

An "intermediate aeon" (*antarakappa*) is so called because, when many beings have met their destruction through the occurrence of one or another of the calamities of weapons, disease, or famine, the continuity of the remaining beings proceeds by the power of wholesome karma; yet from ten years...

Starting from that point, as beings gradually decline through the undertaking of unrighteousness (*adhamma-samādāna*) over the course of an immeasurable lifespan, they eventually become born with a ten-year lifespan;

the occurrence of the destruction of beings through one of the calamities such as disease constitutes this single intermediate eon (*antarakappa*). Thus, by way of these delimited intermediate eons, there are sixty-four intermediate eons.
Others say that one *asaṅkhyeyya-kappa* is equal in measure to twenty intermediate *kappas*. These four *asaṅkhyeyya-kappas* together are called one *mahākappa*.
Thus, first of all, the interval between *mahākappas* is destroyed by fire according to the process of the world’s contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*).
However, at the time when a *kappa* is destroyed by water, then, from the very beginning, the great cloud that destroys the *kappa* arises.
This should be elaborated in the same manner as previously stated; however, this is the distinction:
just as there was a second sun there, so too here a great cloud of caustic water arises to destroy the world-system (*kappa*).

At first raining gently, it gradually rains with massive torrents, filling hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). All lands, mountains, and other things that are touched by the caustic water—
That water, supported on all sides by the wind, dissolves from the earth up to the Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara realms;
thus, it takes up the water of the second jhāna plane as well. Having caused even those three Brahma-worlds to dissolve, it remains striking against the Subhakiṇha realm;
as long as there exists even a minute portion of conditioned phenomena, it does not subside.
But having overcome all conditioned things that follow upon water, it suddenly subsides and vanishes;
below, together with the space, the upper space becomes one vast darkness—all this is exactly as previously described.
However, here it should be understood that the manifestation of the world begins from the Ābhassara Brahma-world downwards when the water has been crossed and crossed again.
After beings pass away from the Subhakiṇha realm, they are reborn in the Ābhassara realms and so forth;
here too, from the great cloud that destroys the eon until the limit of the water that destroys the eon, it is called "contraction" (saṃvaṭṭa), and this constitutes the first incalculable eon.
Thus, four incalculable eons are exactly as previously described. In this manner, after seven great eons have been dissolved by fire seven times, during the eighth great eon—

The destruction by water and its stabilization should also be understood: thus, after the world has been dissolved by fire seven times during each of seven great aeons (mahākappa), it is dissolved by water during the eighth cycle;
when sixty-three great aeons have been completed in this gradual succession, then, having resisted the turn of water, the world is destroyed by wind during the sixty-fourth great aeon. At that time—
"First, the great wind that destroys the aeon arises"—all of this is exactly as previously described. However, this is the distinction:
just as in the aeon destroyed by fire a second sun appears, so too here, for the purpose of destroying the aeon, a wind arises;
it first stirs up fine dust, then coarse dust, soft dust, fine sand, gravel, stones, and so forth.
He causes even massive rocks the size of gabled houses and great trees standing on uneven ground to rise up;
having ascended from the earth into the sky, they do not fall back down, but right there they are reduced to dust and vanish into non-existence.
In due course, a wind arises from beneath the great earth, overturns the earth, and turns it root-upwards into the sky.
The wind hurls even regions of earth measuring a hundred yojanas, and those measuring two, three, four, five, six, or seven yojanas;
having been cast by its force, they shatter in mid-air and vanish into dust.
Even the Cakkavāḷa mountain range the wind lifts up and hurls into the sky; colliding with one another, they are reduced to powder and destroyed.

By this very [fire], destroying the earth-dwelling celestial mansions (*bhūmaṭṭhaka-vimāna*) and the sky-dwelling celestial mansions (*ākāsaṭṭhaka-vimāna*), and having destroyed the six sense-sphere heavens (*chakāmāvacara-devaloka*), it destroys hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

Therein, the world-systems collide with world-systems, the Himavat mountains with Himavat mountains, and Mount Sinerus with Mount Sinerus; having come together, they are reduced to powder and destroyed.
From the earth element up to the Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha realms—these three Brahmā-worlds constitute the plane of the third jhāna.
The wind takes hold there, destroys all three Brahmā-worlds, and comes to rest having struck against the Vehapphala realm.
Thus, having destroyed every conditioned state, it itself perishes; below, together with space, the space above becomes one.
"It becomes a great darkness" is entirely as previously stated. However, here the world first manifests beginning from the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world.
Beings pass away from the Vehapphala realm and are reborn in the Subhakiṇha and other realms;

from that point until the destruction of the aeon by the great cloud of its own kind, up to the cessation caused by the aeon-destroying wind—this is called "contraction" (saṃvaṭṭa), the first incalculable period.
"Four *asaṅkhyeyya*-kalpas make one *mahākappa*"; all this is exactly according to the method explained regarding the fire-dissolution (*tejosaṃvaṭṭa*).
And it has also been said:
"Seven times by fire, and at every eighth time by water."
When sixty-four [aeons] are complete, there may be a single supreme wind.
By fire, the Ābhassara [heaven] below is destroyed; by water, from the Subhakiṇha [heaven] downward;
by wind, from the Vehapphala [heaven] downward—in this way the world is destroyed.
Therefore, because even in a single *kappa* there is no destruction of the three levels of the first jhāna, their existence does not cease throughout the entire *kappa*;
thus, their lifespan should be understood as being measured in terms of *asaṅkhyeyya* (incalculable) *kappas*.
However, from the level of the second jhāna onwards, their lifespan should be understood as being measured by full great *kappas*, and not by *asaṅkhyeyya* *kappas*.

If the limit of the lifespan were to be determined by a full great aeon (*mahākappa*) starting from the level of the second jhāna, how could the lifespan of the Brahmās in the Ābhassara realm and above be complete according to the measure of eight great aeons and so forth?
For indeed, the level of the first jhāna is destroyed by fire seven times; on the eighth occasion, everything up to the Ābhassara realm is destroyed by water, and then—
It is true that during seven cycles the surface of the first jhāna is destroyed by fire, and then on the eighth cycle the surface of the second jhāna is destroyed by water;
thus, having warded off the water-cycle on the eighth turn, it is destroyed by wind as far as the Subhakiṇha realm, whereby sixty-four complete cycles are fulfilled.
This is according to the lower mode of evolution, based on incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*).
One being [lives] for seven great aeons; thus, eight aeons constitute the measure of the lifespan of the Ābhassara Brahmas.

Furthermore, regarding the sixty-four aeons, by way of the incalculable aeons during which the world remains evolved (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī), one hundred and sixty great aeons constitute the measure of the lifespan of the Subhakiṇha Brahmas. Thus it was said by the ancients.
"Seven times seven turns of fire, and water on every eighth;
when sixty-four are completed, there shall be one turn of wind.
So say some.
“By fire, [the world perishes] below the Ābhassara [heaven]; by water, from the Subhakiṇha [heaven] downwards;
by wind, from the Vehapphala [heaven] downwards—thus the world is destroyed.
Regarding this verse, the terms “Ābhassara,” “Subhakiṇha,” and “Vehapphala” are used in the sense of inclusive limit (abhividhi).

And not considering the fact that it was stated [in the *Paṭṭhāna*] even with respect to the state of being level ground, nor the fact that it was stated as a basis for the *paṭṭhāna* (foundations), but rather considering it to be a "progression of grounds" (*bhūmikkama*) in successive order, like the *Suddhāvāsa* grounds, [he said]:
"The five grounds were destroyed by fire; the eight grounds were destroyed by water."
The winds that stand upon the nine levels would then be those that stand upon the world.
In the first [level] there are thirty-two fires; in the second, sixteen at the beginning;
in the middle of the second level is the eighth; that consists of fifty-six vessels.
"In the Ābhassara [heaven] there is the fourth [destruction]; in the Parittasubha [heaven], two [destructions] by water;
in the Appamāṇasubha [heaven], once [by fire]. Water is considered the seventh.
Thus they say; according to their doctrine, the five planes below the Ābhassara are destroyed by fire, and those below the Subhakiṇha...

They say that the eight stages are the "water-stage" (*udakanaṭṭha*). [The phrase] "the rebirth-existence and so forth" was stated with reference to the conclusion of a single existence (*ekabhavapariyosāna*), being taken thus for the purpose of illustrating the levelness [of the process] and for the purpose of cutting through doubt.

Having grasped the meaning of this [passage] incorrectly, he imagines that it was stated with reference only to the similarity [of the states] by way of the rebirth-linking and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
It appears as if illogical and is an extreme misconception, because it contradicts such suttas as the *Aggañña-sutta* and the *Visuddhimagga*;
furthermore, the limit of the eon’s dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭasīmā*) is also contradicted by the statement that "it is destroyed by fire starting from the level of the first jhāna,
by water starting from the level of the second jhāna, and by wind starting from the level of the fourth jhāna."

Therefore, in the cases of "the Ābhassara [deities]," "from the Subhakiṇha [brahmā]," and "from the Vehapphala [brahmā]," the meaning should be understood here according to the sense of inclusion (abhividhi).

Otherwise, just as in the expression "the rain falls above the mountain," there would be no destruction of the Ābhassara, Subhakiṇha, and Vehapphala realms by means of those respective contractions (saṃvaṭṭa).
This is the delimitation of the world's dissolution. Thus, the Buddha...
And the meaning of "rare in the world" has already been stated.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Section on the Destruction of the Aeon, in the *Sīmavisodhana* composed by the Elder Sāgarabuddhi.
3. The Chapter on Nibbāna Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the phrase, "And hearing the true Dhamma.

In this regard, hearing the true Dhamma is indeed difficult to obtain in the world. For the so-called true Dhamma is threefold: the true Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-saddhamma*), the true Dhamma of practice (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*), and...
"The True Dhamma of penetration" (paṭivedhasaddhamma). In this context, the "True Dhamma of the scriptures" (pariyattisaddhamma) refers to the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas.

The "True Dhamma of practice" (paṭipattisaddhamma) refers to the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), the eighty rules of conduct from the Khandhakas, and so forth, including the rules for proper behavior (abhisamācāravatta).
The "True Dhamma of penetration" refers to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Among these, the True Dhamma of the scriptures is indeed the precursor to the other two forms of the True Dhamma.
And the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). Why? Because it is rooted in that; for indeed, in the absence of the scripture (*pariyatti*), there is no such thing as penetration (*paṭivedha*).
When the scripture has disappeared, practice (*paṭipatti*) disappears; when practice has disappeared, realization (*adhigama*) disappears.
For what reason? Because this scripture is the condition for practice, and the scripture alone is also the condition for the realization of practice.
This is the measure. In that regard, both penetration (*paṭivedha*) and practice (*paṭipatti*) may exist or may not exist.
For at one time there were many monks who possessed penetration, such that one had to point with a finger and say, "This monk is an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
On this very island, at one time, even the name of an ordinary monk did not exist. At times, those who fulfill the practice (*paṭipatti*) [are likewise rare].
Sometimes they are many, sometimes few. Thus, both penetration (*paṭivedha*) and practice (*paṭipatti*) may exist or may not exist.
However, for the endurance of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*) alone is the measure;

for a wise person, having heard the Three Piṭakas, fulfills both as did our own Bodhisatta when he had generated the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the seven meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in the presence of Āḷāra.
He asked about the preliminary practice for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He replied, "I do not know.
Then, having gone to Udaka and compared his own attained distinction with him, he asked about the preliminary practice for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Udaka explained it, and immediately upon those words, the Great Being accomplished it; thus indeed is one possessed of wisdom.
A bhikkhu, having heard the Pariyatti, fulfills both [the Sāsana and himself]; therefore, when the Pariyatti stands firm, the Sāsana stands firm.

Just as it cannot be said that water will not remain in a great reservoir if its embankment is solid, nor can it be said that lotuses and other flowers will not bloom when there is water—even so, regarding the Tipiṭaka, which is like the solid embankment of a great reservoir...
When the word of the Buddha exists, it cannot be said that there are no sons of good family who fulfill the practice, for they are like the water in a great lake.
When they exist, it cannot be said that there are no noble persons such as stream-enterers and the rest, for they are like the lotuses and other flowers in those great lakes.
The scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*) alone is by no means the sole authority; for when the scriptural tradition has disappeared, the practice and realization [of the Dhamma] also vanish.
By way of disappearance. In this context, "the teaching" (*pariyatti*) refers to the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Pitakas together with the commentaries;
as long as it remains in the form of the text itself, so long is the teaching complete. As time passes, the kings of the Kali age become unrighteous;
when those kings and ministers are unrighteous, likewise do the inhabitants of the kingdom and the provinces become unrighteous.
Because they are unrighteous, due to their lack of righteousness, the rain does not fall properly from the sky; consequently, the crops do not flourish.
When the crops fail, those who provide requisites are unable to give the necessary provisions to the Saṅgha of monks.
Being distressed for lack of requisites, the monks are unable to support their pupils. As time passes in this way, the sacred scriptures...
They decline; they are no longer able to preserve it by way of its meaning, but preserve it only by way of the text.
Then, as time passes, they are no longer able to preserve even the entire text, and first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka declines.
As it declines, the scripture is lost starting from its summit; for first the Mahāpakaraṇa declines. In that...

When the Yamaka, Kathāvatthu, Puggalapaññatti, Dhātukathā, Vibhaṅga, and Dhammasaṅgaṇī—thus the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—is lost, beginning from its summit, the Sutta Piṭaka is lost. For first the Aṅguttara Nikāya is lost;
in that too, first the Ekādasanipāta... and so on down to... then the Ekanipāta.
Thus, when the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* has been lost, starting from the top, the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* begins to decline; first the *Mahāvagga* is lost.
Starting from that point, the *Saḷāyatanavagga*, the *Khandhavagga*, the *Nidānavagga*, and the *Sagāthāvagga* follow.
Thus, when the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* has been lost, starting from the top, the *Majjhima Nikāya* begins to decline; for first—
The *Upari-pannāsaka* (Final Fifty) is lost; after that, the *Majjhima-pannāsaka* (Middle Fifty); and after that, the *Mūla-pannāsaka* (Root Fifty).
Thus, when the *Majjhima-nikāya* has been lost, the *Dīgha-nikāya* is lost starting from its end:
first the *Pāthiya-vagga* is lost, then the *Mahā-vagga*, and then the *Khandhaka-vagga*. When the *Dīgha-nikāya* has been lost, the *Suttanta-piṭaka* is lost.
It was called [the Jātaka]. Together with the Vinaya Piṭaka, they memorized only the Jātakas. Those who were modest (lajjino) memorized the entire Vinaya Piṭaka;
however, those desiring gain, even when the Sutta Piṭaka was recited, remarked, "There is nothing [of value here]," and so they memorized only the Jātakas.
As time passed, they became unable to even maintain the Jātakas in memory. Consequently, first the Vessantara Jātaka was lost to them.
Then, in reverse order, the Puṇṇaka Jātaka and the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka were lost;
they retained only the Vinaya Piṭaka. As time passed, even that was lost from its summit:
first the Parivāra was lost, then the Khandhaka, the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, and the Mahāvibhaṅga, until finally only the Uposatha Khandhaka remained.
When they preserve it, then the scripture remains unextinguished. As long as even a four-line verse continues among human beings, so long does the scripture remain unextinguished.

When a faithful and devoted king, having placed a purse containing a thousand [pieces of gold] in a golden casket upon the back of an elephant, [declares]: "A four-line verse spoken by the Buddhas..."
"Let whoever knows this take this thousand pieces," he proclaimed by having a drum beaten throughout the city.

But when no one came forward to take it—even after the drum had been beaten once, some did not hear it and others were not listening—when they had beaten it for a third time and still found no taker, the king’s men carried the bag of a thousand pieces back into the royal palace; at that point, it was said that the *pariyatti* (the formal teaching) had disappeared.
Thus, when the *pariyatti* (the scriptures) has disappeared, both the *paṭipatti* (practice) and the *paṭivedha* (realization) have likewise disappeared.
The rarity of hearing the true Dhamma is to be illustrated by the story of Dhammasoṇḍaka:
it is said that not long after the disappearance of the teaching of our own Sammasambuddha Kassapa, the Dhamma-king, there was a prince named Dhammasoṇḍaka, the son of the King of Bārāṇasī.
Having performed the oblation and established himself in the kingdom upon his father’s passing, he became desirous of hearing the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Kassapa.
After ruling for only about a month, our own Sammasambuddha— having likewise ruled as king in this very Bhaddakappa—
was performing a sovereignty comparable to that of a Wheel-Turning Monarch in the city of Bārāṇasī, which resembled the city of the gods, when he thought thus:…
“What kind of splendor is this kingdom of mine, what majesty of sovereignty, when separated from the True Dhamma?
It is like the sky bereft of the sun, like a night devoid of the moon, like an elephant deprived of its tusks,
like the great ocean lacking its shore, like a well-adorned face without eyes, or like a *pārichatta* flower stripped of its fragrance.”
Thinking, "Without the teaching of the Dhamma restricted to four syllables,
this kingdom of mine does not shine," he placed a well-prepared bundle containing a purse of a thousand [coins] upon the frontal globe of his auspicious state elephant using a golden hook,
and caused a drum to be beaten in the great streets of the city of Bārāṇasī, proclaiming: "Whether it be a one-footed, two-footed, or three-footed..."
"Or even one who knows a single four-line verse of the Dhamma—to him I give [this]," he proclaimed by having the drum beaten.

Yet, failing to find anyone who knew the Dhamma, he repeatedly offered two thousand, three thousand, and so on, up to a hundred thousand, two billion, and ten billion villages, market towns, districts, positions of army commander, and positions of viceroy. At the conclusion, he sought a teacher of the Dhamma.
Having failed to obtain [the Dhamma], he gave up his own golden throne and white parasol;
failing to obtain a teacher of the Dhamma, he abandoned the glory of kingship and sacrificed himself, saying, "I shall listen to the Dhamma even as a slave to the teacher of the Dhamma.
Yet, even after saying this, failing to find a teacher of the Dhamma, he became remorseful and said to his ministers, "What use have I for kingship if it means separation from the True Dhamma?"
Having handed over the kingdom and become a seeker of the True Dhamma, King Dhammasoṇḍaka entered the Great Forest.
At the very moment King Dhammasoṇḍaka entered with the intent of hearing the True Dhamma, the Vejayanta Palace of Sakka, the Great King of the Devas,
together with his throne, shook, and the Paṇḍukambala stone seat became warm.
Sakka, the King of the Gods, thought to himself, "For what reason has the Paṇḍukambala stone seat become hot?
Having considered this, he surveyed the world of gods and humans with his thousand eyes. Seeking the Dhamma, he saw the Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka who had entered the forest, and he thought:
"Today, even at the cost of my own life, I shall assume the guise of a rākṣasa..."

"Having demonstrated the fault of birth, old age, sickness, and death throughout the entire body to illustrate this impermanence, and having taught the Dhamma, he should be established right here in my own kingdom," thought Sakka, King of the Devas.
Having formed the appearance of a Yakkha, he showed himself not far from the Bodhisatta, facing him. Upon seeing him, the Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka—
He thought thus: "Could a *rakkhasa* such as this know the Dhamma? Having thought this, and standing at a place not far away, thinking "I shall ask him," he spoke to the *rakkhasa*, addressing him:
"O King of Devas, master of merit! But you, O King of Devas dwelling in this dense forest, do you perhaps know the Dhamma? The deity replied: "Great King, the Dhamma..."
“I know it,” he said. “If you know the Dhamma, then give me a discourse on the Dhamma,” he said.
“I will give you a discourse on the Dhamma; but what kind of honor will you show me, a preacher of the Dhamma? he asked.
“That being the case, after you have given me a discourse on the Dhamma, you shall eat the flesh from my body,” he said.
“I am hungry, Great King, and I am unable to preach the Dhamma,” he said.
“If you eat meat first, who will listen to the Dhamma? the king replied. Again that rakkhasa said, “I am not able to teach the Dhamma.
Again the king said, “My attainment of the Dhamma and your attainment of meat—[you two]...”
“Having understood it, please teach me the Dhamma,” he said.
Then Sakka, the king of the gods, saying, “Very well,” created at no great distance a massive mountain of collyrium, three *gāvutas* in height, and spoke thus:
“Great King, if you were to climb to the summit of this mountain, leap from the sky, and fall into my mouth—”

“I shall teach you the Dhamma while we are in the air; this being so, there will be for you the gain of the Dhamma and for me the gain of flesh,” he said. Having heard his words, King Dhammasoṇḍaka thought:

“In the beginningless cycle of existence, having been a man and being possessed of unrighteousness, I have committed the taking of life and the taking of what is not given solely for the sake of unrighteousness.”
Sexual misconduct includes the pig-butchers, the sheep-slaughterers, the fowlers, the thieves, and the adulterers;
the blood shed when their heads are cut off would be more abundant than the water in the four great oceans.
And the tears shed by those weeping for the sake of their parents and other loved ones would be more abundant than the water in the four great oceans. But this body belongs to the Dhamma.
Thinking, "I shall sell this for a great and pleasing fruit," he said, "Very well, dear sir, let us do so.
Having climbed the mountain and stood upon its peak, he was filled with joy, thinking, "Along with my kingdom, I shall give even my living body for the sake of the True Dhamma.
Then, saying "Preach the Dhamma," he renounced his life for the sake of the True Dhamma.
"Fly up into the air and preach the Dhamma," he said. Then Sakka, the king of the gods,
adorned with all his ornaments in his own celestial form, exceedingly joyful to hear [the teaching], touched him as he descended from the sky with a divine touch,
received him upon his breast, led him to the world of the gods, seated him on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, and honored him with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings.
While teaching the Dhamma to the Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka, he spoke this verse:
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease—their pacification is bliss.”

Thus Sakka, having taught the Dhamma to the Great King Dhammasoṇḍaka, having shown him the splendors of the deva-world, having brought him back from the deva-world and established him in his own kingdom, and having exhorted him to heedfulness, returned once more to the deva-world.

In this way, it should be understood that even the hearing of the true Dhamma is difficult to obtain. Thus, with the disappearance of the scriptures (pariyatti), both practice (paṭipatti) and realization (paṭivedha) also disappear.
And here, three kinds of parinibbāna are to be understood. What are the three kinds of parinibbāna? They are:

the parinibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*), the parinibbāna of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*), and the parinibbāna of the elements (*dhātuparinibbāna*). Among these, the parinibbāna of the defilements occurs at the very seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
for the Blessed One, having established himself upon the earth of virtue with the feet of energy at the seat of enlightenment, by means of the hand of faith...
Having taken up the wisdom-axe that brings about the destruction of karma, one cuts down all greed, hatred, delusion,

distorted attention, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, anger, resentment, hypocrisy, spite, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, agitation, conceit, pride, intoxication, negligence, craving, ignorance, the three kinds of unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, stains, uneven perceptions, discursive thoughts, conceptual proliferation, the fourfold perversion,
the taints, the fetters, the floods, the bonds, the underlying tendencies, the knots, the clingings, the five mental barrennesses, the shackles, the hindrances, and delighting in existence.
The root of dispute, craving, the underlying tendencies of the body and beings, the eight wrong views,

the ten unwholesome courses of action rooted in the nine types of craving, the sixty-two types of speculative views, and the hundred thousand varieties of defilements consisting of the hundredfold wanderings of craving—

all these torments, fevers, and afflictions have been utterly destroyed and dispelled, whether in brief as the five defilements, the formative aggregates, the Mara of Death, or the Mara who is the Son of Deva.
Because they have been rendered non-existent, all defilements (*kilesa*) go to extinction (*nibbāna*), which is cessation (*nirodha*), at the very seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
thus, the extinction of defilements occurs at the seat of enlightenment itself. Here, "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is intended to mean the knowledge of the path to *arahantship*;
for indeed, for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), all defilements reach complete cessation precisely at the moment of the path to *arahantship*.

Those Buddhas who go to Nibbāna are also threefold, according to the distinction between those who understand through a condensed summary (ugghaṭita-viññū), those who understand through analysis (vibhajja-ñū), and those who must be led (neyya).
For this has been stated in the Jātattakī and Sotattakī Nidānas:
"There is one named 'understanding through a condensed summary,' and two who understand through analysis."
The third is to be known by name as the Bodhisatta, who is considered to be of three types:
the Bodhisatta who gains knowledge through a condensed exposition is so named because he is preeminent in wisdom;
the Bodhisatta who gains knowledge through detailed analysis is said to be preeminent in energy.
The one to be led is called "one who abounds in faith"; these are the three types of Bodhisattvas:
[those who will attain enlightenment] in a hundred thousand aeons, four incalculable aeons, and [four more].
Having fulfilled the requisites for enlightenment and received their prophecy in a former life, they proceed.
The Bodhisatta Ugghaṭitaññu attained supreme enlightenment.
Having fulfilled the requisites for enlightenment during the eighth incalculable eon and a hundred thousand aeons, he received his prophecy in the past.
The Bodhisatta Vipassī attained supreme enlightenment;
the Bodhisatta Neyya, however, received his prophecy sixteen hundred thousand aeons ago.
In the past, he had already obtained his prediction.
"Having fulfilled the requisites for enlightenment, he attained supreme awakening.
However, in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "Ānanda, for Buddhas, the minimum limit is four *asaṅkhyeyya*s and one hundred thousand *kappa*s;
the middle limit is eight *asaṅkhyeyya*s and one hundred thousand *kappa*s..."

By the final division, there are sixteen incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) and one hundred thousand aeons. It is stated that these are to be understood according to whether wisdom, faith, or energy is predominant among them:
one who is predominant in wisdom [attains Buddhahood] after four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons;
one predominant in faith after eight incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons; and one predominant in energy after sixteen incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons.

This should be understood. In this regard, although one who is preeminent in wisdom transmigrates through the various wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, his enlightenment is swift due to the predominance of wisdom, arising from the presence of a perfected aspiration.

However, one who is preeminent in faith, because of his dull wisdom, places faith even in what should not be believed; therefore, his enlightenment is slow. One who is preeminent in energy, on the other hand, is dull in both [faith and wisdom].
He believes even what should not be believed and does even what should not be done; for just as King Pasenadi Kosala,
while the Omniscient Buddha was still living, conceived the thought of approaching another’s wife though it was forbidden,
and began to deprive others of life— he was utterly deluded, even upon hearing the sound "Dusana" from the wailing denizens of hell.
Setting aside the Omniscient Buddha, he consulted a brahmin of wrong view; following that man's words, he caused suffering for all people for the sake of sacrifices.
What need is there to speak of when no Buddha had yet arisen?

For instance, when the world had become blind due to the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s teaching, this man, though being a king in Bārāṇasī, [acted] because of a deity dwelling in a *nigrodha* tree.

He began to have one hundred kings, together with their queens, slain for the sake of the sacrifice. Thus, while he was superior in energy yet deficient in both [faith and wisdom], his attainment of full enlightenment was consequently very slow.
In this way, the brevity or length of the time [required] should be understood according to whether one is superior in wisdom, superior in faith, or superior in energy.
It is our own opinion that only the latter method (the last one mentioned) should be praised in this context.
As for the Parinibbāna of the aggregates, it occurred at the Upavattana in the Malla country’s Sal Grove,

between the twin Sāla trees on the full moon day of Vesākha, at the time of dawn; having made the final consciousness indeterminate by means of a great resultant consciousness— similar to a wholesome, unprompted, consciousness associated with joy and knowledge belonging to the preliminary stage of loving-kindness—
among the nineteen moments of the death-consciousness, there was no rebirth-linking consciousness in any state of existence.

It should be understood that, acting as an immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*), it is the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*sabbupadhipaṭinissagga*)—being free from clinging through the defilements of karma and craving—and the abandonment of the aggregates that have been grasped.
For the detailed explanation, however, one should consult the commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta in the Mahāvagga of the Dīgha Nikāya.
Therein, it is said that a man departing for a foreign land embraces his entire circle of kinsmen and kisses them on the head...
As if entering the city of Nibbāna, the Blessed One likewise entered all the twenty-four hundred thousand millions of attainments without exception,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
having emerged from that, he reviewed the factors of jhāna, and with the resultant life-continuum consciousness, which is indeterminate, [he reflected] upon the truth of suffering.
He attained final Nibbāna. In the Pāḷi, however, it is stated: “Having emerged from the fourth jhāna, immediately thereafter the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna.
In this context, there are two kinds of “immediately thereafter”: immediate succession to the jhāna and immediate succession to reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*).
Among these, when one has emerged from the jhāna and entered the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), attaining final Nibbāna right there is called “immediate succession to the jhāna.”

Having emerged from jhāna and again reviewed the factors of jhāna, the "attainment of final Nibbāna right there" refers to the moment immediately following that review for one who has descended into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
However, it should be understood that the Blessed One did not pass away immediately after the jhāna, but rather passed away immediately after the reviewing;
for this very reason he said: "But the Blessed One, having entered jhāna and emerged from jhāna..."
"Having reviewed the factors of jhāna, he attained final nibbāna with a resultant, indeterminate bhavaṅga consciousness, [taking] the truth of suffering as its object.

Regarding this, others say: "What was the object of the Blessed One’s consciousness at the moment of final nibbāna? Was it kamma, or was it the sign of the kamma (kammanimitta) or the sign of the destination (gatinimitta), or was it nibbāna?"
For the Stable One whose mind was established, there were no more inhalations or exhalations;
free from agitation, having undertaken peace,
at that time the Sage brought his sensations to rest with an unflagging mind.

Regarding the verse: "Like the extinguishing of a lamp, there was the liberation of his mind," if one were to connect this by saying, "The sage who, being unshaken, passed away with Nibbāna as his theme," and claim that the consciousness of the Blessed One at the moment of final Nibbāna had Nibbāna as its object—that would be incorrect;
for it is impossible for rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, or the death-moment to have Nibbāna as their object.
Because the *Paṭṭhāna-pāḷi* states, "Nibbāna is a condition for change-of-lineage, purification, and the path by way of object-condition;
Nibbāna is [a condition] for the fruition and for adverting," and because it is intended there that only impulsion and adverting are meant, therefore here:
"The sage who, being unshaken by the attainment of fruition, is called 'unshaken'—being free from craving—having taken as his object the peace that is Nibbāna..."
The construction should be made thus: “Having made it the object, he passed away—that is, he completed and exceeded a lifespan measuring eighty years.

However, some say this: because it has been stated that for one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) who does not arise [in a new existence] anywhere, only such things as the phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as they present themselves become the objective range (gocara) for the final moments of death, and not kamma, the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta), or the sign of the destination (gati-nimitta). Therefore, [they claim] the signs of kamma, the sign of kamma, and the signs of the destination...
To say that [these objects] do not become the object of the death-consciousness of an Arahant is likewise incorrect;

for this is the meaning here: in whatever way, by whatever mode, and as mere phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) such as the aggregates, they appear to the advertence and impulsion consciousnesses until the end of the death-moment of an Arahant whose taints are exhausted and who is not arising in any further state of existence.

It does not go, because there is no further production of existence (bhava). For what reason do the primary elements (bhūta), kamma, the signs of kamma, and the signs of destiny (gatinimitta) not become objects (gocara)?
It is because only that which has been grasped by the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) from the death-consciousness (cuticitta)—namely, a past object—becomes an object.
Regarding the phrase "only name-and-form, etc.," here "name" (nāma) refers to consciousness (citta) and mental factors (cetasika), excluding Nibbāna.

"Form" (*rūpa*) includes the eighteen kinds of form. "Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to both name and form. "Those phenomena which are name-and-form" (*nāmarūpā ca te dhammā*) is the same [as the compound].
Those for which these are the beginning are "name-and-form-phenomena-beginning" (*nāmarūpadhammādi*); that very thing is "having name-and-form-phenomena as its beginning" (*nāmarūpadhammādika*).

By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the six designations (*paññatti*) are included; by this, even *nibbāna* and the impulsion of action (*kriya-javana*) at the time near the death of an *arhat* are also included.
Whether it could serve as an object of consciousness must be determined after investigating our own inclination.

However, it should be understood that for the Blessed One’s mind of Nibbāna, the object is precisely that which was grasped by the rebirth-linking consciousness when he descended from the Tusita heaven and dwelt in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā;
and that, moreover, is solely the sign of the destination (gatinimitta), not the sign of the deed (kamma-nimitta) nor the deed itself (kamma). This is also evident through logical reasoning.
Even according to scripture, it is logical that the cause for his departure was precisely this:
having remained in Tusita City itself as the deity Setaketu for four thousand years by celestial reckoning— which is fifty-seven million six hundred thousand years by human reckoning—
and having seen five portents at the conclusion of that time, he was [instructed] by the Arahant Brahmā of the Suddhāvāsa realm from ten thousand world-systems.
And having approached with the distinguished deities, they said:
"It is time, O Great Hero, for you to arise in a mother’s womb;
saving the world including the gods, awaken to the deathless state."
Being entreated, he performed the five great observations— concerning the time, the continent, the region, the clan, and the mother—
and having descended from the Tusita heaven on the full moon of Āsāḷhī under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha,
amidst nineteen moments of rebirth-linking consciousness, his mind was a wholesome state associated with joy and knowledge, unprompted and preceded by loving-kindness.
He took rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by means of a similar great resultant consciousness (*mahāvipākacitta*).

Prior to the stage of the proximate mental process (*āsannavīthi*) that takes that [rebirth-linking object] as its object, these five factors—namely, direction, time, place, clan, and mother—become the objective field for the rebirth-linking consciousness by way of being the objects of the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*).
This is our conviction (*khanti*), because they frequently arise through their inclination toward, leaning toward, and tending toward those [five factors].
Therefore, in the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* and other works, such as the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvanī*, it is stated:

"At the time of death, there appears either the kamma that produces rebirth-linking in the next existence according to its suitability; or the kamma-sign, which consists of the forms and so forth perceived at the time of performing that kamma and served as its instrument;
or the destination-sign, which is the object to be experienced in the immediately arising existence and served as the basis for enjoyment."
Or, by the power of karma, [consciousness] presents itself at one of the six doors;

thereafter, taking that very object thus presented as its basis, the stream of consciousness—whether pure or defiled, according to the maturing karma and corresponding to the state of existence to be reborn—continues to flow there frequently and predominantly, directed toward that very same productive cause. Or else, that which has become the producer...

Kamma reaches the "door" by way of being freshly performed. However, for one whose death is imminent, at the conclusion of the cognitive process (vīthicitta), either with the destruction of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or by way of falling away, the death-consciousness (cuticitta)—which constitutes the end of the present existence—arises and ceases.
Immediately after that has ceased, taking as its object the very same object previously grasped, [the rebirth-linking consciousness arises].
Whether with a physical basis or without one as appropriate, it arises as the mind designated as "rebirth-linking" by way of connecting to another existence;
it is being produced by a volitional formation rooted in the underlying tendency of craving and enveloped by the underlying tendency of ignorance,
and while being grasped by its associated mental factors, it acts as the precursor to co-nascent states by serving as their foundation.
It is said: "It establishes itself in another existence.

Therein, by the phrase "the stream of consciousness proceeds frequently and predominantly toward that which is bent toward it," he shows that the sign of the destination (gatinimitta), established by the power of karma, arises from one day or two days prior to the stage immediately preceding death, and may even arise for seven days or more than seven days; for it is either pure or defiled.
Or, the sign of the destination (gatinimitta), corresponding to the maturing karma, may persist for a long time, as in the cases of Ariyagāla Tissa,
the Coraghātaka, and others. For instance, the lay follower named Ariyagāla Tissa,
having performed meritorious deeds such as giving throughout his life together with his wife Sumanā on the island of Siṃhala, [saw that sign] at the end of his life upon the bed of death.
As he lay there, the six devas brought their chariots from their respective celestial realms and each praised his own world.
Having heard the words of the deities, the lay follower had the chariot brought from the Tusita heaven set aside and told the others, "Take these remaining chariots and go.
But Sumanā, having heard her husband's words, asked, "Why did he utter such lamentation when death was near?"
Āḷavaka said: Having heard the words of his own wife, he replied, "I am not lamenting;
deities have brought six chariots from the world of the gods, and I am conversing with those deities. When [the king] asked, "Where is she?
he had a flower garland brought and threw it into the air. That flower garland was seen hanging from the front of the chariot.
Having seen [the city], she entered the womb, lay down upon a couch, ceased the flow of breath through her nostrils, passed away, and appeared [in Tusita].
She sent a message to her husband: “…But I have arrived first; why do you delay?
Both of them stood in their chariot and went to the Tusita realm while everyone was looking on. In this matter:
The sign of the husband’s destination appeared clearly to his wife; having been reborn in Tusita-pura even earlier than her husband, she sent a message to him.
By this it should be understood that for Ariyagālatissa, the sign of his destination remained present for a long time.
For in the human world, a long period of time is but a moment in Tusita-pura. Thus it was perfectly pure.
In this manner, the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) manifests for a long duration in accordance with the karma that is about to ripen;

by this method, the accounts of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi, Abhayadhammika, Uppasaka, and others should also be expanded upon. However, for the executioner of thieves, the flames of the fires of hell and so forth manifest for seven days in accordance with the karma that is about to ripen in the Great Hell (*mahāniraya*).
It is said that in the city of Sāvatthī, five hundred thieves were committing acts of robbery outside the city.
Then one day, a man from the countryside, having become one of their number, committed a robbery;
at that time, all those royal officers seized them. When the king saw them, he said, "I grant life to whoever among you is capable of killing all these men.
The five hundred thieves were related to one another and were companions to one another.
They did not wish to kill him; however, a man from the countryside said, "I will kill him," and killed them all.
The king, being pleased with him, appointed him to the office of executioner. He performed the duties of an executioner for twenty-five years.
When the king remarked that he had grown old, he assigned the office of executioner to another. From that point on, he [no longer] performed the work of an executioner.
Having been taken to a certain person, he learned the technique of inhaling breath through the nostrils;

by releasing that breath into the thighs, neck, or other vulnerable spots of those who were to be executed—such as those to be beheaded or have their hands, feet, ears, or noses cut off—he acquired a mantra for killing.
Having informed the king, while performing the work of an executioner using the breath of his nostrils, thirty years passed.
He passed away. Later, having become old, he lay upon his deathbed and was told, "You will pass away in seven days.
At the time of death, there was great agony. He became distressed, making a loud noise as if he had been reborn in the Great Hell.
Terrified by his sound, the people abandoned their houses on both sides and fled. On the day of his death—
The Elder Sāriputta, surveying the world with his divine eye, saw that after this man had died, he was being reborn in the great hell.
Out of compassion for him, the Elder made himself visible at the entrance to the house. The man, becoming enraged, released a blast from his nostrils.
Although he tried to release it up to three times, he was unable to make the Elder disappear; instead, the Elder shone even more brilliantly.
Having seen this, he gladdened his heart and had the milk-rice given to the Elder. The Elder, having pronounced a blessing, departed.
The executioner, recollecting the gift he had given to the Elder, passed away and was reborn in heaven;
the flames of hell and other such torments vanished. He will also become a Paccekabuddha in the future. Thus, even that which is defiled, when it ripens...
The sign of the destination corresponding to one’s own karma also appears for a maximum of seven days. Those who wish to know more should consult the *Sahassavatthu* and the *Sagāthāvagga*.

However, for the Blessed One, due to the force of his pure wholesome karma associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy arising from the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*), these five signs of the destination appear according to the time, island, country, clan, and mother.
Having remained for a long time, they appear. "For a long time" means for about seven days in the human world, but only for a mere moment in the Tusita heaven;

nevertheless, the five portents of the devas become manifest during that period of seven days in the human world, and they appear only to those who possess merit, not to everyone—specifically, not to all those in the human world such as kings, royal ministers, and others, even if they are meritorious.

Upon seeing that [sign], deities of great power perceive it, whereas those of little power do not—just as in the human world, only brahmins, scholars, and others who are skilled in omens recognize them.
Having seen that omen, the powerful deities lead him to Nandavana and entreat him with words such as, "The time has come, O Deva.
Thereupon, Mahāsakka, having performed the fivefold examination regarding the time, the continent, the country, the family, and the mother right there in the Nandavana grove, passed away.
It should be understood that he reached a definitive conclusion: "Taking that as the object, I shall take rebirth in the womb of Mahāmāyā.
In this context, regarding "time," he surveyed the time, thinking: "I shall become a Buddha in the twenty-ninth year of the human world on the full-moon day of Vesākha.
Regarding "continent," he surveyed the continent, thinking: "I shall appear only in Jambudīpa, not in other continents. Regarding "country"...
He surveyed the country, seeing that it must be the Middle Country, and specifically the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), not any other region.
Regarding the clan, there are two clans: the Kṣatriya clan and the Brāhmaṇa clan.

In this regard, at whatever time the Kṣatriya clan is recognized in the world as being of the highest status, such that it is declared, "This alone is the foremost in the world," at that time Buddhas arise only within the Kṣatriya clan.
At whatever time the brahmin caste was regarded as the foremost in the world, at that time Buddhas arose only in the brahmin caste.
But now, they recognize the kshatriya caste alone as the foremost. Even among the kshatriyas, the Śākya kings alone are supreme in the world because of their unadulterated kshatriya lineage;
therefore, [the Bodhisatta thought], "I shall be born only in the Śākya royal family," thus regarding the family.
He looked back. He also looked at his mother, thinking: "My mother shall remain for ten months and seven days;
during this interval, my mother will be free from illness. Now, the Bodhisatta’s mother was already in her final years.

Thus, both by way of reasoning and by way of scripture, it is established that the sign apprehended by the Blessed One’s consciousness of Nibbāna was indeed [the same as] the rebirth-linking consciousness.
It should be understood as being the object:
"The Nibbāna of the Omniscient Victor is the beautiful range of the mind;
it is to be known as the sign of the destination because it is not contradicted by the scriptures."
The final nirvana of the relics will also take place at the very seat of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa). For this has been stated in the *Upari-Paṇṇāsaka*:
"In the future, at the time of the decline of the Dispensation, the relics will assemble here on this island of Tambapaṇṇi;
from the Mahācetiya they will go to the Rājāyatana Cetiya on Nāgadīpa, and from there they will proceed to the Great Bodhi Throne. Even from the abode of the Nāgas..."
Even from the world of the gods, the relics will proceed to the Great Bodhi Throne itself; not even a relic the size of a mustard seed shall perish along the way.

All the relics, having gathered together upon the Great Bodhi Throne like a single mass of gold, becoming one solid whole, will emit six-colored rays that will pervade the ten-thousandfold world system. Then...
Deities from ten thousand world-systems will assemble and, thinking, "Today the Teacher attains final nibbāna; today the Dispensation declines;

this is our last sight of him," they will manifest even greater compassion than on the day the One of Ten Powers passed away—except for those who have reached the state of non-returning and whose taints are exhausted, who are unable to maintain their own physical bodies.
They were unable [to extinguish it], for from the relic-body the fire-element will rise up and ascend as far as the Brahma-world.
As long as there is even a mustard-seed-sized portion of the relics, there will be a single flame; when the relics have been completely consumed, it will be cut off.
Having thus displayed such great majesty, once the relics have vanished, the Dispensation (sāsana) is said to have vanished. Up to this point...
It does not disappear; as long as it has not disappeared, the Dispensation remains.

From the time of the final *parinibbāna* until the relics remain even for the size of a mustard seed, this period must not be understood as being after the time of the Buddha. For as long as the relics persist, the Buddhas persist;
therefore, the arising of another Buddha during this interval is indeed precluded. It is for this very reason that we say so.
After the time of his final Nibbāna, the relics remain;
the Fully Awakened One is as if not yet extinguished, for they are withheld from any other Buddha.
Whether the Fully Awakened One is still living or the Tathāgata has passed away, [the relics remain].
"Whoever performs equal worship, the fruit thereof shall be equal.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Section on Nibbāna, within the Dhamma-vaṇṇanā of the Sīmavisodhana, composed by the Elder Sāgarabuddhi.
4. *Samasīsikaṇḍa* (The Chapter on the Equal-Headed):

Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the phrase, "And the Saṅgha is rare in the world. In this context, "Saṅgha" is twofold, according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) and the conventional sense (*sammuti*).
Among these, the Saṅgha in the ultimate sense consists of the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals, and even the forty [arahants].

There are eight hundred types of persons; thus, there are four kinds [of pairs]. In that regard, by way of summary, there is one pair consisting of the one standing on the path of stream-entry and the one established in its fruit;

one pair consisting of the one standing on the path of once-returning and the one established in its fruit; one pair consisting of the one standing on the path of non-returning and the one established in its fruit;
and one pair consisting of the one standing on the path of arahantship and the one established in its fruit—thus there are four pairs of persons (*purisayuga*). There are four who stand on the paths.

There are eight types of persons consisting of those established in the four fruits. As for the forty persons: there are twenty persons established in the paths—five for each path, such as the one standing on the path to stream-entry, categorized by way of the first jhāna and so forth;
likewise, five for each of the paths to once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship.
Similarly, there are twenty persons established in the fruits—five for each fruit, such as the one established in the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

There are forty persons who are possessors of the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*). Now, since the path (*magga*) lasts for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*), how can there be twenty persons who are possessors of the path? It is said in reply:

because of the influence of either the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*), the jhāna attained through reflection (*sammasitajjhāna*), the individual’s disposition toward jhāna (*puggalajjhāsaya*), or any one of these, there arises the manifestation of factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) corresponding to that particular jhāna.
The four types of persons standing on the path, receiving the designations of "first-jhāna" and so forth, are each divided fivefold;

therefore, there are twenty types of persons standing on the path. Among those, whichever jhāna—whether the first jhāna or another—one enters, and having emerged from it, contemplates formations (*saṅkhāra*), such that insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*) proceeds, that is the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).

Because it serves as the proximate cause for insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*). Whatever jhāna is practiced by one who is contemplating [the aggregates], that is the "jhāna being contemplated.

Thus, the inclination arises in the practitioner: "O, may there be for me a path consisting of five factors similar to the first jhāna, or a path consisting of four factors and so forth, similar to any one of the second jhāna and the rest. This is the aspiration that has arisen.

This is called the inclination of the individual (*puggalajjhāsaya*). In this regard, for one who has entered any one of the jhānas beginning with the first, emerged from it, and then developed the path by contemplating miscellaneous formations (*pakiṇṇakasaṅkhāra*), that path of his resembles that particular foundational jhāna, such as the first jhāna and so forth.
However, if there is no jhāna whatsoever to serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanāpādaka*), [then it is] merely—
When the path has been generated by contemplating one of the jhānas, such as the first jhāna, it resembles that jhāna which was contemplated.

However, when the path is generated after entering a certain jhāna and then contemplating something else, it then resembles one or the other of those two according to the individual's inclination (*ajjhāsaya*).
Thus it is for one whose vehicle is serenity (*samathayānika*).

Because the path-factor consisting of any one of the jhānas, such as the first jhāna, arises for a worldling or for a noble one—either by way of a foundational jhāna, a jhāna attained through insight, or according to the individual’s inclination toward a particular jhāna—there are twenty individuals established on the path based on these personal differences;
likewise, there are twenty established in the fruition. Thus, there are forty noble individuals. Furthermore, if...

However, for such a person, there is no such underlying disposition; rather, having emerged from each successive lower jhāna in forward order and having comprehended the phenomena of each successively higher jhāna, the path produced is similar to the jhāna that was comprehended, regardless of the foundational jhāna.
Or, having emerged from each successively higher jhāna in reverse order, [one comprehends] the phenomena of each successive lower jhāna...
The path produced by reviewing is similar to the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*), as it does not look back toward the jhāna that was being reviewed;

for each successive jhāna is stronger than the preceding one. Regarding the "eight hundred types of persons," there are three kinds of stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*): the "one-seeder" (*ekabījī*), the "family-to-family" (*kolaṅkola*), and the "seven-times-at-most" (*sattakkhattuparama*).
There are three kinds of once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) who have attained the fruit within the realms of sense-desire, fine-materiality, and immateriality.

All of these together amount to twenty-four, by way of the four modes of progress (*paṭipadā*): painful progress with slow direct knowledge (*dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*), painful progress with quick direct knowledge (*dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā*), pleasant progress with slow direct knowledge (*sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*), and pleasant progress with quick direct knowledge (*sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā*).

These include those who attain *parinibbāna* in the interval (*antarā-parinibbāyī*), those who attain *parinibbāna* upon landing (*upahacca-parinibbāyī*), those who attain *parinibbāna* with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*), and those who attain *parinibbāna* without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*).
"One who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm": there are five types in the Aviha [heaven], likewise five in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī [heavens].

In the Akaniṭṭha [heaven], however, there are four—excluding the one who goes upstream—namely, the one who attains nibbāna in the interval, the one who attains nibbāna upon landing, the one who attains nibbāna with exertion, and the one who attains nibbāna without exertion.
Thus, there are twenty-four non-returners (anāgāmin). The dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and the one whose vehicle is calm (samathayānika).
There are two who are Arahants and four who are established on the paths;
thus, all fifty-four become doubled as those belonging to the vehicles of faith (*saddhādhura*) and wisdom (*paññādhura*), making eight hundred noble persons (*ariyapuggala*).
All these noble persons, who were enumerated in detail as "eight hundred," are, in brief, one according to the pairs: the path-attainer and the fruition-attainer for stream-entry (*sotāpatti*).

By means of the passage beginning with "the pairs," there are only four. For this very reason, it is said in the *Ratanaparitta*: "Those individuals who are praised as one hundred and eight—these consist of four pairs.
This classification is obtained by way of a mixture among those established in the paths and those established in the fruits;

however, the classification into meditators (*jhānika*) and insight-workers (*vipassaka*) is obtained only among those established in the fruits, because the path exists for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).
