It is not found among those standing on the path. Therein, the one standing in the fruit of stream-entry is twofold:

by way of one possessing jhāna and by way of a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*). Among them, the person possessing jhāna attains Arahantship in that very existence and attains final Nibbāna;

or, failing to attain it, having gone to the Brahma-world, he is called "one possessing jhāna. However, in the *Mūlaṭīkā*, it is stated that when there is attachment (*nikanti*), ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others [who have attained jhāna]—regarding the jhāna they have obtained as appropriate—...

In the case of those who have become [Arahants] belonging to the pure abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), they are reborn anywhere except there; likewise, even in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), they are reborn by the power of sense-sphere karma.
For it is said: "Monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.
However, because non-returners (*anāgāmin*) have completely abandoned sensual lust, they do not produce attachment toward sense-sphere existences; thus, they are excluded from the sense-world.
It is said: "The plane of what has been obtained is wherever one is reborn.

For it is understood that because attachment to the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) has been abandoned only by the non-returner (anāgāmī), the arising of stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and once-returners (sakadāgāmī) in the sense-sphere existence through the power of sense-sphere karma remains unprevented as long as they still possess attachment;
therefore, "he has gone to the Brahma-world without having reached [the higher planes]; he is a jhānika..."
It should be understood that the term "name" is stated here by way of the majority of cases. Furthermore, the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*) is of three types:
the one-seeder (*ekabījī*), the family-to-family (*kolaṅkola*), and the seven-times-at-most (*sattakkhattuparama*).

Among these, one who—whether in the human world or in the six celestial worlds—obtains only a single rebirth-linking and then attains *arahantship* and passes away into final *nibbāna*, is called a "one-seeder. For such a person, there is only one rebirth-linking in the human world.
In the world of the gods, having taken one or two rebirths, and thus reaching a maximum of three, four, five, or six, one attains *arahantship* and passes into final *nibbāna*;

this is called a "one who goes from family to family" (*kolaṅkolo*). Another, having become a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) in the human world, takes one rebirth in the world of the gods, and then returning once more to the human world, takes one [rebirth];
thus, by way of alternating between the human and divine worlds, there—
By the passage beginning "four here, three there," and so on, up to "one here," it refers to one who, having undergone seven rebirths, attains final nibbāna;

this is called the "seven-times-at-most" (sattakkhattuparama). However, this should be understood as taking rebirths exclusively—either seven times only in the human world or seven times only in the deva worlds—and not mixed. Others, however, say: "seven from here, seven from there..."
Because it is stated, "wandering in saṃsāra," they say that for one who has "seven births at most," this refers to seven rebirths in the human world and seven rebirths in the deva world.

That is incorrect; why? Because it contradicts the canonical text (Pāḷi): "Even though they may be exceedingly negligent, they do not undergo an eighth existence. Furthermore, even a once-returner (sakadāgāmī) is limited to two existences.
It might be thought that because one who has come to the human world twice would have one [return] there and one here—thus obtaining two opportunities—one should not view it in that way.
A *sakadāgāmī* (once-returner) is so called because they come this human world once more;
having reached here, they attain final nibbāna here; having reached there, they attain final nibbāna there; or having reached there, they attain final nibbāna here.
"One who attains final nibbāna there after having arrived here" refers to the fifth among the five types of once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*).
If this is so, one might ask: how can the four types beginning with "one who attains final nibbāna here after having arrived here" be considered once-returners?
They are called once-returners in the sense that they return [to this world] only once more. Because craving for sensual pleasures has been entirely abandoned, [they do not return] to this...

One who does not return to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*); the intended meaning is that they always return only to the Brahma-world by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Let this be so for one who possesses jhāna; but how is it for the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*)?

He too goes having become one who possesses jhāna, for even if he is killed by lions, tigers, and the like along the way, he applies the three characteristics [to his death] and thus becomes one who possesses jhāna.

Having offered [the sacrifice], death indeed occurs; this, however, is called "one who has at most one more existence" (*ekakkhattuparama*) by way of rebirth in the fine-material or immaterial realms.

Noble ones (*ariya*) such as those who have "at most seven more existences" (*sattakkhattuparama*), although they may take many rebirths in the fine-material and immaterial worlds, are said to have "only one rebirth" due to their commonality with the Brahma-world.

An *arahant*, however, is so called because he is devoid of the capacity to do evil (*raha*); furthermore, because he is incapable of being reborn again into existence after attaining *arahantship*, and so forth.

One who is worthy (*arahā*) by way of the meaning of the word is also threefold, according to the categories of the one possessing jhāna (*jhānika*), the one practicing dry insight (*sukkhavipassaka*), and the one who has attained the summit simultaneously with the path (*samasīsī*).
Among these, the one possessing jhāna arrives [at the fruit] by means of the path itself; he is called "one who has attained the analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidāppatta*).

Furthermore, another person, having become one possessing jhāna within the continuum of an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) or a trainee (*sekkha*), produces the path by making jhāna the basis; he too is one possessing jhāna. The one practicing dry insight...
However, there is no such thing as "future-jhāna" that arises together with the path other than the mere destruction of the defilements;

some say that this [jhāna] later falls away. But the "one who reaches the goal simultaneously" (samasīsī) is of three kinds: the one whose posture is simultaneous, the one whose illness is simultaneous, and the one whose life is simultaneous.
Among these, he who—having been endowed with whichever posture among the postures such as standing and so forth—[practices] insight...
One who exerts effort and, having attained Arahantship through that very posture, attains Parinibbāna—this is called "one for whom the end is simultaneous with the posture" (*iriyāpatha-samasīsī*).

Furthermore, one who, having fallen ill, establishes insight while still within the illness, attains Arahantship and passes away from that very illness—this is called "one for whom the end is simultaneous with the illness" (*roga-samasīsī*).
Furthermore, among the thirteen types of "heads," the head of defilements (*kilesa-sīsa*)...
The path of arahantship exhausts ignorance; the death-consciousness exhausts the life-faculty, which is the head of the process of existence.
This is called "that which has its head at the same time as life. In this context, what are the thirteen heads? They are:
the head of impediments, the head of the bond of craving, the head of conceit and misapprehension, the head of the distraction of views, and the head of restlessness and defilements.

It has ignorance as its head for resolution, faith as its head for exertion, energy as its head for establishment, mindfulness as its head for non-distraction, concentration as its head for seeing, wisdom as its head for occurrence, the life-faculty as its head for the domain, and liberation as its head for formations.
And herein, the path-consciousness that exhausts ignorance is able to exhaust the life-faculty; [it is] that which exhausts life—

The final consciousness (*cuticitta*) is unable to eradicate ignorance (*avijjā*); the consciousness that eradicates ignorance is one thing, while the consciousness that eradicates the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is another.
But how is this "head" made equal? By way of equality of occasion (*vāra*).

For at whichever occasion the emergence of the Path occurs, there are five kinds of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*) in the stream-entry path: by way of reviewing the Path, the Fruit, Nibbāna, and the defilements abandoned.
Likewise, there are five knowledges on the path of once-returning, five on the path of non-returning, and four on the path of arahantship because of the absence of remaining defilements.

Thus, having established nineteen moments of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), and having descended into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) to attain final Nibbāna, this exhaustion of both heads by way of these twelve equalities is indeed called "equal. And on the path of arahantship, it is the head of the process (*pavatti-sīsa*).
Although the Path, emerging from the process of existence (*pavatti*), consumes the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) by preventing its further occurrence beyond the moment of death (*cuti*),
it is said that the life-faculty— the head of the process— consumes the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) because it possesses the nature of occurring until the very moment of death.
By means of the Path-consciousness, which brings about the exhaustion of the defilements (*kilesa*), [the fruit] must be produced immediately following itself.

The sections on reviewing are indeed complete. Because they consist of the reviewing of defilements already abandoned by way of their completion, they deserve to be called "sections on the exhaustion of defilements.

For that very reason, having equated the exhaustion of ignorance—the head of the defilements—with the exhaustion of the life-faculty—the head of the process of existence—through this equality of the sections, [the exhaustion of defilements and the exhaustion of life]...
"It should be understood as 'without before or after'"—so it was said. However, in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"That person for whom the exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after is a person who is 'equal-headed' (*samasīsī*).
And here, there are two heads: the head of occurrence (*pavatti-sīsa*) and the head of defilements (*kilesa-sīsa*). Among these, the "head of occurrence" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

Ignorance (avijjā) is called the "head of the defilements" (kilesasīsa). Among these, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is exhausted by the death-consciousness (cuticitta), and ignorance is exhausted by the path-consciousness (maggacitta).
There is no simultaneous arising of these two types of consciousness. However, immediately after the path comes the fruition (phala); immediately after the fruition, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
and having emerged from the life-continuum, the reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa) becomes complete. Is that [reviewing] incomplete? [It is not. By means of the sharp...
"For even when one's head is being cut off with a sword, one or two moments of reflection necessarily arise;

however, because of the rapid succession of mental states (*citta*), the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) and the exhaustion of life appear as if they occur at the same moment," so it is said.
And in the commentary on that passage: "'Of two mental states' refers to the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*) and the path-consciousness (*magga-citta*). 'That'..."
There is a deficiency of conditions. [The javana process] is complete when it occurs seven times; it is incomplete when it occurs five times.
Although it is stated that "one or two [resultants arise]," that statement was made for the sake of euphony.
They say that at the very least, one or two registration-minds (*tadārammaṇa-citta*) occur, meaning that at minimum two arise.
It has been stated. And here, by this passage from the *Aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*: “Complete [consciousness] occurs seven times through the occurrence of impulsion-minds;

incomplete [consciousness] occurs five times,” it is shown that for those who die simultaneously with their attainment (*samasīsī*), there is occurrence seven times in a complete manner and five times in an incomplete manner within the death-proximate cognitive process, by way of reviewing.
It should be understood that the conclusion here is simply that the functional impulsions (kriya-javana) run their course.
Furthermore, because it is stated that "one dies undeluded," it is known that the occurrence of the impulsions at the time near death takes place in a complete cycle of seven.
This being so, regarding the phrase "but when the occurrence is sluggish, as at the time of death and so forth, only five times," the term "sluggish occurrence" [is used].
The qualification may be purposeful. Regarding the phrase “only five times,” here the word “only” (eva) excludes six or seven times during periods of weak occurrence;
however, it permits even six or seven times during periods of non-confusion.

Furthermore, the number of sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) javanas is not fixed, for they reach their full complement even during periods of strength; thus, [it is said]: “during a period of strength of the sense-sphere javanas...”
"In the case of slow functioning, there are seven or six times; however, at the time of death and so forth, there are only five times.
In the case of quick functioning, such as during the Blessed One’s Twin Miracle and similar occasions, there arise four or five moments of javana consciousness consisting of reflection.
Thus, the occurrence [of these moments] by way of an unspecified measure is also mentioned in this section on the "Instruction on Equal Heads" (Samasīsī-niddesa).

Since a process-consciousness (vīthicitta) at the moment of death cannot be found separately, and since final Nibbāna occurs by means of the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta) immediately following the reviewing consciousness, seven impulsion moments (javana-cittāni) are to be expected in their full form;
this is our own view, which should be examined and accepted, or else any more suitable method that may be found should be sought. Thus, [the Sangha is defined] by way of the ultimate Sangha.

When all are combined—the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals, the forty-five types of persons, and even the one hundred and twenty-eight types of persons—it should be understood that the Saṅgha is also difficult to find in this world.
For noble persons (ariyapuggala) are exceedingly rare;
even during the time when the Dispensation (sāsana) exists, since even a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is currently non-existent, this is an investigation into the ultimate Saṅgha.
Furthermore, the conventional Saṅgha consists of those who have received full ordination through the formal procedure of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*);

it is indeed difficult to find. Why? Because it is obtainable only at a time when a Buddha has appeared. For even though hundreds of thousands or more Pacceka Buddhas may arise when no Buddha has appeared, one cannot obtain full ordination in their presence; for in the presence of Pacceka Buddhas—
Because it was impossible for them to give even the meditation subject of going for refuge to sons of good family who had gone forth;
and because those known as paccekabuddhas, like a mute person seeing a dream, were unable to explain to others the true Dhamma they themselves had attained,
they were therefore incapable of ordaining them and directing them to a meditation subject, [saying], "In this way you should wear your robes..."
"In this manner they should be clothed," and by such methods as these, they taught them only the training of proper conduct (*abhisamācārika*).
Therefore, the conventional Saṅgha (*sammuti-saṅgha*) is found at the very time of a Buddha’s appearance. Moreover, they are not difficult to find;
rather, even for a very small act performed with reference to them, there is an incalculable fruit. For this was said by the Blessed One: "But there will be, Ānanda..."
In the future, Ānanda, there will be those belonging to the lineage, with yellow robes around their necks, who are immoral and of evil character.
When people give a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha for the sake of those immoral ones, then, Ānanda, I declare that the offering made to the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable;
yet, Ānanda, by no means whatsoever do I say that an offering made to individuals is equal to an offering made to the Saṅgha.
“I say it is of great fruit. For thus it is stated in the *Uparipaṇṇāsa* in the commentary on the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga*:
“When a gift is given to the Saṅgha by those with yellow robes around their necks, that offering is also incalculable because of the incalculability of its virtues.

Indeed, an offering directed toward the Saṅgha belongs to one who is able to show reverence toward the Saṅgha; for such reverence toward the Saṅgha is difficult to perform. One who [thinks], “That which is directed toward the Saṅgha...”
Having prepared a gift with the thought, "I will give a donation," he goes to the monastery and says, "Venerable sir, please assign one elder for the sake of the Saṅgha.

If, after receiving a novice from the Saṅgha, he falls into a state of mental change, thinking, "I have obtained a novice," then that donation does not go to the Saṅgha. Even if he obtains a great elder... [he thinks], "A great elder..."
Even for one who feels joy thinking, "I have received it," [the gift] does not truly go to the Saṅgha.
However, when someone— whether it be a novice, one who has been ordained, a junior, an elder, a fool, or a wise person—
having received anything from the Saṅgha, becomes free of doubt and, with respect toward the Saṅgha, thinks, "I give this to the Saṅgha," [then the gift goes to the Saṅgha].
If one is able to do so, that gift is said to have "gone to the Saṅgha. It is said that those living beyond the ocean act in this way:
there, a householder who is the owner of a monastery, thinking "I shall give a gift that has gone to the Saṅgha," requests from the Saṅgha, saying, "Give me one monk.
Having obtained a single monk of immoral conduct, he [prepares] a sitting place...
Having had the ground leveled, having prepared a seat, having tied a canopy above, and having honored [the Sangha] with perfumes, incense, and flowers, he washed his feet and anointed them;
then, as if performing an act of prostration toward the Buddha, he gave gifts to the Sangha with deep reverence.
After the meal, that bhikkhu, for the purpose of looking after the monastery, went to the house door and said, "Give me a hoe."
An *upāsaka* arrived and, while still seated, kicked a pickaxe with his foot and said, "Take it!
People said to him, "It was impossible for you to show such honor to him this morning; now there is not even a trace of respect left. What is this?
The *upāsaka* replied, "That gentleman’s devotion belongs to the Saṅgha, not to him. [This concludes] the section on the offering given to the Saṅgha by one wearing the saffron robe around his neck.
But who purifies it? The eighty great elders, such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, purify it;
moreover, although those elders have long since attained final nibbāna, starting from them down to the present day, those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) while still living purify it indeed.

For in this way, a gift becomes of great fruit both on account of the donor and on account of the recipient. Regarding the donor, the Vessantara Jātaka should be told, for Vessantara... [gave] to one of immoral conduct.
Having given his two sons, Jālī and Kaṇhājina, who were like the eyes of the brahmin Jūjaka, he caused the earth to quake.
He caused the earth to quake because of the greatness of the volition directed toward omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). Thus, it is of great fruit even from the perspective of the donor.
Furthermore, regarding the recipient, the story of the thief-killer given to the Elder Sāriputta should be told. [The thief-killer...]

Indeed, in Sāvatthī there was a certain man from the countryside who, having committed the work of an executioner for twenty-five years, continued to perform that work even in his old age for another thirty years, cutting off ears, noses, and so forth by means of the breath from his nostrils alone;
thus fifty-five years passed while he was engaged in the work of an executioner. Even as he lay upon his deathbed, by the power of his own karma—
He was distressed, making a great noise as if he had been reborn in the Great Hell; terrified by his sound, the people abandoned their houses on both sides and fled.
Then, the Elder Sāriputta, surveying the world with his divine eye, saw him and, out of compassion for him, stood at the door of his house. He [the man] became enraged.

Although he tried three times to blow it out with the breath from his nose, being unable to extinguish it, and seeing the Elder shining with great splendor, he was filled with extreme faith and gave him the milk-rice he had prepared for his own sake.
The Elder, having increased his merit, departed. Recalling the gift given to the Elder, the executioner was reborn in heaven; thus it was.
It is also of great fruit because of the recipient. It is of great fruit because of both;
this should be understood as the case with the gifts given by Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and others to the one headed by the Buddha.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Whether toward the Tathāgata, the Fully Awakened One, or toward his disciple, when the mind is full of serene confidence, there is no such thing as a small gift.
Thus, the Buddhas are inconceivable; the qualities of the Buddhas are inconceivable.”
“For those with faith in the inconceivable, the result is inconceivable.
Thus, the state of being of great fruit should be understood by way of both [the donor and the recipient].

It is indeed fruitless from the perspective of either the donor or the recipient—just as, for example, the specific offerings made to teachers such as Makkhali Gosāla and others by their own followers who held wrong views.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusa grass;
he does not equal even a sixteenth part of those things that are conditioned.”

For this very reason, the Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four purifications of offerings. These three—namely, the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—are called “jewels” (ratana) in the sense that they produce delight for the virtuous.
For it has been said:
“Honored, of great value, incomparable, and rare to behold;”
“Because it is enjoyed by beings who are peerless, it is therefore called a ‘jewel’ (ratana).
And what is called a jewel is twofold, by way of being sentient or insentient.

Therein, the insentient consists of the wheel-jewel, the gem-jewel, or whatever else such as gold and silver not bound to sense-faculties. The sentient consists of those beginning with the elephant-jewel and horse-jewel, ending with the counselor-jewel.”
Or whatever else is bound to the faculties. Of these two kinds, the sentient jewel is declared to be the foremost.
Why? Because insentient jewels—such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls—are brought forward for the purpose of adorning sentient jewels, such as hand-jewels and the like.
Sentient jewels are also of two kinds: animal jewels and human jewels.
Among these, the human jewel is declared to be the foremost. Why? Because the animal jewel serves as a mount for the human jewel.
The human jewel is also twofold: the woman-jewel and the man-jewel. Among these, the man-jewel is declared to be the foremost. Why?
Because the woman-jewel enters into the role of an attendant to the man-jewel.
The jewel among men is also twofold: the householder-jewel and the homeless-jewel; therein, the homeless-jewel is declared to be supreme.

Why? Because even a wheel-turning monarch, the foremost among householders, having bowed down with the fivefold prostration, attended upon, and served the homeless-jewel who is endowed with virtues such as morality, attains celestial and human prosperity.
At the end, one attains the perfection of Nibbāna. The jewel of the homeless life is also twofold, according to the noble ones (ariya) and worldlings (puthujjana).

The jewel of the noble ones is also twofold, according to those in training (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha). The jewel of those beyond training is also twofold, according to those who practice pure insight (sukkha-vipassaka) and those whose vehicle is serenity (samatha-yānika).

The jewel of those whose vehicle is serenity is also twofold: those who have attained the perfection of discipleship (sāvaka-pāramī) and those who have not. Among these, [the jewel] that has attained the perfection of discipleship...

It is declared to be supreme. Why? Because of the greatness of its qualities. Even compared to the jewel of a disciple who has attained perfection, the jewel of a *paccekabuddha* (solitary enlightened one) is declared to be supreme.

Why? Because of the greatness of its qualities. For even many hundreds of disciples like Sāriputta and Moggallāna do not approach even a hundredth part of the qualities of a *paccekabuddha*. Compared to the *paccekabuddha*, the jewel of a *sambuddha* (fully enlightened one)...

It is declared the foremost. Why? Because of the greatness of his qualities, even all the Paccekabuddhas who sit cross-legged throughout the entire Jambudīpa without their knees touching one another do not equal even a fraction, a number, or a calculable part of the qualities of a single [Buddha].
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless... [etc. ...the Tathāgata is the foremost among them."

"...is declared supreme," and so forth. Thus, by way of extracting the meaning of these three phrases—"The Buddha is rare in the world, the hearing of the True Dhamma is also [rare], and the Saṅgha is rare in the world"—the entire meaning has been fully stated.
Thus ends the commentary on the Saṅgha in the *Sīmavisodhana* composed by the Elder Sāgarabuddhi.
The Fourth Chapter: The Section on Equal Heads.
The Miscellaneous Section.
Now follows the sequence for the commentary on the passage beginning with "Good persons are rare. For indeed, in this world, good persons...
They are indeed exceedingly rare. "True persons" (*sappurisa*) refers to supreme beings endowed with excellent qualities.
By relying on them, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth, and beings subject to death are liberated from death. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Indeed, Ānanda, by coming to me as a good friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), beings are liberated from birth; beings subject to aging are liberated from aging."
Furthermore, according to the word "and so forth," only a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is called a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitta) who is endowed with all excellent qualities.

If one does not find such a person, one may rely on noble individuals (ariyapuggala) such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others. If even they are not available, one must find a good friend who has entirely abandoned [unwholesome states] and is intent upon the auspicious goal;
for this was said by the ancients:
“Dear, respected, and inspiring; one who speaks and is patient with what is said;

one who delivers profound discourse and does not urge [one] toward what is inappropriate”—a wise person endowed with such qualities as these, standing on the side of progress, is indeed rare in the world. What kind of person is the wise one?
The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the eighty great disciples, and other disciples of the Tathāgata— such as Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Vidhura, Sarabhaṅga, Mahosadha, Sutasoma,
Nimi-rāja, Ayoghara-kumāra, Akatti-paṇḍita, and others— should be understood as "wise ones. Like protection in times of fear, like lamps in the darkness,

or like the acquisition of food and drink when overcome by the sufferings of hunger and thirst, they are capable of destroying all fears, calamities, and misfortunes for those who act according to their word.

For it is so: by relying on the Tathāgata, incalculable and immeasurable gods and humans have attained the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) and established themselves in the Brahma-world or been reborn in the world of the gods.

Having inspired confidence in the Elder Sāriputta and having attended upon the Elder with the four requisites, eighty thousand who were virtuous were reborn in heaven; likewise [those who did so] for Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others.
Some disciples of the Teacher Sunetta were reborn in the Brahma-world;
some were reborn in companionship with the Paranimmitavasavatti gods... [and so on] ...some were reborn in companionship with great householder families.
For it has been said: "Monks, there is no fear for one who is wise; there is no calamity for one who is wise."

“An affliction comes from the wise. Furthermore, the wise person is like a fragrant substance such as tagara or garlands, while one who associates with them is like a leaf used to wrap that fragrant substance.
For it is said in the Nāradajātakaya:
“If a man wraps tagara with a palāsa leaf;”
"Even the winds blow fragrant; such is the result of associating with the wise.
When the wise Akitti was offered a boon by Sakka, lord of the devas, he spoke thus:
"One should see the wise, hear the wise, and dwell together with the wise."
"Engage in conversation and discourse with the wise, and you will find it pleasing.
What has the wise one done for you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa;
why do you long for the sight of the wise one?"
The wise person follows the right method and does not employ what is improper;
he becomes more excellent than other men and does not become angry when spoken to rightly.
He understands discipline; it is good to be in his company.
Furthermore, even when associating with those true persons (sappurisa), one hears speech never heard before that brings benefit to both worlds; for it has been said:
“The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is supreme: speak the Dhamma, not what is contrary to the Dhamma—this is the second [criterion].
Speak what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant—this is the third. Speak the truth, not what is false—this is the fourth.”
“The speech that the Buddha utters for the attainment of Nibbāna,
for the making of an end to suffering— that indeed is the supreme among speeches.

It is precisely through the condition of relying upon and attending to true persons, and by means of engaging in wholesome deeds such as giving, that they are liberated from the suffering of the woeful states.
For this has been said: "Moreover, it is meritorious deeds alone that are of great benefit to living beings, because they provide protection from the suffering of hell and other realms;
and for those [beings] as well, the recollection of such benefits and gratitude are causes for attaining various distinguished qualities—such as being praised by the virtuous—and so forth.
This was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, two persons are rare in the world. Which two?'"

"Two: he who acts first, and he who is grateful and mindful of what has been done. Furthermore, even at times such as those during the *Vidhura-paṇḍita-jātaka* and the *Mahosadha-jātaka*, they properly employ those who follow their word for the sake of success in this world and the next.

By means of the steadfast application of orderly work, through knowledge of the proper time, acting appropriately, being untiring, through balance in exertion and energy, and through non-addiction, they avoid transgressing the right time, doing what is inappropriate, and failing to act or acting with laxity.
Occupations such as cattle-rearing and trade, when free from unwholesome states (akusala) and the like, are undertaken through one’s own skill or that of one’s wife, children, slaves, or laborers;
these serve as causes for obtaining wealth, grain, and prosperity in this very life.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"One who acts appropriately, is steadfast, and possesses the energy of exertion finds wealth;
but for one whose habit is to sleep by day, who shows no diligence in rising at night,
who is ever negligent and addicted to drink— it is impossible for such a person to maintain a household."
"Too cold, too hot, too much diarrhea"—
thus do matters pass by for the youth who has neglected his duties.
But he who regards neither cold nor heat as mere blades of grass...
“Having performed the duties of a true person, he does not depart from happiness.
And: “For one who amasses wealth and squanders it upon others alone, his riches go toward accumulation, just as an anthill is built up.”
Such distinguished types of true persons (sappurisa) are extremely rare in the world.

By contrast, through their absence, base persons (duppurisa)—foolish folk who are found even when one does not seek them—cause those who associate with them to sink further into the suffering of *saṃsāra* amidst other people; they do not grant liberation from existence (*bhava*).
For instance, there were the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, as well as Devadatta, Kokālika, and Modaka Tissa.
Khaṇḍadeviyāputta, Samuddadatta, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others in the past obtained long-lasting suffering;
these and other such beings are fools who, like a house set ablaze by fire, destroy themselves and those who follow their words because of their own wrong grasp.
For instance, through Devadatta, King Ajātasattu, Kokālika, and others [met with ruin].
At that time, other individuals as well were reborn in the woeful states.
Had King Ajātasattu not killed his father at the time he was listening to the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, he would have become a stream-enterer;
however, because he killed his father, without even reaching the path and its fruit, he will boil in the Iron Cauldron for sixty thousand years and afterwards will become a Paccekabuddha.

“Kokālika, too, failing to show respect for the elder monks Sāriputta and Moggallāna, was reborn in the Mahāniraya hell, in a place within that hell where the lotuses are counted; he fell into the Paduma hell...

[as before] ...And as for the monk who was reborn in the Paduma hell, it was the monk Kokālika, who had harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna. In this context, “a certain monk” refers to—

To a certain bhikkhu who was sitting there, his name and clan unknown, and who had asked the question, "Venerable sir, how long indeed is the lifespan in the Paduma hell?", he spoke thus: "Long, bhikkhu, is the lifespan in hell;
it is not easy to calculate it as 'this many years,' or 'this many hundreds of years,' or 'this many..."
“Is it possible, Bhante, to provide a simile for ‘thousands of years’ or ‘hundreds of thousands of years’?
“It is possible, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a Kosalan cartload of sesame seeds consisting of twenty khāris.
If a man were to remove a single sesame seed from it at the end of every hundred or thousand years, [the exhaustion of that load would take longer than the aeon].”
“Indeed, bhikkhus, that Kosalan sesame-cartload of twenty khāris would be exhausted and consumed more quickly by this method than even a single Abbuda hell.
Just as, bhikkhus, is one Abbuda hell, so too is one Nirabbuda hell,” and so forth.
“Twenty khāris” means, according to the Magadhan measure, four...
In the kingdom of Kosala, one *pattha* is a measure. Four *patthas* make an *āḷhaka*; four *āḷhakas* make a *doṇa*; four *doṇas* make a *mānikā*; four *mānikās* make a *khārī*.
Twenty *khāris* make a cartload of sesame seeds (*tilavāha*). A "cartload of sesame seeds" refers to a cart filled with sesame.
Regarding the "Avīci hell": there is no separate hell named Avīci; rather, it is within the Avīci [hell]...
Thus, by way of the *abbuda* calculation, the corresponding period is called "the *abbuda* hell. This same method applies to the *nirabbuda* and subsequent hells as well.
Therein, the calculation of years should be understood in this way, as it has been said: "One hundred times one hundred thousand makes a *koṭi*;
likewise, one hundred thousand *koṭis* is what is called a *pakoṭi*. One hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is what is called a *koṭipakoṭi*. One hundred thousand *koṭipakoṭis*..."
"A *nahuta* [is the next unit]. A hundred times a hundred thousand *nahutas* is a *ninnahuta*. A hundred times a hundred thousand *ninnahutas* is one *abbuda*.
Twenty times that is a *nirabbuda*. This same method applies everywhere; and this calculation is difficult for those who are unacquainted with it. Thus it was said:
"It is not easy to calculate," some say, referring both to the variety of lamentations therein and the variety of the workings of karma.
They say these names were obtained [in this way]. Others, however, say it was due to the causes of his speech; such is the explanation in the *Ṭīkā* and *Netti*.

And just as Dīghavidāghāta fell prone for sixty *yojanas* into the Great Hell and is cooked there until the end of the Buddha-interval, and just as the five hundred families who delighted in his views have arisen in his very companionship.
They are cooked in the great hell. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Just as, monks, a reed-hut or a grass-hut, when struck by fire, burns down the gabled houses—those plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with doors fitted and windows closed—even so, monks, whatever fears arise, all arise from the fool.”
No calamities whatsoever arise from the wise; no afflictions whatsoever... [and so on] ...no [calamities or afflictions arise] from the wise.
Thus, monks, the fool is full of danger while the wise person is free from danger; the fool is beset by calamities while the wise person is free from calamities;
the fool is beset by afflictions while the wise person is free from afflictions. Furthermore, the fool is like a putrid fish, while the wise person is like a bowl tied to that putrid fish.
One who associates with such a person becomes like a rotting fish. One falls into a state of being discarded and loathed by the wise. This has also been stated in the Nāradajātakaya:
“When a man carries a rotting fish on the tip of a blade of kusa grass, the kusa grass itself reeks of rot;
so too is the association with fools.”
When Sakka, the lord of the devas, was granting boons, the wise Akatti also spoke thus:
“May I neither see nor hear a fool, nor dwell together with a fool;
may I neither engage in conversation or discourse with a fool, nor take pleasure in him.”
What has this fool done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa;
for what reason, Kassapa, do you not wish to see this fool?
This witless man leads one astray and yokes one to what is burdensome.
"One of poor judgment is better when he is superior; he becomes agitated when spoken to rightly.
He does not understand discipline; it is good not to see him.
Thus, all fears and calamities arise solely through association with fools and the wicked, and not through service to the wise; for truly noble persons are exceedingly rare.
Now:
“Human birth is difficult to obtain, and the arising of a Buddha is difficult to obtain;
the perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to obtain, and the True Dhamma is most difficult to obtain.”
The turn has come for the commentary on this verse. Therein, "human birth is hard to obtain" means that even the state of being human is indeed difficult to find;
the rarity of the human condition is to be understood through such similes as that of the blind tortoise.
It is said that once there was a farmer who, having plowed for three years along the bank of the Ganges and obtained not even a little [crop], split his plowshare in two.
Having broken them, he threw them into the Gaṅgā; by the current of the river Gaṅgā, one was carried upstream and one downstream.
Thus, as two plowshares were being swept away in the Gaṅgā, after a long time, one would be above and one below;
only when the two came together would they join back into their original state. At that moment, there was a blind tortoise that surfaces only once every hundred thousand years.
At the moment he was plunging down, his neck was positioned between two plowshares;
this moment is indeed difficult to obtain, and in the same way, human existence is also difficult to obtain.

For, failing to attain human existence, one wanders only among the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, asuras, and animals, unable even to lift up one's head for one, two, or three intervals between Buddhas.
The four intervals between Buddhas, by way of one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), exceed the range of calculation for beings being cooked in hell;

likewise, even in the realms of ghosts, asuras, and animals, with an extremely minute individual existence (*attabhāva*)— measuring no more than a fraction of a sesame seed, a grain of rice, or a mustard seed,
specifically the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, or eighth part of a kalā— one occupies a spot on the ground no larger than the space covered by a finger.
They exceed even the range of calculation for the extremely minute beings seated there;
indeed, who else besides those possessed of supernormal powers (iddhimanta) would be able to count them?
Being blinded by delusion, they do not understand even the dark and light sides [of kamma], and thus, even when hundreds or thousands of Buddhas arise, they do not hear the word "Buddha."
Having thus transcended [the lower realms], even human existence is indeed difficult to obtain. Even when human existence is attained, the time of a Buddha’s appearance is exceedingly rare.
Even during the time of a Buddha’s appearance, the perfection of the opportune moment—consisting of rebirth in a favorable state while possessing right view—is difficult to find.
Furthermore, because one who teaches the True Dharma is also rare, and even when such a teacher exists, the hearing of the True Dharma is difficult due to the deficiency of one's own faculties.
It should be understood that the perfections of the moment (*khaṇasampatti*)—such as human existence and so forth, categorized as "hard to obtain" (*dullabha*) and so on—are indeed difficult to find.

Regarding the phrase "the perfection of the moment is hard to obtain": the perfection of the moment, which consists of a favorable rebirth for the performance of wholesome deeds (*kusala*), is indeed rare;

for even in the Middle Country, one may be born in a border region, or at a time when one is an immaterial being, a non-percipient being, an animal, a hungry ghost, or in hell, or else one may be deficient in limbs such as the eyes and so forth.
Even when the constituent factors are complete, those who possess wrong view do not possess the opportune moments known as "wholesome rebirths.
For people living in border regions delight and take pleasure only in the ten unwholesome courses of action, such as killing;
they are of a violent nature and do not even know the virtues of the Triple Gem. This is also the case for formless beings (*arūpin*), due to their lack of hearing the voice of others.
They do not even attain the path of stream-entry, nor do they obtain such things as the sight of a Buddha.

Furthermore, during the periods of non-percipient beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings, the occurrence of even those beings who have fulfilled the perfections is considered outside the scope of conventional reckoning.

Even when born into families possessing right view, one who lacks eyesight fails to see the jewels of the Buddha and the Saṅgha; and one who lacks the faculty of hearing is deprived even of hearing the Dhamma.

Due to being like a deaf-mute and so forth, they do not undertake what is wholesome. Even when encountering a Fully Enlightened Buddha—who is endowed with all the factors, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide aura, and who has become the object of the sense-field of the eyes for all people—they do not even consider him as one to be gazed upon with the eye of serene confidence;
rather, through mental corruption, they take up a hostile attitude toward him on occasions such as the Twin Miracle.
Even many who hold wrong views are reborn in the great hells. Thus, even the attainment of a moment of rebirth in a favorable state is indeed difficult to find.

As it is said: “Human birth is difficult to obtain, The arising of a Buddha is difficult to encounter, The attainment of a favorable moment is difficult, And the True Dhamma is most difficult to find.”
The meaning of this verse has already been explained.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled the Section on Miscellaneous Matters, in the *Sīmavisodhana* composed by the Elder Sāgarabuddhi.
Thus, one hundred years after the Parinibbāna of the Teacher, in the city of Sīrikhetta—
known as “Isinagara” because it was built by a sage (*isi*) and serving as the residence for kings such as Dvattapāda and others— on a mountain ridge on the opposite bank of the river Erāvatī,
stands the Great Golden Thūpa; [this is] of the donor of that thūpa, the great righteous king Satthivisa.
In the year 2312 of the era of the Dispensation, because he caused the ordination ceremony (*upasampadā-kamma*) to be performed without casting water into the river—
having failed to thoroughly investigate the words spoken in the *Vimativinodanī*, which was intended to bring great benefit to those sons of noble family who had gained faith in the Dispensation,
by means of both their verbal consistency and logical consistency— he incurred defeat (*parājaya*) within the Dispensation.
A treatise that removes defects of boundaries and elucidates the perfection of boundaries has come forth by way of providing a means for censuring those of noble birth.
And at this point, having served as preceptor to the Great Elder—who was a field of glory, a city, and a village of his domain; who was the venerable teacher of the Great Dhamma King;
who was a master of great grammar; who was a bearer of the Tipiṭaka; and whose renowned name was "Mahāveyyākaraṇa Tipiṭakadhara Saddhammakovida"—[the work was composed].
In this most excellent wheel of the teaching of the final Conqueror, which is the dwelling place of those for whom wisdom is predominant,
[the work was carried out] by the teacher of the community of residents, Gaṇavācaka Vinayadhara Mahāsāmi, and by the royal preceptor Tipiṭaka Nāgatthera; acting as teachers,

they abandoned improper livelihoods such as medical practice and running errands on foot, and together with the Saṅgha communities who were pure in livelihood through right means of subsistence, they became the Saṅgha of donors for Sirikhettanagara.
On the southern side, on the ridge of the Dīgha mountain, on the sandy bank of the river Erāvatī,
having performed the ritual throwing of water (*udakukkhepa*) together with those observing the boundary (*sīmā*), [the Venerable] Sāgarabuddhi—

being twenty years of age and having received full ordination (*upasampadā*) through a formal act (*kamma*) consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) by those authorized to do so, without committing the tenfold failure of expression (*byañjanavipatti*) regarding that *udakukkhepasīmā*— was [ordained] by his teachers.
The treatise named *Sīmavisodhanī*, composed by the monk who has assumed this name, which removes the decline of the Dispensation,
is completed. Thus far, this *Sīmavisodhanī*— which is subtle and well-considered— has been explained together with its classifications and modes of occurrence.
In the renowned city called Sirikhettā, formerly known by another name,
in the region of the south, where a lofty dwelling had been constructed,
there lived a bhikkhu well-known by the name Sāgarabuddhi.
When I was twenty years of age, this treatise was well conceived.
This treatise composed by me has reached completion without confusion;
thus may the intentions of all living beings be swiftly fulfilled.
As long as even the name of the Buddha— the World-Chief, the Tathāgata— endures,
so long may this book remain, dispelling the darkness within the Teaching.
From the peak of existence above down to the Avīci hell below, [may it endure].
May all those beings who roam upon the earth throughout the entire universe likewise experience exactly equal results through my merit;
may our king, the illuminator of the Teaching, live for a long time.
Ruling according to the Dhamma of kings, may I be free from illness together with my kinsmen;
through this meritorious deed, may I be so in birth after birth.
Illuminating the teaching within the dispensation of the Son of the Sakyas—
"When the True Dhamma perishes and the surface of the earth has become blind,
I shall then be in the world of the gods, in the supreme abode of the Tusita heaven.
The *Sīmavisodhanī* is completed.
